After this module you can

- Recognise 8 equipment types from a photo
- Explain why “80,000 lb” is not the cargo weight
- Work out pallet counts and freight height limits
- Pick the right equipment for a load posting
- Ask the 4–5 questions each equipment type needs
- Avoid the four classic equipment booking mistakes

pages.title: Wrong equipment = wrong load
pages.markdown:
2

Module 2 · Equipment & freight matching

Wrong equipment  
= wrong load

A 53′ van at a 48′-only dock. A reefer set to the wrong temperature. A box truck with no liftgate at a house. A flatbed without the tarps the load needs. Each mistake costs a load, a fee or a claim — and each is prevented by knowing the equipment and asking one question.

No rates in this module. The old manuals printed “$ per mile” for each truck type. Rates change with market, lane and season — they are taught with live data in Module 7.

pages.title: Eight kinds of equipment you will dispatch
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.0 · The equipment family

# Eight kinds of equipment you will dispatch

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/lineup.jpg)

### Three big families

- **Enclosed:** dry van, reefer, box truck, Sprinter van, curtainside. Freight is protected from weather; loaded from the rear (or side, for curtainside).
- **Open deck:** flatbed, step deck and specialised trailers. Freight that is too big, heavy or awkward for a box; loaded by forklift or crane; must be secured and often tarped.
- **Capacity only:** power only — a tractor that pulls someone else’s trailer.

> **[KEY RULE] The first check on every load**
>
> Before rate, before broker, before anything: **can this truck carry this freight — size, weight, temperature, loading method and gear?** If the answer is “no” or “not sure,” you are not ready to call.

Which equipment will you dispatch most? In Pakistani dispatch offices, beginners usually start with **dry van, box truck and power only**. Reefer and flatbed often come later because they add temperature and securement risk.

pages.title: Tractor-trailer vs straight truck
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.0 · Anatomy

# Tractor-trailer vs straight truck

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/anatomy.jpg)

### Words you must use correctly

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Tractor** (power unit) | The truck with the engine and cab. Pulls a trailer. |
| **Semi-trailer** | The trailer. Its front rests on the tractor’s fifth wheel. |
| **Fifth wheel / kingpin** | The coupling. The trailer’s kingpin locks into the tractor’s fifth wheel. |
| **Landing gear** | Legs that hold the trailer up when it is dropped. |
| **Tandem axles** | Two axles together. Trailer tandems often slide to balance weight. |
| **Straight truck** | Cab and cargo box on one frame, e.g. a box truck. |

### Why the difference matters to you

A tractor can **drop** one trailer and **hook** another. That makes **drop-and-hook** loads and **power-only** work possible. A straight truck cannot drop its box: it must wait while it is loaded and unloaded.

Weight and licensing also differ. Tractor-trailers are combination vehicles (Class A CDL). Box trucks are single vehicles whose licence depends on their weight rating (page 14).

> **[FACT] Three weight words**
>
> **GVWR** = the maximum a vehicle is rated to weigh, loaded (on a door sticker). **Tare** = what it weighs empty. **Payload** = what it can carry = the legal maximum minus the tare.

pages.title: 80,000 lb is the whole truck, not the cargo
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.0 · The weight truth

# 80,000 lb is the whole truck, not the cargo

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/weight.jpg)

### The federal numbers

On the Interstate system, FHWA’s rules are: **80,000 lb gross** (unless the bridge formula gives less), **20,000 lb on a single axle**, **34,000 lb on a tandem axle**. The **bridge formula** limits weight on groups of axles according to how far apart they are, to protect bridges.

So the cargo is whatever remains after the **tractor, fuel, driver and trailer** are counted, and only if it is spread so that no axle group is overweight.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “Dry van max payload = 45,000 lb” / “Flatbed max = 48,000 lb”**
>
> These are rough real-world examples, **not legal limits**. A heavy tractor and a steel trailer carry less; a light tractor and an aluminium trailer carry more. Your old manual also claimed “mountain areas lower payload to 30–40k” — there is no such general rule.

> **[KEY RULE] The dispatcher habit**
>
> Every truck gets a **“max weight”** in your notes, confirmed by the carrier: *“Truck 12 legal up to 44,500.”* Never book to a generic number from a PDF.

pages.title: Width, length and height: who sets the limit?
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.0 · Size rules

# Width, length and height: who sets the limit?

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/sizes.jpg)

### What FHWA says

- **Width:** 102 inches (8′6″) is the federal maximum on the National Network. Wider = over-dimension.
- **Length:** states must allow semitrailers of **at least 48′** on the National Network; many allow 53′ (and some longer, grandfathered).
- **Height:** “There is no Federal vehicle height requirement.” States set their own — most between **13′6″ and 14′**.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “13′6″ is the legal height”**
>
> There is **no single federal height limit**. 13′6″ is common in the East; 14′ is common in many Western states; bridges and tunnels can be lower. Flatbed and step-deck freight must be checked against the route.

> **[FACT] What this means for vans**
>
> Vans are built to about 13′6″ tall so they can run almost everywhere. Height becomes your problem mainly with **open-deck** freight (pages 22–24).

pages.title: The 53-foot dry van
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.1 · Dry van

# The 53-foot dry van

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/spec_dv53.jpg)

### Read the sheet like a dispatcher

The two numbers that decide most van loads are **pallet positions (26)** and **legal weight**. A load of 26 light pallets fills the floor long before it reaches the weight limit: it **cubes out**. A load of 18 pallets of paper can reach the weight limit with floor space left: it **weighs out**.

Vans load at **docks**. The trailer floor sits about 4 feet off the ground, the same height as a warehouse dock, so forklifts drive straight in.

### What dry vans haul

Palletised or boxed goods that need weather protection but **no temperature control**: retail and grocery dry goods, paper, packaging, beverages, electronics, household goods, auto parts — like the printed boxes on load #12354.

### What they can’t

Frozen or temperature-sensitive food (reefer), freight taller than about 9′ or wider than the doors, and freight that must be loaded from the top or side with a crane (flatbed / curtainside).

pages.title: Pallet math: cube vs weight
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.1 · Dry van

# Pallet math: cube vs weight

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/pallets.jpg)

### Straight vs turned

A standard U.S. pallet is **48″ × 40″**. Loaded **straight** (48″ side along the trailer), two pallets fit side by side and 13 rows fit in a 53′ van: **26 pallets**. **Turned** (40″ along the trailer, 48″ + 48″ across), 15 rows fit: **up to 30**, but only if the trailer is wide enough inside and the shipper loads it that way.

> **[TRY IT] Worked example**
>
> A posting says: **“24 pallets, 42,000 lb, 53′ dry van.”** Floor: 24 ≤ 26 ✓. Weight: 42,000 lb — you must ask the carrier whether this truck is legal at 42,000. If the truck’s max is 43,500 ✓. If it is 41,000 ✗.

### Questions that uncover problems

- **“Palletised or floor-loaded?”** Floor-loaded (loose boxes) takes hours to load and unload by hand.
- **“Stackable?”** Some pallets can be double-stacked, which changes the space needed.
- **“Pallet size?”** Not every pallet is 48 × 40; oversized pallets mean fewer fit.
- **“Exact weight?”** Remember load #12354: the RC said 2,000 lb, the BOL said 5,729 lb.

> **[KEY RULE] Say it back**
>
> “So that’s **24 pallets, non-stackable, 42,000 pounds**, dock to dock.” Reading back catches mistakes on the call itself.

pages.title: The 48-foot dry van — and when length matters
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.1 · Dry van

# The 48-foot dry van — and when length matters

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/spec_dv48.jpg)

### Why 48′ still exists

Older docks, tight city streets, some yards and some customers were built around shorter trailers. A few postings say **“48′ max”** or **“no 53′”**. Most carriers today run 53′ vans; some also have 48′.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Classic mistake: wrong length**
>
> The receiver only accepts 48′ trailers. Your 53′ shows up and is turned away at the gate: no delivery, redelivery fees, a furious broker. **Ask:** “Any length restriction at pickup or delivery?”

| Question | 48′ van | 53′ van |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Pallets (straight / turned)** | 24 / up to 28 | 26 / up to 30 |
| **Weight capacity** | Similar — depends on the truck | Similar — depends on the truck |
| **Fits “48′ max” locations** | ✓ | ✗ |

> **[TRY IT] Quick check**
>
> A load is **25 pallets, 20,000 lb, “48′ max at delivery.”** Can your 48′ van take it? No: 25 pallets needs more than 24 straight positions, unless the shipper can turn them. Ask the broker how the pallets are loaded.

pages.title: Inside the van: gear, doors and variants
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.1 · Dry van

# Inside the van: gear, doors and variants

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/vangear.jpg)

### Securement applies to vans too

FMCSA’s cargo-securement rules apply to **all cargo-carrying commercial vehicles** in interstate commerce, including enclosed vans. Freight that shifts can break through doors, tip the trailer or be damaged. Loads may require **straps, load bars or blocking**, and brokers sometimes ask for “2 load bars” or “straps required.”

### Swing doors vs roll-up door

Most 53′ vans have **swing doors**. Some vans and many box trucks have a **roll-up door**, which sits inside the opening and can reduce usable door height. It rarely matters, until the freight is tall.

#### Curtainside van (DAT: VC)

Side curtains slide open so a forklift can load from the side. Used for rolls, long items, or where rear loading is impossible.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “Curtain-side is still filtered under V”**
>
> DAT now lists **Van w/ Curtains (VC)** as its own type. Use current platform categories, not old cheat sheets.

pages.title: Van variants and what they really mean
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.1 · Dry van

# Van variants and what they really mean

| DAT type | Name | What it means | When it matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **V** | Van | Standard enclosed dry van | The default for general freight |
| **VA** | Van Air-Ride | Air-bag suspension gives a softer ride | When the posting / broker requires air-ride |
| **VM** | Van w/ Team | Two drivers take turns so the truck keeps moving | Time-critical loads that need team service |
| **VC** | Van w/ Curtains | Curtainside, side-loading | Side loading required |
| **VG** | Van Lift Gate | Van with a liftgate | No-dock delivery with a van |
| **VZ** | Van Hazmat | Van hauling placarded hazardous materials | Only if carrier + driver are hazmat-qualified |
| **VP** | Van w/ Pallet Exchange | Driver swaps empty pallets for loaded ones | Pallet exchange loads — ask how it works |
| **VV** | Van Vented | Van with vents for airflow | Some produce / commodities needing ventilation |

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “VA is mandatory for fragile freight”**
>
> Air-ride is a **load requirement when the posting, broker or shipper asks for it**, not an automatic rule for glass or electronics. Read the requirements and ask.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “VM = loads over 700 miles”**
>
> VM means a **van with a team**. No 700-mile rule exists. Use it when the load needs team service **and** your carrier has team drivers.

> **[FACT] “VR — van or reefer”?**
>
> Older manuals teach VR. It did not appear in DAT’s current equipment list when this module was checked (Sep 2026), so it is not taught as a core code. Check the live platform in Module 6.

pages.title: The straight box truck
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.2 · Box truck

# The straight box truck

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/spec_box26.jpg)

### Where box trucks shine

Shorter local and regional runs, partial loads, deliveries to **stores, homes, job sites and businesses without docks**, and freight too small for a 53′ van. Many new small carriers and owner-operators start with a box truck, so you may dispatch them early in your career.

### The numbers that trip beginners

- **Payload is small** — often 8,000–12,000 lb, not 45,000.
- **Interior sizes vary** — ask for inside length, width, height and door opening.
- **Liftgate is not standard** — confirm it exists and its capacity.

Remember load #12354: a 26′ box truck, and the BOL weight was nearly three times the RC weight. On a box truck that difference really matters.

pages.title: Who can drive it? CDL and the 26,001 lb line
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.2 · Box truck

# Who can drive it? CDL and the 26,001 lb line

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/cdl.jpg)

### FMCSA’s classes, in plain words

- **Class A:** combinations of 26,001 lb or more where the towed unit is over 10,000 lb — every tractor-trailer.
- **Class B:** a **single vehicle** with a GVWR of 26,001 lb or more — heavier box trucks.
- **Class C:** smaller vehicles that carry **placarded hazmat** or **16+ passengers**.

A box truck rated at **25,999 lb** and driven without hazmat usually needs **no CDL**. The same-size box rated at **33,000 lb** needs a **Class B**.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “14–22 ft = non-CDL, 24–28 ft = CDL”**
>
> The licence depends on the **GVWR and the use** (hazmat, passengers), **not the length of the box**. Two 26′ trucks can need different licences.

> **[KEY RULE] Where to find the GVWR**
>
> The manufacturer’s certification label on the **driver’s door jamb**. Ask the carrier for it when you onboard a box truck and write it in your truck notes.

pages.title: Dock or no dock? Liftgate and pallet jack
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.2 · Box truck

# Dock or no dock? Liftgate and pallet jack

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/dock.jpg)

### The questions for every box-truck stop

- “Is there a **dock** at pickup and at delivery?”
- “Is it **residential** or a business with a dock?”
- “Is a **liftgate** required? Does the driver need a **pallet jack**?”
- “Is there a **forklift** on site, or does the driver unload?”
- “How heavy is the heaviest pallet?” (It must be within liftgate capacity.)

#### Reefer box truck (DAT: Straight Box Truck – Reefer)

Box trucks can also be refrigerated. Treat them like a reefer: setpoint, mode, pre-cool if required.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “VG is the box-truck liftgate code”**
>
> DAT lists VG as **Van Lift Gate**. Box trucks have their own types: **Straight Box Truck**, **Straight Box Truck – Reefer**, **Straight Box Truck Hazmat**. Treat the liftgate as a **capability you confirm**, not a code to memorise.

pages.title: Box truck vs 53′ dry van
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.2 · Box truck

# Box truck vs 53′ dry van

#### Box truck

#### 53′ dry van trailer

| Feature | Box truck (26′ typical) | 53′ dry van |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Units** | One vehicle: cab + box on one frame | Tractor + separate trailer |
| **Floor** | About 12 pallets | 26 pallets (up to 30 turned) |
| **Cargo weight** | Often 8,000–12,000 lb | Often 42,000–45,000 lb |
| **Licence** | No CDL if GVWR ≤ 26,000 (and no hazmat); Class B above | Class A CDL |
| **Stops** | Docks, homes, stores, job sites (with liftgate) | Mostly docks |
| **Typical runs** | Local / regional, partials, LTL-style | Regional / long haul, full truckload |
| **DAT search** | Straight Box Truck types + broad “Partial” van search | V (and variants) |

> **[KEY RULE] DAT’s own advice for small equipment**
>
> Run **two searches**: one with the specific equipment type (Straight Box Truck, Sprinter Van), and a broad **Van Standard / Van Specialized** search with **Partial** selected, because “brokers don’t always post them under specific truck types.”

pages.title: The refrigerated trailer (reefer)
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.3 · Reefer

# The refrigerated trailer (reefer)

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/spec_reefer.jpg)

### Why a reefer holds a bit less

Thick insulated walls, floor and roof make the inside **narrower and lower** than a dry van, and the unit, insulation and fuel make the trailer **heavier**, so it can carry less weight. Its floor has **grooves** so cold air can return to the unit underneath the pallets.

**The unit** on the front wall: a diesel engine and compressor with its own fuel tank.

### Continuous vs cycle (start-stop)

**Continuous:** the unit runs all the time and air always moves, the usual choice for fresh produce and many sensitive loads. **Cycle / start-stop:** the unit switches off when the temperature is reached and restarts when needed. It saves fuel and is often used for frozen goods. **The shipper decides**; the RC or BOL usually says which.

**Inside:** the air chute along the ceiling, insulated walls, grooved floor.

pages.title: Cold air, and what “temperature control” means
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.3 · Reefer

# Cold air, and what “temperature control” means

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/reefer_air.jpg)

### Three kinds of reefer freight (examples)

| Type | Typical example | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Frozen** | Ice cream, frozen meat — often around 0°F or below | Setpoint, cycle vs continuous, pre-cool |
| **Chilled / fresh** | Dairy, fresh meat — often mid-30s °F | Tight temperature windows |
| **Produce** | Fruit, vegetables — varies by product | Usually continuous; some products must not freeze |

These are examples to build intuition. **The only temperature that counts is the one on the load instructions / RC.**

> **[KEY RULE] A reefer can often haul dry freight**
>
> With the unit off, a reefer is an insulated van. Carriers often take dry loads as backhauls. Ask the broker whether a reefer is acceptable for a van load, and check the extra trailer weight.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “No temperature log = no claim defence”**
>
> Too absolute. Temperature records are **important evidence**, and FDA’s rule says carriers must be able to show they kept the requested temperature **when asked**. Outcomes of claims depend on the contract and the facts.

pages.title: Before you book a reefer: five questions
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.3 · Reefer

# Before you book a reefer: five questions

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/reefer_flow.jpg)

1. **“What is the setpoint?”** Write the exact number and °F. Never guess.
2. **“Continuous or cycle?”**
3. **“Is pre-cooling required, and to what?”**
4. **“Frozen, chilled or produce? What temperature is the product loaded at?”**
5. **“Any temperature recording or download needed at delivery?”**

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Say it out loud — reefer read-back**
>
> “So that’s **34 degrees Fahrenheit, continuous**, pre-cool to 34 before loading, fresh chicken, temperature download at delivery. Correct?”

### What FDA’s rule actually says

The FSMA sanitary-transportation rule says that before loading food that needs temperature control, the loader must make sure the refrigerated compartment is **“adequately prepared … including precooling, if necessary.”** Shipper and carrier can agree how temperature is monitored, and carriers must show they kept the requested temperature **“only upon request.”**

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “Pre-cool the trailer 2 hours before loading”**
>
> No universal 2-hour rule exists. **Pre-cool when the shipper or the load instructions require it**, to the temperature they give, and always verify the setpoint before loading.

Why it matters: a wrong setpoint can mean a **rejected load** worth tens of thousands of dollars and a claim against your carrier.

pages.title: The flatbed
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.4 · Flatbed

# The flatbed

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/spec_flat48.jpg)

### Why flatbed is a different world

With a van, the box protects the freight. With a flatbed, **the driver builds the protection**: straps, chains, edge protectors, blocking and tarps. Loading is usually from the **sides or top** by forklift or crane, so the freight can be long, heavy or awkward.

Flatbed loads therefore depend on **dimensions, weight and gear**, not just the letter “F.”

### Tarps in one minute

- **Lumber tarps** — large, cover tall stacks.
- **Steel tarps** — smaller, for lower loads like coils or beams.
- **“Drop”** — how far the tarp hangs down the sides: 4′, 6′, 8′. A posting may say “8′ drops required.”
- **Smoke tarp** — covers the front of a load against exhaust.

DAT now shows handling requirements (tarps, chains, coil racks) on flatbed loads. Match them to what the truck carries.

pages.title: Flatbed freight and gear
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.4 · Flatbed

# Flatbed freight and gear

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/flatgear.jpg)

### Gear checklist to confirm with the carrier

| Gear | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| **Straps + winches** | Most general freight |
| **Chains + binders** | Steel, machinery, heavy items |
| **Tarps** (size, drop) | Weather protection when required |
| **Edge protectors / corner guards** | Protect straps and freight edges |
| **Dunnage / lumber** | Blocking, lifting freight off the deck |
| **Coil racks** | Steel coils (commodity-specific rules) |

> **[KEY RULE] The division of responsibility**
>
> **The driver and carrier** are legally responsible for securing the load correctly. **The dispatcher** is responsible for not booking a load the truck can’t secure, so confirm gear **before** saying yes.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Over-dimension is a specialist area**
>
> Freight wider than 8′6″, taller than the route allows, or heavier than legal limits needs **state permits**, sometimes escorts and route surveys. Beginners should not book over-dimension loads without an experienced dispatcher.

pages.title: The tiedown rule — and the “4 chains” myth
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.4 · Securement

# The tiedown rule — and the “4 chains” myth

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/tiedowns.jpg)

### FMCSA’s general rule, in plain words

For an article that is **not blocked** from moving forward (by a headboard or other cargo): **1 tiedown** if it is 5 ft or shorter and 1,100 lb or lighter; **2 tiedowns** if longer than 5 ft (up to 10 ft) or heavier than 1,100 lb; above 10 ft, **2 for the first 10 ft plus 1 for every extra 10 ft or part of it**. The combined working load limit of all tiedowns must be **at least half the cargo’s weight**.

> **[TRY IT] Worked example**
>
> A 32-ft bundle of steel beams, not blocked: first 10 ft → 2, remaining 22 ft → 3 more (10 + 10 + 2). Minimum **5 tiedowns**, and commodity rules may require more.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “Minimum 4 chains per flatbed load”**
>
> No such universal rule exists. The count depends on **length, weight, whether the cargo is blocked, the working load limits**, and **commodity-specific rules** for logs, lumber, metal coils, paper rolls, concrete pipe, vehicles, heavy machinery and boulders.

You don’t need to calculate securement for the driver. You need to know enough to ask: “What does this load need, and does our truck have it?”

pages.title: The step deck (drop deck)
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.4 · Step deck

# The step deck (drop deck)

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/spec_step53.jpg)

### How to spot one

Look for the **step**: a short upper deck over the tractor, then a drop to a long, lower deck. In the photo the lower deck is loaded with long steel pieces. A **flatbed** is one flat deck at about 5 feet.

DAT has **SD** (Step Deck) and **FD** (Flatbed or Step Deck). FD postings accept either, so height may not be critical.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “Step deck = no permit needed for medium machinery”**
>
> A step deck **reduces loaded height**, which may keep a load legal. But permit need depends on the **total dimensions and the states on the route**. It never guarantees permit-free movement.

pages.title: Flatbed or step deck? Do the height math
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.4 · Height math

# Flatbed or step deck? Do the height math

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/clearance.jpg)

> **[TRY IT] Worked example: a 9′6″ machine**
>
> On a flatbed: 5′0″ deck + 9′6″ = **14′6″**, over a 13′6″ or 14′ limit ✗. On a step deck: 3′6″ + 9′6″ = **13′0″**, under 13′6″ ✓, if every state and bridge on the route allows it. **Use real deck heights from the carrier**, not typical ones.

### Other open-deck equipment (awareness only)

| Type | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Conestoga (CN)** | Flatbed or step deck with a rolling tarp system, like a covered wagon |
| **Double drop** | Very low well between two raised decks, for tall freight |
| **RGN / lowboy** | Heavy haul; the front detaches so machinery can drive on |
| **Hotshot** | Pickup truck pulling a gooseneck flatbed, for smaller urgent loads |

#### Gooseneck trailer used in hotshot work

Real photo from your manual. Hotshot (pickup + gooseneck) is a growing niche. DAT lists Flatbed Hotshot (FH) and Van Hotshot (VH).

> **[KEY RULE] Know your limits**
>
> Heavy-haul and over-dimension freight (RGN, lowboy, permits, escorts) is a specialist job. Learn to **recognise** it and pass it on until you are trained.

pages.title: Power only: the tractor without a trailer
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.5 · Power only

# Power only: the tractor without a trailer

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/spec_po.jpg)

### How a power-only load works

1. Your driver goes to a yard or shipper and **hooks a trailer** that is already loaded (or empty).
2. Checks the trailer: tyres, lights, brakes, doors, **seal number**. Photos before leaving.
3. Hauls it to the receiver or another yard and **drops** it.
4. Sometimes takes an **empty trailer back**. Ask whether that is paid.

> **[KEY RULE] Why beginners see many power-only loads**
>
> Some shippers and brokers keep their own trailer pools and just need tractors. Power only has **no trailer to own or maintain**, and it moves fast with drop-and-hook. DAT has also added power-only specialty variants in 2025.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] The insurance question**
>
> When your carrier pulls someone else’s trailer, the trailer owner usually wants **trailer interchange** (or similar) insurance. Confirm your carrier has it before booking.

pages.title: Sprinter and cargo vans: small, fast, specific
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.5 · Sprinter / cargo van

# Sprinter and cargo vans: small, fast, specific

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/spec_sprinter.jpg)

### Where cargo vans fit

Urgent, small and high-value freight: auto parts to stop a production line, medical supplies, electronics, time-critical partials. Loads are often **posted and gone within minutes**, pick up the same day, and run long distances non-stop (sometimes with a team).

**Smaller vans** (like this mid-size van) carry even less. Always get the real inside dimensions and payload.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “Sprinter codes are VH, MV, VL” / “MV = Mini Van”**
>
> On DAT today, **MV = Moving Van** and **VH = Van Hotshot**. DAT has explicit **Sprinter Van**, **Sprinter Van Hazmat**, **Sprinter Van Temp-Controlled** and **Sprinter Van Team** types.

> **[KEY RULE] Search like DAT recommends**
>
> Run a **specific** search (Sprinter Van types) and a **broad** Van Standard / Van Specialized search with **Partial** selected.

pages.title: Hazmat, tankers, teams and over-dimension
pages.markdown:
Lesson 2.5 · Special cases

# Hazmat, tankers, teams and over-dimension

#### Hazardous materials (hazmat)

Placarded hazmat needs a driver with a **hazmat endorsement** on the CDL and a carrier set up for hazmat (registration, insurance, procedures). DAT types include VZ, RZ, FZ and SB-Hazmat. **Never book hazmat unless your carrier and driver are qualified.**

#### Tankers

Liquids and gases in bulk. Specialised equipment, and a tanker endorsement is required for the driver. Recognise it; beginners rarely dispatch tankers.

#### Over-dimension

Wide, tall, long or heavy loads that need permits, sometimes escorts and specific routes. DAT: FO, LO.

#### Team service

Two drivers take turns driving, so the truck can move almost non-stop within hours-of-service rules. Used for urgent, long loads. DAT marks it with **VM, RM, FM** or “Team” variants. Only book team loads if your carrier really has a team on that truck.

#### Pallet exchange

The shipper or receiver swaps empty pallets for loaded ones. It can cost the carrier time or money if the pallets aren’t returned. Ask how it works (VP, RP).

> **[KEY RULE] One-line rule for special equipment**
>
> If a load has an extra letter (Z, M, P, O, T…) or the word “Hazmat / Team / Over-dimension,” **stop and confirm the carrier and driver are qualified and equipped** before you call.

pages.title: Match the freight to the equipment
pages.markdown:
Putting it together

# Match the freight to the equipment

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/matching.jpg)

#### 1Read the freight

Commodity, weight, pallets or dimensions, temperature, hazmat.

#### 2Read the stops

Dock or no dock, residential, length limits, loading method (forklift, crane, side, rear).

#### 3Match your truck

Type, size, confirmed max weight, gear (tarps, chains, liftgate), driver qualifications.

> **[KEY RULE] If any of the three steps is unclear, ask before you negotiate**
>
> A rate conversation about a load your truck can’t legally or physically do is wasted time, and a booked load you have to cancel damages your carrier’s reputation with that broker.

pages.title: Equipment types on the load board
pages.markdown:
Putting it together

# Equipment types on the load board

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/codes.jpg)

### How to learn codes the right way

- Memorise the **core**: V, VA, VM, VC, R, RA, F, FD, SD, PO, SB.
- Know that the **second letter adds a feature** (A air-ride, M team, Z hazmat, P pallet exchange, T tarps, C chains/curtains…).
- For everything else, **use the platform’s equipment selector** and read the load details.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Why old code sheets are dangerous**
>
> Platforms add and rename types. DAT added explicit Sprinter, box-truck and power-only specialty types and flatbed handling attributes in 2025. A code sheet from an old PDF can make you search for the wrong truck or miss loads.

pages.title: Four mistakes this module prevents
pages.markdown:
Putting it together

# Four mistakes this module prevents

![](/assets/diagrams/m02/mistakes.jpg)

| Mistake | What happens | The question that prevents it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Wrong length** | Turned away at the gate; redelivery, maybe a TONU dispute | “Any length restriction at pickup or delivery?” |
| **Wrong temperature** | Product damaged, load rejected, claim against the carrier | “Setpoint and mode?” + read it back + check the RC |
| **No liftgate** | Freight can’t be unloaded; failed delivery | “Dock or no dock? Liftgate and pallet jack needed?” |
| **Missing gear** | Driver refused at the shipper or rejected by the receiver | “What tarps, chains, straps or load bars are required?” |
| **Overweight** | Illegal truck, fines, load must be split | “Exact weight?” vs the truck’s confirmed max |

pages.title: The questions to ask, by equipment
pages.markdown:
Your equipment checklist

# The questions to ask, by equipment

| Equipment | Always ask | Extra checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Every load** | Commodity · weight · pallet count / pieces · dimensions if unusual · pickup and delivery type (dock / live / drop) | Special requirements in the posting notes |
| **Dry van** | Palletised or floor-loaded · stackable · length limits | Air-ride, team, load bars, straps |
| **Box truck** | Dock or no dock · residential · liftgate · pallet jack | Inside dimensions, door type, driver licence |
| **Reefer** | Setpoint · continuous or cycle · pre-cool | Product type, temp recording, clean trailer |
| **Flatbed** | L × W × H · tarps (size, drop) · chains / straps | Loading method, edge protection, over-dimension? |
| **Step deck** | Exact freight height · deck height · ramps | States on the route and their height limits |
| **Power only** | Whose trailer · loaded / empty · where it goes after | Interchange insurance, seal, trailer inspection |
| **Sprinter** | Weight · pallet size · door / liftgate | Hazmat, temp, team, same-day pickup |

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Say it out loud — drill 4: the equipment questions**
>
> Practise this with a broker who has just said “It’s a dry van load, Joliet to Atlanta.”  
>   
> **“Great. What’s the commodity and the total weight? How many pallets — are they stackable? Is it dock to dock, live load and live unload? Any length restriction, load bars or air-ride needed?”**  
>   
> Then do the same for a reefer (“What’s the setpoint — continuous or cycle? Pre-cool required?”) and a flatbed (“Dimensions? Tarps — what size drop? Chains or straps?”).

pages.title: Visual quiz: name it, then ask your first question
Module 2 check
pages.markdown:
Module 2 · Check yourself

# Module 2 check

Answer on paper, then use the key. Aim for 10 of 12.

1. What is the difference between a tractor-trailer and a straight truck, and why does it matter for drop-and-hook loads?
2. The federal gross limit is 80,000 lb. Why can’t a 53′ dry van usually carry 80,000 − 0 lb of cargo? Give the example math.
3. How many 48″ × 40″ pallets fit in a 53′ van straight? Turned? In a 26′ box truck?
4. True or false: “The federal height limit is 13′6″.” Explain.
5. A 26′ box truck has a GVWR of 25,999 lb. Does the driver need a CDL to haul general freight? What if the GVWR were 33,000 lb?
6. Name four things you ask before booking a box truck to a residential address.
7. Explain continuous vs cycle mode, and who decides which is used.
8. What does FDA’s rule say about pre-cooling? What was wrong with the old manual rule?
9. A 25-ft article on a flatbed, not blocked: minimum number of tiedowns under FMCSA’s general rule?
10. A machine is 9′10″ tall. Flatbed deck 5′0″, step-deck lower deck 3′4″. What is the loaded height on each, and which could be legal where the limit is 13′6″?
11. What do MV, VH, VM and VC mean on DAT today?
12. What must be true before you book a placarded hazmat load?

pages.title: Answers — Module 2 check
pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers — Module 2 check

**1.**

A tractor-trailer is two units: the tractor can drop one trailer and hook another. A straight truck’s box is on the same frame and can’t be dropped. Drop-and-hook and power-only work need a tractor.

**2.**

80,000 lb is the gross for the whole vehicle. Example: 80,000 − tractor/fuel/driver 19,000 − trailer 15,000 = 46,000 lb on paper, and axle limits and real loading usually make it less. Ask the carrier for the truck’s max.

**3.**

26 straight, up to 30 turned (if the inside width and loading allow); about 12 in a 26′ box truck.

**4.**

**False.** There is no federal vehicle height limit. States set limits, mostly 13′6″–14′, and routes can be lower.

**5.**

25,999 lb GVWR, no hazmat → usually **no CDL**. 33,000 lb GVWR → **Class B CDL**. Length doesn’t decide it.

**6.**

Any four: dock or no dock; residential?; liftgate required?; pallet jack?; forklift on site?; heaviest pallet weight vs liftgate capacity; inside dimensions.

**7.**

Continuous: the unit runs all the time. Cycle/start-stop: it switches off at the setpoint and restarts as needed. The shipper decides; it’s usually on the RC or BOL.

**8.**

The compartment must be adequately prepared, “including precooling, if necessary.” The old “always 2 hours” rule is not in the regulation. Follow the shipper’s instructions.

**9.**

First 10 ft → 2; remaining 15 ft → 2 more (10 + 5) = **4 tiedowns** minimum, plus any commodity-specific rules.

**10.**

Flatbed: 5′0″ + 9′10″ = **14′10″** ✗. Step deck: 3′4″ + 9′10″ = **13′2″** ✓ under 13′6″, if every state and bridge on the route allows it.

**11.**

MV = Moving Van · VH = Van Hotshot · VM = Van w/ Team · VC = Van w/ Curtains.

**12.**

The driver has a hazmat endorsement and the carrier is set up for hazmat (registration, insurance, procedures), and the truck can be placarded correctly. Otherwise, don’t book.

## Answers — visual quiz

| # | Equipment | A good first question | # | Equipment | A good first question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Reefer box truck | “Setpoint and mode?” | 5 | Curtainside van | “Side-load required?” |
| 2 | Gooseneck flatbed (hotshot) | “Weight and dimensions?” | 6 | Reefer trailer (unit) | “Setpoint, continuous or cycle?” |
| 3 | Flatbed trailer | “Tarps and chains needed?” | 7 | Box truck | “Dock or liftgate?” |
| 4 | Small cargo van | “Real weight and size?” | 8 | Tanker | “Hazmat / tanker endorsed?” (specialist) |

pages.title: Answers — twelve postings
pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers — twelve postings

| # | Equipment (DAT) | The question you must ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 53′ reefer (R) | Exact setpoint and mode (cycle OK?) — and can this reefer carry 40,500 lb? |
| 2 | Box truck + liftgate (SB) | Liftgate and pallet jack needed? Heaviest fixture weight? |
| 3 | Flatbed with coil racks + chains (F · FC) | Does our truck have coil racks and enough chains? Is it legal at 44,000 lb? |
| 4 | 53′ dry van (V) | Floor-loaded or palletised? (26 pallets = the full floor; weight is fine.) |
| 5 | Power only (PO) | Trailer type and condition, seal, and does the carrier have trailer interchange insurance? |
| 6 | Sprinter / cargo van | Can the driver pick up within the hour? Pallet size fits the doors? |
| 7 | Step deck with ramps (SD) | Exact deck height: 3′6″ + 9′8″ = 13′2″. States on the route? Ramps on the truck? |
| 8 | 48′ dry van (V) | Do we have a 48′ trailer? A 53′ will be refused. |
| 9 | Reefer (R), continuous | Pre-cool to what temperature? Temperature record needed? |
| 10 | Flatbed with 8′ drop tarps (F · FT) | Does the truck carry lumber tarps with 8′ drops? Legal at 46,000 lb? |
| 11 | Box truck with liftgate (SB) | Liftgate capacity vs pallet weight; pallet jack; residential access for the truck? |
| 12 | Hazmat van (VZ) | Is the driver hazmat-endorsed and the carrier hazmat-qualified? If not, don’t book. |

> **[KEY RULE] Notice the pattern**
>
> Almost every answer includes a **capability check** (gear, size, temperature, licence) **and** a **weight check** against the specific truck. That pattern is the habit this module builds.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.markdown:
Reference

# Glossary

**Air-ride** — Suspension using air bags for a smoother ride (VA, RA).

**Blocking / bracing** — Wood or other material built around cargo to stop movement.

**Box truck** — Straight truck with an enclosed cargo box.

**Bridge formula** — Federal formula limiting weight on axle groups by their spacing.

**Continuous mode** — Reefer unit runs all the time.

**Cube out** — Trailer floor or space is full before reaching the weight limit.

**Curtainside** — Van with sliding side curtains for side loading (VC).

**Cycle / start-stop** — Reefer unit switches off at setpoint, restarts when needed.

**Deck height** — Height of a flatbed or step-deck deck above the ground.

**Drop (tarp)** — How far a tarp hangs down the side: 4′, 6′, 8′.

**Drop-and-hook** — Leaving one trailer and taking another instead of waiting to load.

**Dunnage** — Material used to fill gaps or support cargo (wood, airbags).

**E-track** — Metal rails on van walls for straps and load bars.

**Fifth wheel** — Coupling plate on the tractor that holds the trailer’s kingpin.

**Floor-loaded** — Freight loaded loose on the floor, not on pallets.

**GVWR** — Gross vehicle weight rating: maximum loaded weight of a vehicle.

**Kingpin** — Pin under the trailer’s nose that locks into the fifth wheel.

**Landing gear** — Legs that support a dropped trailer.

**Liftgate** — Powered platform that lowers freight to the ground.

**Load bar** — Bar wedged across a van to hold freight in place.

**Over-dimension** — Freight exceeding legal width, height, length or weight.

**Pallet jack** — Hand tool for moving pallets.

**Payload** — Cargo weight a truck can legally carry.

**Power only** — Tractor pulling a trailer it doesn’t own (PO).

**Pre-cool** — Cooling a reefer trailer before loading, when required.

**Reefer** — Refrigerated, temperature-controlled trailer or truck.

**Setpoint** — The temperature the reefer unit is set to hold.

**Step deck** — Flatbed with an upper and a lower deck (SD).

**Straight truck** — Truck with cab and cargo body on one frame.

**Tandem** — Pair of axles. Trailer tandems often slide.

**Tare** — Empty weight of a vehicle or trailer.

**Tiedown** — Strap, chain or similar used to secure cargo.

**Weigh out** — Reaching the weight limit before the space is full.

**WLL** — Working load limit of a tiedown.

Start here

# How to use this module

You don’t need to become a geography teacher. You need **speed**: when a load pops up, you should know in five seconds roughly where it goes, which way the truck will travel, which interstates it will use, and what the appointment is in Pakistan time.

### Study rhythm (about 7 hours, spread over a week)

- **Day 1 (1.5 h):** states and codes. Do the state drill until you score 24/24.
- **Day 2 (1.5 h):** regions, DAT zones, freight hubs. City drill: 18/20 in under 3 minutes.
- **Day 3 (2 h):** interstates, corridors, the four lanes.
- **Day 4 (1.5 h):** time zones, conversion, traps. Lane practice and the check.
- **Every day after (10 min):** redo one drill. Geography is memory — repetition wins.

> **[KEY RULE] The five-second lane test**
>
> For any load, say out loud: **direction · main interstate(s) · rough distance · time zones at each end · one risk** (mountains, big city, border, dead market). By the end of this module you should manage it for any major lane.

Contents

About the maps

All maps were drawn for this course from official U.S. boundary data. Interstates are drawn **simplified** — straight lines between major cities on each route — so they show the idea, not every curve. For real trips the driver uses a truck-specific GPS or routing tool.

pages.title: A load posting is a tiny map
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.1 · Why geography

# A load posting is a tiny map

A typical load-board line

**09/30**   V   **JOLIET, IL**   DH-O 12   →   **CHARLOTTE, NC**   42,000 lb   53′   Full

### What an experienced dispatcher “sees” in that line

- **Where:** Joliet is just south-west of Chicago. Charlotte is in North Carolina, in the Southeast.
- **Which way:** south-east, around 750–800 miles. A full day and a half of driving.
- **Which roads:** down through Indianapolis, Cincinnati and West Virginia (or a similar route).
- **When:** Joliet is Central Time; Charlotte is Eastern. The clock moves forward one hour.
- **After:** Charlotte is a decent freight market — the truck should find a reload.

### What a beginner sees

Two names and a number. Then they book it, and find out afterwards that the delivery is in the wrong time zone, the driver can’t make it, or the truck is stuck in a place with no freight going home.

> **[KEY RULE] Geography comes before rates**
>
> You can’t judge a rate, check hours of service, or plan a reload until you know where the load is going. That is why this module comes before HOS (Module 4) and load economics (Module 7).

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/route_jol_clt.jpg)

Preview: the Joliet → Charlotte lane read on the map. You will study it on page 16.

pages.title: The 50 states and their codes
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.1 · States and codes

# The 50 states and their codes

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/map_states.jpg)

### How codes appear on real paperwork

Always **City, ST**: “Lebanon, OH”, “Owensboro, KY”. The two letters are U.S. Postal Service codes, the same everywhere: load boards, rate confirmations, BOLs, ELDs.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] The same city name in many states**
>
> There are Springfields in IL, MO, MA, OH and more; Columbus in OH, GA and MS; Portland in OR and ME. **Never write a city without its state**, and repeat it on the phone: “Portland, **Oregon**?”

### A study method that works

1. Learn the **big shapes first**: CA, TX, FL, the Great Lakes, the East Coast.
2. Then learn **by region** (next pages), not alphabetically.
3. Then drill the **confusing codes** (page 6).
4. Test yourself on the blank-map drill (page 10) until you score 100%.

Alaska and Hawaii appear in the corner (not to scale). You will rarely dispatch there; the lower 48 states are where almost all truckload work happens.

pages.title: The codes that cause real mistakes
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.1 · States and codes

# The codes that cause real mistakes

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/tricky.jpg)

### Memory hooks

- **MI**chigan — “MI” are its first two letters. **MS** = MiSsissippi (the S sounds).
- **MO** = Missouri (“Mo” is a nickname). **MT** = MonTana.
- **AK** = AlasKa (the K). **AR** = ARkansas.
- **IA** = IowA (first and last letter). **ID** = IDaho.
- **NE** = NEbraska; **NV** = NeVada.

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Say it out loud**
>
> Read these as a broker would: **“Joliet, Illinois · Owensboro, Kentucky · Springfield, Missouri · Des Moines, Iowa · Boise, Idaho · Jackson, Mississippi · Lansing, Michigan.”** Then cover the names and say the codes.

pages.title: Regions: how people talk about the map
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.1 · Regions

# Regions: how people talk about the map

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/map_census.jpg)

### Region words you will hear on calls

| Word | Usually means | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Northeast** | New England + NY, NJ, PA | “We have a lot going into the Northeast.” |
| **Southeast** | GA, FL, AL, SC, NC, TN (often MS) | “Truck wants to head Southeast.” |
| **Midwest** | IL, IN, OH, MI, WI, IA, MN, MO… | “Midwest freight is steady.” |
| **Texas triangle** | Dallas–Houston–San Antonio/Austin | “Plenty of loads inside the triangle.” |
| **West Coast** | CA, OR, WA (Pacific Northwest = OR, WA) | “Reefer out of the West Coast.” |
| **Mountain West** | CO, UT, ID, WY, MT, NV, AZ, NM | “Long empty miles out west.” |

These informal words are not exact. When it matters, ask: “Which states?”

pages.title: DAT zones: search a whole region at once
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.1 · Load-board zones

# DAT zones: search a whole region at once

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/map_dat.jpg)

### How dispatchers use zones

DAT One lets you type a zone instead of a city: a destination of **Z3** finds loads going anywhere in AL, FL, GA, MS or TN. You can enter several: **Z7, Z8, Z9** (or Z7Z8Z9).

Zones are perfect for **“where can my truck go next?”** searches, and for a carrier who says “anything heading Southeast.”

> **[TRY IT] Try it**
>
> Your truck delivers in Memphis tomorrow. The carrier wants it home in Georgia by Friday. Which zone would you search as the destination? (Answer at the back.)

Zones are a DAT feature (checked Sep 2026). Truckstop and other boards have similar region searches. Module 6 covers the search screens.

pages.title: Where the freight is
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.1 · Freight hubs

# Where the freight is

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/map_hubs.jpg)

| Hub | Known for (long-standing) | Hub | Known for (long-standing) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **LA / Long Beach + Inland Empire** | Largest U.S. port complex; huge warehouse region east of LA | **Chicago** | Rail and distribution crossroads of the country |
| **Dallas–Fort Worth** | Texas and Southwest distribution; many interstates meet | **Atlanta** | Southeast distribution hub (I-75, I-85, I-20) |
| **Memphis** | Central location, river, rail, air-cargo hub | **Columbus / Indianapolis** | Midwest distribution; a day’s drive to much of the U.S. |
| **Harrisburg (central PA)** | Distribution for the Northeast (I-81, I-76, I-83) | **Houston** | Port, petrochemicals, Gulf Coast freight |
| **Savannah** | Major East Coast container port | **Laredo / El Paso** | Mexico border crossings; Laredo is the busiest land port for freight |

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Hubs are not “hot markets”**
>
> A hub produces freight all year. A **hot market** — where loads outnumber trucks this week — changes with season, weather and the economy. Never memorise a hot-market list; check live data (Module 7).

pages.title: State-code drill
pages.markdown:
Drill

# State-code drill

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/map_statequiz.jpg)

Write the two-letter code for each numbered state. Do it without looking at page 5. **Target: 24/24.** Repeat daily until it takes under two minutes. Answers at the back.

> **[KEY RULE] Why the confusing ones first**
>
> Most real-world code mistakes come from these 24 states. If you know them perfectly, the rest are easy.

> **[TRY IT] Level up**
>
> After 24/24: take a blank piece of paper, draw a rough U.S. outline, and write in all 48 lower states by region. Check against page 5. Repeat weekly.

pages.title: City drill: 20 freight cities
pages.markdown:
Drill

# City drill: 20 freight cities

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/map_quiz.jpg)

Write the city and its state code for each number. **Target: 18/20 in under 3 minutes.** Then say each one with its time zone: “Number 3, Dallas, Texas — Central.” Answers at the back.

> **[KEY RULE] Add the interstate**
>
> Level 2: for each city, name one interstate that runs through it (Atlanta — I-75, I-85, I-20; Dallas — I-35, I-20, I-30, I-45). Use the map on page 13 to check.

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Say it like a broker**
>
> “I have a load **Memphis, Tennessee to Columbus, Ohio**.” Say three pairs from the drill, and for each, say the direction: “North-east.”

pages.title: The numbering code
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.2 · Interstates

# The numbering code

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/numbering.jpg)

### FHWA’s rules, in plain words

- **Odd numbers run north–south.** The lowest (I-5) is on the West Coast; the highest (I-95) on the East Coast.
- **Even numbers run east–west.** The lowest (I-10) is in the far south; the highest (I-90, I-94) in the north.
- **Numbers ending in 0 or 5** are the long, major routes: I-5, I-10, I-35, I-40, I-80, I-95…
- **Three digits:** the last two digits are the parent route. An **even first digit** means a loop or connector (I-285 around Atlanta); an **odd first digit** means a spur (I-575 off I-75).

> **[TRY IT] Use the code**
>
> Without a map: is I-65 more east or west than I-35? Does I-20 run north–south or east–west, and is it north or south of I-40? (Answers at the back.)

> **[FACT] Interstates are the freight backbone**
>
> FHWA’s Primary Highway Freight System is about 41,800 miles, and about 38,000 of those miles are Interstate. Most long-haul truckload miles run on these roads.

pages.title: Freight corridors
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.2 · Corridors

# Freight corridors

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/map_corridors.jpg)

### Why corridors matter to a dispatcher

- **Reloads are easier** along a busy corridor: cities along it generate loads in both directions.
- **Your carrier’s preferred lanes** are often corridors: “We like I-35 and I-40.”
- **Ports and borders** feed corridors: I-5 and I-10 from the California ports, I-35 from Laredo, I-95 from the East Coast ports.

> **[KEY RULE] Plan in corridors, not single loads**
>
> An owner-operator from Dallas may want to run **I-35 north** and come back **I-35 south** each week. Knowing the corridor helps you find the second load before the first one delivers.

Descriptions show long-standing freight flows. Volumes and rates on each corridor change with season and economy; check live data (Module 7).

pages.title: Lane 1: Dallas, TX → Atlanta, GA
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.2 · Reading a lane

# Lane 1: Dallas, TX → Atlanta, GA

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/route_dal_atl.jpg)

### The five questions for every lane

1. **Direction:** which way is the truck moving?
2. **Main interstate(s):** which 1–3 roads carry most of the trip?
3. **Distance:** roughly how many miles, or how many driving days?
4. **Time zones:** the zone of each stop, and any change on the way.
5. **One risk:** mountains, weather, a big city, a border, a weak market for the next load.

> **[TRY IT] Worked example: the time-zone trap**
>
> On day 2 the truck leaves **Birmingham, AL at 2:00 PM CT** for the last 150 miles to Atlanta, about 2.5 hours. It arrives around **4:30 PM on Central time**, but the receiver works on Atlanta time: **5:30 PM ET**. If receiving closes at 5:00 PM ET, the truck is late, even though a Central-time plan said he had time.

Real driving time depends on hours-of-service rules, traffic and breaks (Module 4). Here we only practise the clock.

pages.title: Lane 2: Joliet, IL → Charlotte, NC
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.2 · Reading a lane

# Lane 2: Joliet, IL → Charlotte, NC

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/route_jol_clt.jpg)

### Several interstates, one direction

Long lanes often use several interstates. You don’t have to memorise every change; know the **big turning points**: Indianapolis, Cincinnati, then the mountains of West Virginia down to Charlotte.

This is the lane from Module 0’s message. At about 750–800 miles it is **more than one legal driving day**, so the pickup and delivery times must allow for a 10-hour break (Module 4).

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Terrain and weather**
>
> I-77 through West Virginia and Virginia has long grades and can see snow and fog in winter. Mountain routes are slower and use more fuel. Ask the driver about conditions, and don’t plan tight appointments through the mountains in winter.

pages.title: Lane 3: Laredo, TX → Chicago, IL
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.2 · Reading a lane

# Lane 3: Laredo, TX → Chicago, IL

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/route_lar_chi.jpg)

### Cross-border freight

Laredo sits on the Mexican border and is the busiest U.S.–Mexico land port for freight. Mexican trucks bring loads across. U.S. carriers often pick up at warehouses in **Laredo** and haul north on **I-35** into Texas and on to the Midwest.

The whole lane stays in **Central Time**, a rare easy one. But at about 1,400+ miles it is a **2–3 day** trip for a solo driver.

> **[FACT] Border words you will hear**
>
> **Cross-dock** — freight moved from a Mexican trailer to a U.S. trailer in a warehouse. **Transload** — similar. **Bonded / in-bond** — freight still under customs control; it needs special handling and carrier authorisation. Treat in-bond loads as specialist until trained.

### Major land border crossings for trucks (awareness)

| Crossing | Border | Main interstate from there |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Laredo, TX** | Mexico | I-35 north (Texas → Midwest) |
| **El Paso, TX** | Mexico | I-10 east/west, I-25 north |
| **Otay Mesa (San Diego), CA** | Mexico | I-5 / I-805 / I-15 north |
| **Detroit, MI** | Canada (Windsor) | I-75, I-94, I-96 |
| **Buffalo, NY** | Canada (Ontario) | I-90, I-190 |

Cross-border work needs extra documents and carrier set-up (customs brokers, in-bond rules, Canadian/Mexican authority). As a beginner, you mostly dispatch the U.S. side, from a warehouse near the border.

pages.title: Lane 4: load #12354 on the map
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.2 · Reading a lane

# Lane 4: load #12354 on the map

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/route_leb_owb.jpg)

### Back to the real load from Module 1

Lebanon, Ohio is just north-east of Cincinnati. Owensboro, Kentucky is on the Ohio River in western Kentucky. The truck runs down toward **Louisville**, then west, and crosses from **Eastern into Central Time** on the way.

Pickup 7–8 AM ET; delivery 12 PM CT, which is 1 PM ET. With about 240 miles and an hour of loading, the timing is **tight but possible**, which is exactly what the map and the clock tell you before booking.

> **[KEY RULE] Kentucky has two time zones**
>
> Louisville, Lexington and eastern Kentucky are **Eastern**. Owensboro, Bowling Green and western Kentucky are **Central**. Tennessee, Indiana, Florida and Michigan also have two zones; check the city, not just the state.

### The clock on load #12354 (February = U.S. winter)

| Event | Local time | Eastern | Pakistan |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pickup window opens, Lebanon OH | 7:00 AM ET | 7:00 AM | 5:00 PM |
| BOL printed (driver loaded) | 7:55 AM ET | 7:55 AM | 5:55 PM |
| Crosses into Central Time (western KY) | clock goes back 1 h | — | — |
| Delivery appointment, Owensboro KY | 12:00 PM CT | 1:00 PM | 11:00 PM |
| POD deadline (72 h after delivery) | Thu 12:00 PM CT | 1:00 PM | Thu 11:00 PM |

pages.title: A truck is not a car: routes, restrictions, seasons
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.2 · Truck routing

# A truck is not a car: routes, restrictions, seasons

#### Truck GPS, not car GPS

A car route from Google Maps can send a 13′6″ truck under a 12′ bridge, onto a parkway where trucks are banned, or down a road with a weight limit. Drivers use truck-specific GPS; dispatchers use truck mileage tools.

#### Miles: road vs straight line

Road miles are always more than the straight-line distance on a map, sometimes much more around lakes, mountains and cities. Rates are paid on the miles on the RC or the broker’s mileage system; check them.

## Classic restrictions and seasonal risks

| Situation | What happens | Dispatcher habit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **New York parkways** | Commercial vehicles are banned from parkways around NYC and Long Island; low bridges catch trucks every year | Deliveries in NYC/NJ: driver must follow truck routes |
| **Big-city delivery** | Tight docks, traffic, time windows, tolls | Ask about access; allow extra time |
| **Mountain passes** | Long grades on I-70 (Colorado), I-80 (Wyoming/Utah), I-5 (Grapevine, Siskiyou), I-77/I-81 (Appalachians) | Allow more time; ask about weather and chains |
| **Winter closures** | Snow, ice and wind can close parts of I-80 in Wyoming, I-70 in Colorado and others | Check road conditions; build buffer days |
| **Hurricanes / floods** | Gulf and Atlantic coasts, summer–autumn | Watch forecasts for FL, TX, LA, the Carolinas |
| **Hazmat routes** | Some tunnels and routes ban hazmat (e.g. Colorado’s Eisenhower Tunnel on I-70) | Hazmat loads need hazmat routing |

pages.title: Where will the truck be after this load?
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.2 · Thinking ahead

# Where will the truck be after this load?

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/nextload.jpg)

### Headhaul, backhaul and dead ends

**Headhaul** = the direction where freight is plentiful and pays well. **Backhaul** = the return direction, often with fewer loads or lower rates. Some destinations sit at the **end of the map** (the Florida peninsula, the far Northeast, remote Mountain West areas), so trucks often leave with lower rates or empty miles.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Don’t hard-code market opinions**
>
> Many dispatchers say “Florida is mostly inbound” or “the Northeast is hard to get out of.” Such patterns shift with season (produce, holidays) and the economy. Treat them as **questions to check with live load-to-truck data** (Module 7), not facts.

pages.title: Four main zones, plus Arizona
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.3 · Time zones

# Four main zones, plus Arizona

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/map_tz.jpg)

### Cities you must know by zone

| Zone | Freight cities |
| --- | --- |
| **Eastern** | New York, Philadelphia, Harrisburg, Atlanta, Charlotte, Columbus, Detroit, Indianapolis, Louisville, Miami, Jacksonville, Savannah |
| **Central** | Chicago, Joliet, Dallas, Houston, San Antonio, Laredo, Memphis, Nashville, St. Louis, Kansas City, Minneapolis, New Orleans |
| **Mountain** | Denver, Salt Lake City, Albuquerque, El Paso, Boise, Cheyenne — and Phoenix (MST, no DST) |
| **Pacific** | Los Angeles, Inland Empire, Oakland, Sacramento, Portland, Seattle, Las Vegas, Reno |

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Split states catch beginners**
>
> **El Paso, TX** is Mountain while the rest of Texas is Central. **Pensacola, FL** is Central. **Nashville** is Central, **Knoxville** Eastern. **Gary, IN** (next to Chicago) is Central, **Indianapolis** Eastern. **Owensboro, KY** is Central, **Louisville** Eastern.

> **[FACT] Arizona and Hawaii**
>
> Most of Arizona does not use daylight saving time, so Phoenix has the **same clock as Los Angeles in summer** and the **same clock as Denver in winter**. Hawaii never changes either. DOT lists Hawaii, most of Arizona and the U.S. territories as not observing DST.

pages.title: Your shift against the U.S. day
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.3 · Your clock

# Your shift against the U.S. day

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/time_summer.jpg)

U.S. summer time (until 1 Nov 2026). Eastern offices open at 5 PM Pakistan time.

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/time_winter.jpg)

U.S. winter time (1 Nov 2026 – 14 Mar 2027). Everything moves one hour later in Pakistan.

pages.title: Convert any appointment
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.3 · Conversion

# Convert any appointment

![](/assets/diagrams/m03/convert.jpg)

### The gap table (memorise)

| Zone | Mar – Nov | Nov – Mar |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ET** | +9 h | +10 h |
| **CT** | +10 h | +11 h |
| **MT** | +11 h | +12 h |
| **Arizona** | +12 h | +12 h |
| **PT** | +12 h | +13 h |

> **[KEY RULE] Going the other way**
>
> A driver calls at **11:30 PM PKT** in October and says “I’ll be there in 3 hours.” Where is he? In Central Time it is 1:30 PM, so he arrives around 4:30 PM CT. Subtract the gap to get U.S. time; add it to get Pakistan time.

> **[FACT] Tool, not crutch**
>
> Keep a world clock on your screen with ET, CT, MT, PT and PKT. But learn the gaps by heart: on a fast broker call you won’t have time to search.

pages.title: Seven time traps — and how to avoid them
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.3 · Time traps

# Seven time traps — and how to avoid them

| # | Trap | Example | Habit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Different zones at each end** | Dallas pickup CT, Atlanta delivery ET | Write each stop in its own zone |
| 2 | **Zone change mid-trip** | Lebanon OH (ET) → Owensboro KY (CT): the clock goes back | Calculate the ETA in the receiver’s zone |
| 3 | **Date change in Pakistan** | “Mon 4 PM ET” in winter = **Tue** 2 AM PKT | Write the day with every PKT time |
| 4 | **Clock-change weekends** | Sun 1 Nov 2026 and Sun 14 Mar 2027 — your gaps change overnight | Put both dates in your calendar |
| 5 | **Arizona** | Phoenix = LA time in summer, Denver time in winter | Treat AZ as “+12 all year” |
| 6 | **Split states** | El Paso TX is Mountain; Pensacola FL is Central | Check the city, not the state |
| 7 | **The driver’s log clock** | Federal rules require the driver’s record of duty status to use the time standard of the driver’s **home terminal**, which may differ from the local appointment time | When discussing hours, confirm which clock the driver means |

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] A real-world cost**
>
> An appointment missed by one hour can mean a **rescheduled delivery the next day**, a lost layover day for the driver, a late fee on the RC, or the broker giving the next load to someone else. Most of these mistakes are pure clock errors.

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Say it out loud: confirming an appointment**
>
> “So delivery is **Thursday, 8 AM Eastern**, at the receiver in Charlotte — correct?” Always say the **day**, the **time** and the **zone**.

> **[KEY RULE] In your load notes**
>
> PU **Wed 09:00 CT** (Wed 19:00 PKT) · DEL **Thu 08:00 ET** (Thu 17:00 PKT). 24-hour format avoids AM/PM mistakes.

pages.title: Four worked scenarios
pages.markdown:
Lesson 3.3 · Worked scenarios

# Four worked scenarios

#### A · Summer, Chicago shipper

Broker: “Pickup is tomorrow, Wednesday, 6:00 AM at the shipper in Chicago.” It is 30 September.  
  
**Chicago = CT, summer → +10.** 6:00 AM CT = **4:00 PM Wednesday PKT**. The driver should be rolling there during your early shift. Confirm by 3 PM PKT.

#### B · Winter, New Jersey receiver

Delivery Friday 2:00 PM in Newark, NJ, in December.  
  
**Newark = ET, winter → +10.** 2:00 PM ET = **12:00 AM (midnight) Saturday PKT**. The POD will arrive after midnight your time: note it as Saturday.

#### C · Phoenix, July

Receiver in Phoenix opens at 5:00 AM.  
  
**Arizona = MST all year → +12.** 5:00 AM = **5:00 PM PKT**. In July that is also 5:00 AM in Los Angeles, since AZ has the same clock as PT in summer.

#### D · Cross-zone ETA

Driver leaves Nashville (CT) at 1:00 PM CT for Knoxville (ET), about 3 hours away.  
  
Arrives about 4:00 PM **CT** = **5:00 PM ET** Knoxville time. If the receiver closes at 4:30 PM ET, he will be late. Same state, different zones!

> **[KEY RULE] The pattern in every scenario**
>
> **Find the zone → apply the season gap → check the date → think about the receiver’s clock.** Four steps, every time, until they become automatic.

pages.title: Module 3 check
pages.markdown:
Module 3 · Check yourself

# Module 3 check

1. What do odd and even interstate numbers tell you? Where would you expect I-5 and I-95?
2. What does a three-digit interstate starting with an even digit usually mean? With an odd digit?
3. Name the main interstate(s) for Dallas → Atlanta, and the time zone of each city.
4. Which DAT zone would you search for loads going to Texas or Oklahoma?
5. Why is Laredo important to U.S. trucking, and which interstate starts there?
6. Give two differences between a truck route and a car route.

Odd = north–south, even = east–west. I-5 on the West Coast (lowest odd, far west); I-95 on the East Coast.

Even first digit: loop or connector around/through a city (I-285). Odd first digit: spur off the main route (I-575).

Z7 (AR, LA, OK, TX).

It is the busiest U.S.–Mexico land port for freight; cross-border freight flows north on I-35.

Any two: truck GPS avoids low bridges and weight limits; trucks are banned from some roads (e.g. NY parkways); hazmat routes; road miles for rates come from truck mileage systems.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.markdown:
Reference

# Glossary

**Backhaul** — The return direction of a lane, often with fewer or cheaper loads.

**Beltway / loop** — Interstate that circles a city (even-first-digit 3-digit number).

**Border crossing / port of entry** — Official crossing point with Mexico or Canada.

**Census region** — Official U.S. regions: Northeast, Midwest, South, West.

**Corridor** — A route with large, steady freight volumes.

**CT / ET / MT / PT** — Central, Eastern, Mountain, Pacific time.

**DAT zone** — Load-board region code Z0–Z9 used for searches.

**Daylight saving time (DST)** — U.S. summer time, second Sunday in March to first Sunday in November.

**DH-O / DH-D** — Deadhead to origin / from destination on a load board.

**Headhaul** — The direction where freight is plentiful and pays well.

**Home terminal time** — The time standard the driver’s log must use.

**Hub** — City or area that generates freight all year.

**Hot market** — An area where loads outnumber trucks right now.

**I-xx** — Interstate highway number.

**In-bond** — Freight still under customs control; specialist handling.

**Lane** — Origin → destination pair, e.g. Dallas → Atlanta.

**MST** — Mountain Standard Time; Arizona uses it all year.

**PHFS** — Primary Highway Freight System (FHWA).

**PKT** — Pakistan Standard Time, UTC+5, no DST.

**Road miles** — Actual driving miles, always more than straight-line distance.

**Split state** — A state with two time zones.

**Spur** — Short interstate branching off a main route (odd first digit).

**Texas triangle** — Dallas–Houston–San Antonio/Austin freight region.

**Truck route** — Road legal and safe for large trucks.

# How to use this module

In Module 3 you learned **where** a load goes and **when** the appointment is. Now you learn whether the **driver** can legally do it. A load that breaks hours-of-service rules is not a load, however well it pays.

### Study rhythm (about 7 hours)

- **Session 1 (2 h):** the four clocks. Learn them until you can explain each in one sentence.
- **Session 2 (1.5 h):** the log grid and the ELD. Read both example days line by line.
- **Session 3 (2 h):** the feasibility formula and the three trip plans.
- **Session 4 (1.5 h):** the 20 booking cases, the drill and the check.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction to your OMNITECH manual**
>
> The manual says a solo driver can legally do “600 legal miles / 10 hr.” **That is not the law.** The law limits **hours**, not miles: 11 hours of driving inside a 14-hour window, a 30-minute break after 8 hours of driving, and a 60/70-hour cycle. In practice a solo driver averages about **500–550 miles** on a good day.
