pages.title: The driver’s clock decides what you can book
pages.markdown:
4

Module 4 · HOS, ELD & feasibility

The driver’s clock  
decides what you can book

Hours-of-service (HOS) rules exist because tired drivers cause crashes. Every U.S. truck driver in interstate commerce works under them, and most record their hours on an electronic logging device (ELD) like the one pictured. As a dispatcher you never touch the logs, but you must plan every load inside them.

pages.title: The four clocks
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.1 · The rules

# The four clocks

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/big4.jpg)

### The FMCSA rules, word for word (property carriers)

- **11-hour driving limit:** “May drive a maximum of 11 hours after 10 consecutive hours off duty.”
- **14-hour limit:** “May not drive beyond the 14th consecutive hour after coming on duty, following 10 consecutive hours off duty.”
- **30-minute break:** required “when they have driven for a period of 8 cumulative hours without at least a 30-minute interruption.”
- **60/70-hour limit:** “May not drive after 60/70 hours on duty in 7/8 consecutive days.” A 34-hour off-duty period restarts it.

> **[KEY RULE] Memorise it as one sentence**
>
> **“After 10 off: 11 driving, inside 14, break after 8, and never over 70 in 8.”**

> **[FACT] Pilot programs are not new rules**
>
> In August 2026 FMCSA announced two pilot programs (a flexible sleeper split and a way to pause the 14-hour window for up to 3 hours). Pre-tests ran in 2026 with a handful of drivers; a full test with 512 drivers is planned for 2027. **The rules on this page still apply to everyone else.**

pages.title: 11 and 14: the two daily limits
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.1 · The rules

# 11 and 14: the two daily limits

#### The 11-hour driving limit

Counts only **driving** time. After 10 consecutive hours off, the driver has 11 hours of driving. When they are used up, he can still do other work (fuel, paperwork) but **cannot drive** until he takes another 10 hours off.

#### The 14-hour window

Starts when the driver first comes **on duty** (any work, not just driving) and runs for 14 hours straight. **It does not stop** for breaks, meals, waiting or loading. After the 14th hour, no more driving until 10 hours off.

## Three worked examples

| The driver’s day | 11-hour clock | 14-hour clock | Result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| On duty 06:00, drives 11 h with a 30-min break and 1 h of other work, off at 18:30 | 11 h used — limit reached | Window closes 20:00 | **Legal.** Stopped by the 11-hour limit. |
| On duty 06:00, waits 5 h at the shipper, drives from 13:30 | Can drive until 20:00 = 6.5 h | Window closes 20:00 | **Stopped by the 14-hour window** with 2.5 h of driving unused. |
| On duty 05:00, drives 4 h, 1 h breakfast off duty, drives 7 h | 11 h at 17:00 (break taken) | Window closes 19:00 | **Legal.** The breakfast hour counted toward the window, not the 11. |

> **[KEY RULE] The question that matters most**
>
> When a driver says “I have 8 hours,” ask: **“8 hours of driving, or 8 hours left in your shift?”** They are different clocks, and the smaller one decides.

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/window.jpg)

pages.title: The 30-minute break
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.1 · The rules

# The 30-minute break

### What triggers it

**8 cumulative hours of driving** without an interruption of at least 30 consecutive minutes. Cumulative means driving time adds up across stops shorter than 30 minutes: 3 h + 15-min fuel stop + 5 h = 8 h, and a break is now due.

### What counts as the break

Any **30 consecutive minutes** not driving: off duty, sleeper berth, **or on duty not driving** (e.g. loading), or a mix taken back to back. So a 45-minute loading stop after 6 hours of driving resets the 8-hour count.

| Sequence | Break needed? |
| --- | --- |
| Drive 5 h → load 1 h → drive 5 h | **No** — loading 1 h interrupted the driving |
| Drive 4 h → fuel 20 min → drive 4 h | **Yes** — 20 min is too short; 8 h reached |
| Drive 8 h straight | **Yes** — 30 min before more driving |
| Drive 7 h → sleeper 10 h → drive 7 h | **No** — the rest period reset everything |

> **[FACT] Planning shortcut**
>
> For plans, add **30 minutes for every 8 hours of driving**, unless a stop at a shipper or receiver already gives the driver 30 minutes.

## Where breaks fit in a real day

| Situation | How the break is handled | Dispatcher tip |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Long run, no stops** | Driver stops at a truck stop or rest area after ≤ 8 h of driving | Add 30 min to the ETA |
| **Pickup mid-day** | 30+ min of loading counts as the break | No extra time needed |
| **Fuel + meal stop** | If 30 consecutive minutes, it is the break | Suggest combining them |
| **Parking at night** | Truck parking is scarce in many areas after dark | Plan the rest stop before the window closes |

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Truck parking is a real constraint**
>
> A driver whose window closes at 20:00 must be **parked** by then, not just “near” a truck stop. On the East Coast and near big cities, truck stops can be full by early evening. Ask the driver where he plans to park.

pages.title: The weekly limit: 60/7 or 70/8
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.1 · The rules

# The weekly limit: 60/7 or 70/8

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/cycle.jpg)

### Which one applies?

A carrier that does **not** operate every day of the week uses 60 hours in 7 days. A carrier that operates **every day** may use 70 hours in 8 days. Most long-haul carriers use **70/8**. The ELD knows which one the driver is on.

**All on-duty time counts** toward the cycle, driving and non-driving (loading, waiting, inspections).

> **[KEY RULE] Why dispatchers watch the cycle**
>
> A driver with only 4 cycle hours left can’t take a 10-hour trip today, however fresh he feels. On a Friday you may need to plan a **34-hour restart** at home, or give hours back by planning short days.

> **[TRY IT] Try it**
>
> A driver has worked 11, 12, 10, 13, 0, 9, 11 hours in the last 7 days (70/8). How many hours can he work today? (Answer at the back.)

pages.title: The sleeper-berth split
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.1 · The rules

# The sleeper-berth split

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/sleeper.jpg)

### The rule in plain words

A driver with a sleeper berth can split the 10-hour rest into two periods: one of **at least 7 consecutive hours in the sleeper berth**, and another of **at least 2 hours** (off duty or sleeper). Together they must add up to **at least 10 hours**. When paired correctly, neither period counts against the 14-hour window.

FMCSA’s summary lists the pairings: 7/3, 8/2, 7.5/2.5 and so on.

> **[KEY RULE] How dispatchers use it**
>
> A driver stuck for 3 hours at a slow shipper might log that time in the sleeper and use it as the short half of a split. That can save a delivery. But the **calculation belongs to the driver and his ELD**. You ask; you don’t decide.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Beginner mistake**
>
> Planning a trip that only works “if he splits” without asking the driver. Many drivers dislike splits because the sleep is broken. Plan on a normal 10-hour rest unless the driver offers a split.

pages.title: Adverse conditions, short-haul, PC and yard moves
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.1 · Special rules

# Adverse conditions, short-haul, PC and yard moves

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/exceptions.jpg)

| Rule | Plain meaning | Dispatcher note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Adverse driving conditions** | 11-h and 14-h limits can be extended by up to 2 hours for conditions the driver didn’t know about when he started (snow, fog, a closure) | Never plan a trip that depends on it |
| **Short-haul exception** | Within 150 air miles, back within 14 hours: time records instead of logs | Common for local box trucks. Ask the carrier which drivers use it |
| **Personal conveyance** | Off-duty personal movement of the truck | Never to advance a load; FMCSA guidance allows e.g. moving to the nearest safe rest spot |
| **Yard move** | Movement inside a yard, logged as on duty | Not for public roads |

pages.title: The rules on one page
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.1 · Summary

# The rules on one page

| Rule | Limit | Resets with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Driving** | 11 h | 10 consecutive hours off (or valid sleeper split) |
| **Window** | No driving after the 14th hour on duty | 10 consecutive hours off (or valid split) |
| **Break** | 30 min after 8 cumulative hours of driving | Any 30 consecutive minutes not driving |
| **Cycle** | 60 h / 7 days or 70 h / 8 days on duty | Rolling; or a 34-hour off-duty restart |
| **Sleeper split** | ≥ 7 h sleeper + ≥ 2 h, total ≥ 10 | — |
| **Adverse conditions** | + up to 2 h on the 11 and 14 | Unexpected conditions only |
| **Short-haul** | 150 air miles, 14-hour day | Time records instead of logs |

## Miles per day, realistically

≈ 500–550

**miles on a full solo day**: 11 h × about 50 mph average including towns, traffic and fuel.

≈ 350–450

**miles on a day with a pickup or delivery**, because stops eat into the 14-hour window.

≈ 1,000+

**miles per 24 h for a team**, two drivers taking turns, each within his own limits.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Why “600 miles a day” is dangerous**
>
> If you promise a broker 600+ miles a day for a solo driver, the trip only works if he speeds, skips breaks or falsifies his logs. Plan on 500–550 on full driving days and less on pickup and delivery days.

pages.title: What an ELD is and what it records
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.2 · The ELD

# What an ELD is and what it records

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/eld.jpg)

### How it works

The ELD connects to the truck’s engine. When the truck moves, it switches the driver to **Driving** automatically and records time, location and engine data. The driver selects the other statuses. Officers at roadside inspections can view or receive the logs.

Carriers usually give dispatchers a login to the ELD provider’s **web portal**, where you can see every driver’s clocks and location.

> **[FACT] If the ELD breaks (49 CFR 395.34)**
>
> The driver notes the malfunction, notifies the carrier in writing within 24 hours, rebuilds his logs on paper for today and the previous 7 days, and keeps paper logs until the ELD is fixed. The carrier has 8 days to repair or replace it.

> **[KEY RULE] You read the ELD; you never edit it**
>
> Drivers can propose edits for genuine mistakes (e.g. forgot to switch to off duty), and the ELD keeps the original record. **Asking a driver to change his hours so a load “works” is illegal.**

pages.title: Reading the log grid
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.2 · The log grid

# Reading the log grid

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/log_legal.jpg)

### How to read it

- Four rows: **off duty, sleeper berth, driving, on duty not driving**.
- The line moves between rows as the driver’s status changes; the grid covers 24 hours, midnight to midnight.
- Totals on the right always add up to **24:00**.
- Times follow the driver’s **home-terminal** time zone (49 CFR 395.8), which may differ from the local time of the stop.

> **[TRY IT] Read this day**
>
> When did the 14-hour window start and end? When was the break taken, and why then? How many driving hours were left at 18:00? (Answers are on the graph itself.)

pages.title: Same driver, same window — 5 hours of waiting
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.2 · The log grid

# Same driver, same window — 5 hours of waiting

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/log_detention.jpg)

### What the detention cost

He waited 5 hours on duty at the shipper, so the window closed at 20:00 with only 8.5 hours of driving done. That is about **125 miles fewer** than planned. If tomorrow’s delivery assumed a full day of driving, it is now late.

> **[KEY RULE] What you do when detention starts**
>
> 1 · Note the arrival time (and get proof: check-in slip, ELD location). 2 · Tell the broker when the RC’s free time is running out. 3 · **Re-plan the next appointment** immediately using the hours actually left. Detention pay comes in Module 10.

pages.title: Four numbers before every booking
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.2 · Reading the clocks

# Four numbers before every booking

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/panel.jpg)

### How to ask when you have no portal access

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Say it out loud — asking for hours**
>
> **“Hi Carlos, before I book tomorrow’s load: how many drive hours and shift hours do you have left right now, and how much on your 70? When does your break come due?”**

> **[KEY RULE] Write them down with the time**
>
> “Carlos, Tue 21:10 PKT: drive 6:12 · shift 8:40 · break in 2:10 · cycle 31:15.” The clocks change every minute; the note shows when you asked.

### What the four numbers let you do

| Number | Question it answers | Example use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Drive left** | How far can he drive today? | 6:12 × 50 ≈ 300 miles more today |
| **Shift left** | When must he stop, even with drive hours left? | Can he still load (1.5 h) and then drive? |
| **Break in** | When is a 30-min stop due? | Add 30 min to the ETA if no loading stop comes first |
| **Cycle left** | Can he do a multi-day trip this week? | A 3-day trip needs ≈ 30+ on-duty hours |

pages.title: The feasibility formula
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.3 · Feasibility

# The feasibility formula

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/formula.jpg)

### The method in one line

**Start time + stop time + driving (miles ÷ 50) + breaks + rest periods + buffer = ETA.** Convert the ETA to the **receiver’s time zone** and compare with the appointment. Then check that the driver’s current clocks and cycle allow it.

> **[FACT] Why 50 mph?**
>
> Trucks often cruise at 60–70 mph on interstates, but fuel stops, towns, traffic, weigh stations and construction bring the real average down. 50 mph is a common, safe planning figure. Some carriers use 45 (cities, mountains) or 55 (open highway).

pages.title: A one-day trip: load #12354
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.3 · Trip plan 1

# A one-day trip: load #12354

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/trip_leb_owb.jpg)
![](/assets/diagrams/m04/route_leb_owb.jpg)

| Step | Calculation | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Load at shipper | On duty 6:45 ET, BOL printed 7:55, leave ≈ 8:10 | Depart 8:10 AM ET |
| Drive | 240 mi ÷ 50 mph = 4.8 h | Arrive ≈ 12:58 PM ET |
| Convert | ET → CT: minus 1 h | **11:58 AM CT** vs 12:00 PM CT appointment |
| Clocks | ≈ 6 h on duty, 4.8 h driving: no break needed, window fine | **Legal — but no buffer** |

pages.title: A two-day trip: Joliet → Charlotte
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.3 · Trip plan 2

# A two-day trip: Joliet → Charlotte

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/trip_jol_clt.jpg)

| Step | Calculation (Central Time) | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wed pickup | On duty 8:30, loaded 9:00–10:30 | Depart 10:30 · window closes 22:30 |
| Drive 1 | 8 h = 400 mi → 18:30; 30-min break → 19:00 | 400 mi done |
| Drive 2 | 3 h = 150 mi → 22:00 (11 h driving used) | 550 mi done · stop |
| Rest | 10 h off: 22:00 → 08:00 Thu | Clocks reset |
| Drive 3 | 240 mi ÷ 50 = 4.8 h → 12:48 CT | **1:48 PM ET** arrival |
| Compare | Appointment Thu 2:00 PM ET | **Legal, 12-minute buffer — too tight** |

> **[KEY RULE] What you do with a tight plan**
>
> Before booking, ask the broker: **“Can we get a 4 PM delivery, or FCFS until 5?”** or propose an earlier pickup. If the broker can’t move it, tell the carrier exactly how tight it is and let them decide.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] This fixes the Module 0 message**
>
> Mike’s message said “DEL Thu 2 PM” for a 750–800-mile trip picked up Wed 9 AM. Now you can see why that answer is risky: only minutes of buffer, and I-77 through the mountains in winter.

pages.title: A three-day trip: Laredo → Chicago
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.3 · Trip plan 3

# A three-day trip: Laredo → Chicago

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/trip_lar_chi.jpg)

### How to estimate long trips fast

1. Divide the miles into full driving days of about **550 miles** (11 h × 50).
2. Reduce the first day for loading (and the last for unloading).
3. Add a **10-hour rest** between days.
4. 1,430 mi → 550 + 550 + 330 = **3 driving days**.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] When a broker asks for the impossible**
>
> “Pick up Laredo Monday, deliver Chicago Tuesday” is ~1,430 miles in about 30 hours. That is **team** freight. Say so politely: *“That’s a team transit. With a solo driver the earliest is Wednesday midday.”*

> **[FACT] Team drivers**
>
> Two drivers take turns: one drives up to 11 h while the other rests in the sleeper. A team can cover 1,000+ miles in 24 hours. Only offer team service if the carrier really has a team.

pages.title: Yes, no, or “only if…”
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.3 · The decision

# Yes, no, or “only if…”

| Your calculation shows… | Decision | What you say / do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ETA well before the appointment** (2 h+ buffer), clocks and cycle OK | YES | Proceed to negotiate and book. |
| **ETA within 1 h of the appointment** | ONLY IF | Ask for a later appointment or FCFS window; tell the carrier the risk. |
| **ETA after the appointment** | NO (as posted) | “Can the delivery move to…?” If not, don’t book. |
| **Driver can’t reach pickup on time** with his current hours | NO | Don’t promise it. Offer the realistic pickup time. |
| **Not enough cycle hours** | NO or re-plan | Plan a restart or a shorter load. |
| **Only works with a split, team or adverse-conditions extension** | ONLY IF | Only if the driver or carrier confirms it is real and safe. |

> **[KEY RULE] The honest-ETA habit**
>
> Brokers remember dispatchers whose trucks arrive when promised. It is better to lose a load by being honest than to book a load that arrives late, costs a fee, and damages the carrier’s name.

## Common hour-eaters to ask about

#### Live load / unload

Driver waits while freight is loaded: 1–3 h, sometimes more.

#### Detention history

“How long do they usually take?” Brokers often know.

#### Big cities

Traffic in LA, Chicago, NYC, Atlanta can double the time.

#### Weather & mountains

Snow, wind, grades: slower average speed.

pages.title: Before you say “yes” to a load
pages.markdown:
Lesson 4.3 · Checklist

# Before you say “yes” to a load

### The driver

- Where is he now, and when will he be empty?
- Drive hours, shift hours, break due, cycle hours **right now**
- When does his 10-hour rest end?
- Home-time plans, personal limits (e.g. no night driving)

### The load

- Pickup window: appointment or FCFS? Live load or drop?
- Miles from the truck to pickup (deadhead) + loaded miles
- Delivery window and **time zone**
- Known delays: detention history, city, weather, mountains

### The calculation

- Drive time = miles ÷ 50
- + 30-min breaks · + 10-h rests · + stop time · + buffer
- ETA converted to the receiver’s zone
- Buffer of at least 1–2 hours?

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Say it out loud — the honest ETA**
>
> **“With a solo driver, loading at 9 Central, I can have him in Charlotte around 2 PM Eastern Thursday, but that’s tight. Could the receiver take him at 4, or first come first served?”**

> **[KEY RULE] Deadhead counts too**
>
> The drive from where the truck is now to the pickup uses the same clocks. A load 150 miles away costs 3 hours of driving before loading even starts.

pages.title: What a dispatcher must never do
pages.markdown:
Safety

# What a dispatcher must never do

![](/assets/diagrams/m04/coercion.jpg)

### The coercion rule

49 CFR 390.6: a motor carrier, shipper, receiver or transportation intermediary (and their agents) may not coerce a driver to operate a truck in violation of the safety rules, including hours of service. FMCSA’s rule came into force in 2016, and drivers can report coercion to FMCSA.

As the carrier’s dispatcher you are acting for the carrier. A message like “Just run it, nobody will know” is exactly the evidence an investigator looks for.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Falsified logs**
>
> Editing, faking or “fixing” records of duty status to hide violations is illegal for the driver and the carrier. ELDs keep an audit trail of every edit. If a trip only works with a false log, **it doesn’t work**.

> **[KEY RULE] Your script when the driver says no**
>
> **“Understood — safety first. I’ll let the broker know and re-plan.”** Then do exactly that, early.

pages.title: Twenty booking cases (1–12)
pages.markdown:
Practice

# Twenty booking cases (1–12)

For each: **yes / no / only if**, plus the reason in one line and the calculation where needed. Use miles ÷ 50 for driving time. Answers at the back.

1

Truck 12 has **3:00 of drive time** left. The pickup is **180 miles** away. Can he reach it today?

2

The driver has **5 hours** left on his 70-hour cycle. Tomorrow’s load needs about 9 hours on duty. Can you book it?

3

On duty at **06:00**, waited at the shipper, loaded at **13:00**. How many hours can he still drive today?

4

The driver has driven **8 hours straight** and is 60 miles from the receiver. Can he keep driving?

5

Drove 5 h, then 45 minutes loading. How many more hours can he drive today, and does he need another break first?

6

Solo, **1,100 miles**, pickup Mon 8:00 AM, delivery Tue 5:00 PM, same time zone, 1 h loading. Feasible?

7

Dallas pickup Mon 7:00 AM CT (1.5 h loading), Atlanta delivery Tue **8:00 AM ET**, 780 miles. Feasible?

8

A broker says: “Your driver can do 600 miles today, right?” What do you answer?

9

The driver says: “I can make it if I fix my log later.” What do you do?

10

A local box-truck carrier runs within about 80 miles of its yard and is back each evening. How might its drivers record hours?

11

Unexpected heavy snow slowed the driver. He reaches his 11 hours 30 minutes from delivery. What are the options?

12

The driver’s 10-hour rest ends at **04:00 CT**. The pickup appointment is **05:00 CT**, 40 miles away. OK?

pages.title: Twenty booking cases (13–20)
pages.markdown:
Practice

# Twenty booking cases (13–20)

13

Laredo pickup Mon 8:00 AM; the broker wants Chicago delivery **Wed 8:00 AM**. Solo driver. Answer?

14

It is 23:00 PKT in October. The driver’s window closes at 17:00 CT. How much window is left?

15

Delivery at 06:00 ET, 250 miles away. The driver’s rest ends at 01:00 ET and pre-trip takes 15 minutes. On time?

16

The driver has been held **4 hours** at the shipper. Tomorrow’s delivery assumed a full driving day today. What do you do?

17

The driver wants to use his 3-hour wait as part of a sleeper-berth split. Who decides, and what do you do?

18

The load requires team service. Your carrier has only solo drivers. Book it?

19

The driver has used his 11 hours, but 2 hours remain in his 14-hour window. Can he fuel and do paperwork?

20

A broker offers a $200 bonus “if your driver gets there a few hours earlier than he legally can.” Your answer?

> **[CHECKLIST] Target**
>
> At least **17 of 20**. If you miss any HOS case, re-read pages 4–10. If you miss a time-zone case, revisit Module 3.

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Say it out loud — drill 6: refusing an unsafe request politely**
>
> Broker: “Can’t your guy just push through tonight?”  
>   
> **“I understand the timing is tight. He’s out of hours at 8 PM Central and needs his 10-hour break, so the realistic delivery is 10 AM tomorrow. I can send you a tracking update when he’s rolling. Would 10 AM work for the receiver?”**  
>   
> Calm, factual, and offering a solution. Practise until it sounds natural.

pages.title: Module 4 check
pages.markdown:
Module 4 · Check yourself

# Module 4 check

1. State the 11-hour, 14-hour, 30-minute and 60/70-hour rules in your own words.
2. Does the 14-hour window stop while the driver waits at a dock? Why does that matter?
3. What counts as the 30-minute break?
4. What resets the weekly cycle completely?
5. Describe the sleeper-berth split and one pairing that works.
6. What was wrong with “600 legal miles / 10 hr” in the old manual?
7. Which planning speed does this module use, and roughly how many miles is a full solo driving day?
8. Name four things an ELD records automatically or displays to the dispatcher.
9. What must a driver do if his ELD malfunctions?
10. Which time zone does a driver’s log use?
11. What is coercion under 49 CFR 390.6, and who can be responsible?
12. An ETA shows arrival 20 minutes before the appointment. What is your decision and what do you say?

> **[FACT] ELD malfunctions (49 CFR 395.34)**
>
> If the ELD malfunctions, the driver must note it, give the carrier written notice within 24 hours, reconstruct his records for the current 24 hours and the previous 7 days, and keep paper logs until it is fixed. The carrier must repair or replace it within 8 days, unless FMCSA grants an extension.

pages.title: Answers — booking cases
pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers — booking cases

**1.**

**No.** 180 ÷ 50 = 3.6 h of driving > 3:00 left.

**2.**

**No** (as planned). 5 h of cycle < 9 h needed. Plan a 34-h restart, or a smaller load.

**3.**

Until the window closes at 20:00 → **7 hours** (≈ 350 mi). The long wait already counts as his break.

**4.**

**No**, not until he takes a 30-minute break.

**5.**

**6 more hours** (11 − 5), window permitting. No break needed first: the 45-min loading reset the 8-hour count.

**6.**

**No as posted.** Day 1: depart 9:00, 550 mi by 20:30; rest to 06:30. Day 2: 550 mi + break → ≈ 18:00, an hour late, before unloading. Ask for a later delivery, or it needs a team.

**7.**

**No.** Day 1: ≈ 550 mi by 20:00 CT; rest to 06:00. Remaining 230 mi = 4.6 h → 10:36 CT = **11:36 AM ET**. Ask for noon ET or later.

**8.**

“For a solo driver we plan 500–550 miles on a full driving day, and less on pickup day. Here’s a realistic ETA…”

**9.**

Refuse. Falsifying logs is illegal. Re-plan honestly and tell the broker.

**10.**

Possibly the **short-haul exception** (150 air miles, back within 14 h): time records instead of logs/ELD. The carrier confirms which drivers qualify.

**11.**

The **adverse driving conditions** rule may allow up to 2 more hours for unexpected conditions. **The driver decides** whether it applies and is safe; you don’t pressure.

**12.**

**Yes, but tight.** Pre-trip ~15 min + 40 mi ≈ 0.8 h → about 05:05. Ask the shipper whether a few minutes late is acceptable, or plan the rest to end earlier next time.

**13.**

**No.** ~1,430 mi = 3 solo driving days; the earliest is Wed ~12:30 CT. Offer Wed afternoon, or it needs a team.

**14.**

October: PKT = CT + 10, so 23:00 PKT = 13:00 CT → **4 hours** of window left.

**15.**

**No.** 01:15 + 5 h = 06:15 ET, 15 min late. Ask for 07:00 or FCFS.

**16.**

Recalculate with the hours actually left, and **tell the broker early** with a new ETA. Document the detention (Module 10).

**17.**

**The driver** (and his ELD). Once he confirms the split, you plan around it.

**18.**

**No.** Don’t book team freight without a real team.

**19.**

**Yes.** Other on-duty work is allowed; only driving is not, until 10 hours off.

**20.**

Decline. It invites an HOS violation (coercion risk) and endangers the driver and the public.

pages.title: Answers — module check
pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers — module check

**1.**

11 h driving after 10 h off; no driving after the 14th hour on duty; 30-min break after 8 cumulative hours of driving; no driving after 60 h / 7 days or 70 h / 8 days on duty.

**2.**

No. Waiting eats the window, so the driver loses driving hours and the next appointment may fail.

**3.**

Any 30 consecutive minutes not driving: off duty, sleeper, on-duty-not-driving (e.g. loading), or a mix.

**4.**

A 34-hour (or longer) off-duty restart.

**5.**

≥ 7 h in the sleeper + ≥ 2 h off duty or sleeper, total ≥ 10 h (e.g. 7/3 or 8/2). Paired correctly, neither period counts against the 14-hour window.

**6.**

The law limits hours, not miles, and 600 miles in 10 h requires a 60 mph average: unrealistic without speeding or violations.

**7.**

50 mph → about 500–550 miles on a full driving day.

**8.**

Any four: duty status, driving time, location, engine hours/miles, remaining drive/shift/break/cycle time.

**9.**

Note it, notify the carrier in writing within 24 h, reconstruct the current day + previous 7 days, keep paper logs until repaired.

**10.**

The time standard of the driver’s home terminal.

**11.**

Forcing a driver to break safety rules (e.g. HOS). Motor carriers, shippers, receivers and transportation intermediaries (and their agents) can be responsible.

**12.**

Only if. Ask the broker for a later window or FCFS; tell the carrier the risk. A 20-minute buffer is not enough.

**p.7.**

11 + 12 + 10 + 13 + 0 + 9 + 11 = 66 h, so 70 − 66 = **4 hours** today.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.markdown:
Reference

# Glossary

**11-hour limit** — Maximum driving after 10 consecutive hours off.

**14-hour window** — Period after coming on duty; no driving after its end.

**30-minute break** — Required after 8 cumulative hours of driving.

**34-hour restart** — 34+ consecutive hours off duty that resets the 60/70 cycle.

**60/70-hour cycle** — On-duty limit over 7 or 8 consecutive days.

**Adverse driving conditions** — Unexpected conditions allowing up to 2 extra hours.

**Coercion** — Forcing a driver to break safety rules; banned by 49 CFR 390.6.

**Cycle hours** — On-duty hours left in the 7/8-day period.

**Deadhead** — Empty miles to reach a pickup; uses the same clocks.

**Drive time left** — ELD figure: driving hours remaining today.

**ELD** — Electronic logging device recording duty status.

**FCFS** — First come, first served: a window instead of a fixed time.

**HOS** — Hours of service: federal driver work-time rules.

**Home terminal time** — Time standard used on the driver’s log.

**Live load / unload** — Driver waits while freight is loaded or unloaded.

**Off duty** — Not working.

**On duty (not driving)** — Working but not driving: loading, inspections, waiting.

**Personal conveyance** — Off-duty personal use of the truck; never to advance a load.

**RODS** — Record of duty status (the log).

**Short-haul exception** — 150 air miles / 14 h: time records instead of logs.

**Shift left** — Time remaining in the 14-hour window.

**Sleeper berth** — Rest in the truck’s sleeping compartment.

**Split sleeper** — 7+ h sleeper + 2+ h rest = the 10-hour rest.

**Team** — Two drivers taking turns so the truck keeps moving.

**Yard move** — On-duty movement inside a yard.

pages.title: How to use this module
pages.markdown:
Start here

# How to use this module

Before any broker gives your carrier a load, the broker checks that the carrier **exists, is authorised, is insured and is who it says it is**. You are the person who collects, checks and sends those documents. Do it well and setups take minutes; do it badly and loads are lost.

### Study rhythm (about 6 hours)

- **Session 1 (1.5 h):** identifiers, Motus, SAFER, L&I. Look up a real carrier on SAFER yourself.
- **Session 2 (2 h):** the packet: W-9, COI, NOA, bank details, dispatch agreement.
- **Session 3 (1 h):** broker setup and verification.
- **Session 4 (1.5 h):** the packet audit, the agent-call drill and the check.

> **[TRY IT] Do it live**
>
> Open **safer.fmcsa.dot.gov** and search any real company by USDOT number, for example one from a truck photo or a news article. Compare what you see with page 7. SAFER is free and public.

pages.title: Paper before freight
pages.markdown:
5

Module 5 · Carrier onboarding & documents

Paper before freight

Every document in this module comes from your OMNITECH manual: a real FMCSA authority certificate, W-9, certificate of insurance, notice of assignment, voided check and carrier profile. They are samples from different companies, and in the audit exercise you will find out why that matters.

pages.title: USDOT, MC and authority status
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.1 · Identifiers

# USDOT, MC and authority status

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/ids.jpg)

### How they appear in real life

- A broker on the phone: **“What’s your MC?”** You answer with the carrier’s docket number.
- A rate confirmation: carrier name, **MC and DOT** (remember load #12354’s RC).
- On the truck door: the **USDOT number** and company name.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction to older course notes**
>
> Some 2025 articles claimed “MC numbers are being eliminated.” FMCSA’s May 2026 Motus notice says docket numbers are **still issued**, the MC/MX/FF prefixes are unchanged, and **existing USDOT and docket numbers don’t change**. New registrants get a letter suffix on the USDOT number.

### What Motus changed (2025–26)

- New online registration system; all users verify identity with **Login.gov**, an anti-fraud step.
- **USDOT suffixes** for new registrants (C = property carrier, B = broker, and others). Not required on trucks.
- **One docket number per new authority**.
- A pending application now shows its **reason**, e.g. “Pending – Process Agent (Form BOC-3) Filings.”

pages.title: The operating-authority certificate
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.1 · The certificate

# The operating-authority certificate

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/mc_annot.jpg)
> **[KEY RULE] A certificate is history; SAFER is today**
>
> The certificate proves authority was **granted** on its service date. It stays valid only “as long as the carrier maintains compliance” with insurance and process-agent rules. **Always confirm current status on SAFER / L&I**, because an authority can be revoked while the paper certificate still looks perfect.

pages.title: How an authority starts — and stays alive
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.1 · Authority life cycle

# How an authority starts — and stays alive

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/timeline.jpg)

| Term | What it is | Why a dispatcher cares |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Common authority** | Authority to haul for the general public for hire (what most carriers have) | Must be ACTIVE to take broker freight |
| **BOC-3** | Filing that names process agents (people who accept legal papers) in each state | No BOC-3 → authority stays pending |
| **BIPD insurance filing** | The insurer files liability proof with FMCSA (BMC-91/91X); $750,000 minimum for general freight | Cancelled filing → authority can be revoked |
| **MCS-150** | Company census (trucks, drivers, operations); update at least every 2 years | Very old date can mean an inactive or careless carrier |
| **UCR** | Unified Carrier Registration: annual fee for interstate carriers | Unpaid UCR can mean fines at inspection |
| **IRP / IFTA** | Apportioned plates and fuel-tax reporting for trucks crossing states | Carrier’s job; affects which states the truck can run legally |

> **[FACT] “New authority” and brokers**
>
> Many brokers wait until an authority is about **90 days old** before giving loads, or give only lower-value freight at first. Others accept new carriers with extra checks. That is broker policy, not law, and it varies. When you start with a new carrier, **ask which big brokers have already approved them**.

pages.title: Reading SAFER
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.1 · SAFER

# Reading SAFER

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/safer.jpg)

SAFER’s Company Snapshot gives “a concise record of a company’s identification, size, cargo, inspection and out-of-service summary, crash data and safety rating (if any)” (FMCSA). Deeper safety data sits in SMS (the Safety Measurement System).

pages.title: Licensing & Insurance: status and filings
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.1 · Licensing & Insurance

# Licensing & Insurance: status and filings

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/li.jpg)

### SAFER vs L&I in one line each

**SAFER**: who the company is, its size and its safety record. **L&I**: its authority types and statuses, insurance filings, and BOC-3. Both are free FMCSA lookups, and brokers and onboarding platforms check both automatically.

> **[TRY IT] Read the screen**
>
> On this L&I screen: is the carrier allowed to broker loads? How much liability insurance is on file, and is that above the federal minimum? (Answers at the back.)

## Practice: what do these lookup results mean?

| # | You see… | Your conclusion |

| 1 | SAFER: Operating Authority Status “NOT AUTHORIZED” |  |
| 2 | SAFER: Out of Service Date 08/12/2026 |  |
| 3 | L&I: Common authority “Pending – FMCSA Review” |  |
| 4 | L&I: BIPD required $750,000 · on file $0 |  |
| 5 | SAFER: MCS-150 date 2019, 1 power unit |  |

pages.title: The carrier onboarding packet
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.2 · The packet

# The carrier onboarding packet

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/packet.jpg)

### Day one with a new carrier

1. Sign the **dispatch agreement**.
2. Collect the six documents (PDF, clear, current).
3. Run the eight checks (page 18).
4. Fill in the carrier profile: trucks, trailers, equipment, lanes, home time, floor rate, contacts.
5. Ask which brokers already have the carrier set up.

> **[KEY RULE] One clean PDF packet**
>
> Save one combined, clearly named file: **“BlueLine\_Packet\_2026-09.pdf”** (MC cert + W-9 + COI + NOA or bank letter). Brokers love fast, clean packets, and it shows the carrier is professional.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Protect the documents**
>
> A packet contains tax IDs and bank details. Fraudsters use stolen packets to impersonate carriers. Send it only to verified brokers, through their official setup link or verified email (Module 8).

pages.title: The W-9
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.2 · W-9

# The W-9

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/w9_annot.jpg)
> **[FACT] Why a broker needs it**
>
> Brokers pay carriers and may have to report those payments to the IRS. The W-9 gives them the carrier’s legal name and taxpayer ID (EIN, or SSN for a sole proprietor). **You never give tax advice**; you just make sure the form is current, complete and matches the other documents.

pages.title: The COI, line by line
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.2 · Certificate of insurance

# The COI, line by line

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/coi_annot.jpg)

> **[KEY RULE] The 60-second COI check**
>
> **1** Insured = exact legal name · **2** dates cover today and the delivery date · **3** auto liability ≥ broker minimum · **4** cargo ≥ load value / broker minimum · **5** truck on the schedule · **6** exclusions vs the freight · **7** agent contact to verify · **8** certificate holder = the broker.

> **[TRY IT] Try it on the sample**
>
> Using the annotated COI above: which of the eight checks pass, and which fail? (Answer in the packet audit at the back.)

pages.title: Insurance types a dispatcher must understand
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.2 · Insurance

# Insurance types a dispatcher must understand

| Coverage | What it covers | Law / typical broker ask | Dispatcher check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Auto liability (BIPD)** | Injury and damage the truck causes to others | FMCSA min. $750,000 general freight · brokers usually $1,000,000 | Limit, dates, truck covered (scheduled autos) |
| **Motor truck cargo** | Damage to or loss of the freight being hauled | Not federally required for general freight · brokers often ≥ $100,000 | Limit vs load value; exclusions (reefer breakdown, electronics, theft) |
| **General liability** | Non-driving incidents, e.g. damage at a customer’s dock | Some brokers / shippers ask ($1M) | Present if the broker requires it |
| **Physical damage** | The carrier’s own truck and trailer | Carrier’s choice / lender | Rarely asked by brokers |
| **Non-owned trailer / interchange** | Trailers the carrier pulls but doesn’t own | Needed for power-only and drop trailers | Present before any power-only load (Module 2) |
| **Workers’ compensation** | Employee injuries (state rules) | Some brokers ask, or an exemption form | Owner-operators may be exempt |

> **[KEY RULE] What the sample COI teaches**
>
> • **Auto $1M, cargo $250K**: meets most broker norms.  
> • **Scheduled autos**: only listed trucks are covered, so ask for the schedule when a new truck is added.  
> • **Non-owned trailer $50K**: OK for power only up to that value.  
> • **Reefer breakdown included**: important for reefer loads.  
> • **Insured blank and dates expired**: this copy would be rejected.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] A COI is not a guarantee**
>
> ACORD 25 says it is “issued as a matter of information only and confers no rights upon the certificate holder.” Policies can be cancelled after the COI is printed. That is why brokers **call the agent** or use monitoring services, and why you re-check before new setups.

> **[FACT] Certificate holder requests**
>
> Each broker wants its name in the certificate-holder box. You email the carrier’s insurance agent: *“Please issue a COI to ABC Logistics, [address], certificate holder.”* Agents usually send it straight to the broker.

pages.title: Factoring and the Notice of Assignment
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.2 · Factoring

# Factoring and the Notice of Assignment

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/noa_annot.jpg)

### How factoring works

The carrier sells its invoices to a factoring company, which pays the carrier within a day or two, minus a fee, then collects from the broker when payment is due. The **NOA** legally tells the broker: “pay the factor, not the carrier.”

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Why it matters to you**
>
> If the broker pays the carrier directly after receiving an NOA, the factor can make the broker **pay twice**. So brokers take NOAs seriously. If your carrier changes factoring companies, the old factor must send a **release letter** before the new NOA takes effect. Keep both on file.

pages.title: Bank details and the dispatch agreement
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.2 · Payment details & your agreement

# Bank details and the dispatch agreement

#### Voided check (sample from your manual)

Shows the **routing number** (bank, 9 digits) and **account number** so a broker can pay by ACH. Many carriers send a **bank letter** instead. Not needed if the carrier factors: the NOA replaces it.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Bank-change fraud**
>
> A classic scam: an email “from the carrier” asks the broker to change the bank account. Brokers verify changes by phone with a known contact. If your carrier changes banks, **tell brokers by phone as well as email**.

### Spot the error on the sample

The printed check number is **3256**, but the label under it says “Cheque Number **5337**.” It’s a small thing on a teaching picture, but it is exactly the kind of mismatch you must notice on real documents.

### The dispatch agreement

The written relationship between you (or your employer) and the carrier. It supports the **carrier-agent** position from Module 1: you act for one carrier, paid by that carrier, and you never handle broker money. The next page shows what it should cover.

> **[KEY RULE] Authority to sign**
>
> Brokers often ask the person completing setup: “Are you authorised to sign for the carrier?” Only say yes if your dispatch agreement says so. Otherwise send the agreement to the owner for signature.

pages.title: What a dispatch agreement should cover
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.2 · Dispatch agreement

# What a dispatch agreement should cover

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/agreement.jpg)

### Typical fee structures (examples)

| Model | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| **% of gross** | E.g. 5–10% of each load’s line-haul pay (practitioner range, varies) |
| **Flat per load / week** | Fixed amount regardless of rate |
| **Salary (employee)** | Dispatch company pays you; the carrier pays the company |

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Not legal advice**
>
> This page shows common contents, not a template to sign. When you start, your employer or carrier will provide the agreement. If you later set up your own business, have a U.S. transportation attorney review yours.

pages.title: Broker carrier setup
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.3 · Broker setup

# Broker carrier setup

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/flow.jpg)

### What the broker sees

Setup platforms pull FMCSA data automatically: authority, insurance filings, safety data, sometimes identity signals and monitoring alerts. The broker adds its own rules: authority age, minimum insurance, safety thresholds, factoring company, sometimes a phone call to the carrier using the number on FMCSA records.

> **[KEY RULE] Speed tips**
>
> • Keep the carrier’s profile complete on the big platforms.  
> • Have the insurance agent’s email ready for certificate-holder requests.  
> • Answer the broker’s verification call quickly, from a number they can match.  
> • Start setup **before** negotiating hard on a new broker’s load if it is time-sensitive.

pages.title: The broker’s carrier profile form
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.3 · Broker setup

# The broker’s carrier profile form

**Real carrier profile form** from your OMNITECH manual (a broker called Metro Express): legal name, contacts, states served, services, equipment by type, references.

### Fill it in from your carrier notes

- **Legal name** exactly as on the MC certificate and W-9.
- **Dispatch day and night phone**: your number and the owner’s. Make sure you can answer.
- **States served**: the carrier’s real lanes. Over-ticking every state gets you spam.
- **Equipment**: exact types (53′ van, 26′ box truck with liftgate…) from Module 2.
- **Special requirements**: hazmat, team, pallet exchange. Tick only what is true.
- **References**: brokers the carrier already hauls for.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Never exaggerate capabilities**
>
> Ticking “hazmat” or “reefer” for a carrier that isn’t qualified gets loads offered that you can’t legally haul, and can void insurance coverage on a claim.

### Other things brokers may ask

Broker–carrier agreement signature, payment terms or quick-pay option, factoring details, ELD provider and tracking consent, safety or accident history, and a recently signed W-9.

pages.title: Verifying your own carrier
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.4 · Verification

# Verifying your own carrier

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/verify.jpg)

### Why check your own carrier?

Because the broker will. If insurance has lapsed or the authority is inactive, the setup fails, or worse, a load moves without valid coverage. Catching it first protects your carrier, your reputation and the load.

> **[KEY RULE] Repeat the live checks**
>
> SAFER and L&I status and COI dates can change any day. Re-check them **monthly**, **before each new broker setup**, and **whenever the carrier mentions insurance changes**.

pages.title: Document red flags
pages.markdown:
Lesson 5.4 · Red flags

# Document red flags

![](/assets/diagrams/m05/flags.jpg)
> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Say it out loud — drill 7: verifying a COI with the agent**
>
> Call the phone number on the COI (or the insurer’s official number):  
>   
> **“Hi, this is Jawad, dispatcher for Blue Line Transport, MC 1298456. I’m confirming a certificate of insurance dated September 15, 2026. Can you confirm the auto liability and cargo policies are active, the limits are $1 million and $100,000, and that the 2022 Freightliner, VIN ending 4471, is on the schedule? Also, are there any cargo exclusions for reefer breakdown?”**  
>   
> Write down the name of the person, the date and the answers.

> **[FACT] Monitoring services**
>
> Brokers often use monitoring tools (e.g. Carrier411 in your manual’s screenshot, or the onboarding platforms) that alert them to insurance cancellations, authority changes and reports from other brokers. The Carrier411 screenshot shows “FreightGuard” reports such as “cancelled after accepting load.” A carrier’s behaviour follows it.

pages.title: Onboarding interview + module check
pages.markdown:
Practice

# Onboarding interview + module check

### Questions to ask a new carrier on day one

1. Legal name, MC, USDOT, and who is authorised to sign?
2. How many trucks and trailers, which types, and the VIN/unit numbers?
3. Insurance agent’s name, phone and email?
4. Do you factor? With whom? Is the NOA current?
5. Which brokers are you already set up with?
6. Preferred lanes, home time, minimum rate (Module 7)?
7. Freight you won’t haul (hazmat, food, high value)?
8. ELD provider, and can I have dispatcher access?

### Module 5 check

1. What is the difference between a USDOT number, an MC number and authority status?
2. Did Motus eliminate MC numbers? What did it change?
3. Which two FMCSA lookups do you use, and what does each show?
4. What is the FMCSA minimum liability for a general-freight carrier, and what do brokers usually ask?
5. Why can a COI be current on paper but not valid?
6. What does “scheduled autos” mean for a dispatcher?
7. What does an NOA tell a broker, and what happens if it is ignored?
8. Name four things a dispatch agreement should cover.
9. Name five document red flags.
10. Why must packets be sent only through verified channels?

pages.title: Answers — lookups and packet audit
pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers — lookups and packet audit

### L&I screen (page 8)

**.**

No: broker authority is NONE. $1,000,000 BIPD is on file, above the $750,000 federal minimum.

### Lookup results (page 8)

| # | Conclusion |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Cannot haul for hire across state lines. Stop. |
| 2 | Ordered out of service. Cannot operate. Stop. |
| 3 | Authority not yet granted. Can’t take broker loads yet. |
| 4 | No liability filing: authority will be or is revoked. Stop. |
| 5 | Census not updated for years; ask the carrier to update the MCS-150 and confirm it is active. |
| 6 | Has both carrier and broker registrations: legal, but confirm which role it plays on each load. |

### Packet audit (page 20) — problems

1. **Names don’t match:** MC certificate = ABC Company LLC; W-9 = Fantastic Tacos, LLC; NOA = Amagination Reaality, LLC. Three different companies!
2. **COI “Insured” box is blank**: no carrier named.
3. **COI expired**: policy period ended 04/01/2023.
4. **COI certificate holder is blank**: the broker would need its own certificate.
5. **W-9 is an old revision** (Oct 2018); the IRS’s current version is March 2024. The address (Phoenix) doesn’t match the MC certificate (Jacksonville).
6. **NOA MC number (1406468) differs** from the certificate (MC-1395526).
7. **Voided check**: the account holder is a person (John Doe), not the company; the cheque number label doesn’t match. And if the carrier factors (NOA), payment goes to the factor, so the check shouldn’t be used.

> **[KEY RULE] Lesson**
>
> Each document looks fine alone. Together they are clearly not one carrier. **Always cross-check names, numbers, addresses and dates across the whole packet.**

pages.title: Answers — module check
pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers — module check

**1.**

USDOT = identity and safety record; MC = operating authority to haul for hire; status = whether that authority is active today.

**2.**

No. Docket numbers are still issued and existing numbers don’t change. Motus added USDOT suffixes for new registrants, Login.gov identity checks, one docket per new authority, and pending-reason displays.

**3.**

SAFER: identity, size, inspections, crashes, rating, operating status. L&I: authority types and statuses, insurance filings, BOC-3.

**4.**

$750,000 BIPD for general freight; brokers usually want $1,000,000 auto liability and often ≥ $100,000 cargo.

**5.**

A COI is information only; the policy can be cancelled after printing, or the truck may not be on it. Verify with the agent.

**6.**

Only the trucks listed on the policy are covered. The dispatched truck must be on the schedule.

**7.**

Pay the factoring company, not the carrier. If ignored, the broker may have to pay twice.

**8.**

Any four: parties; services; authority to sign; compensation paid by the carrier only; carrier decides on loads; no brokering; payments go directly to carrier or factor; term; confidentiality.

**9.**

Any five: names don’t match; expired COI; insured blank; truck not on policy; cargo exclusions; authority inactive; contact mismatch; surprise NOA; bank-change request by email.

**10.**

Packets hold tax IDs and bank details. Fraudsters use them to impersonate carriers and redirect payments.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.markdown:
Reference

# Glossary

**ACORD 25** — Standard certificate-of-insurance form.

**Authority** — FMCSA permission to operate for hire (common/contract/broker).

**BIPD** — Bodily injury and property damage (auto liability) insurance.

**BMC-91 / 91X** — Insurer’s liability filing with FMCSA.

**BOC-3** — Filing naming process agents in each state.

**Cargo insurance** — Covers the freight being hauled.

**Certificate holder** — Party (e.g. a broker) named on a COI.

**COI** — Certificate of insurance.

**Dispatch agreement** — Contract between the carrier and its dispatcher.

**Docket number** — MC / MX / FF authority number.

**EIN** — Employer Identification Number (tax ID).

**Factoring** — Selling invoices to a factor for fast cash.

**L&I** — FMCSA Licensing & Insurance records.

**Login.gov** — Federal identity-verification service used by Motus.

**MCS-150** — Carrier census form; update every 2 years.

**Motus** — FMCSA’s registration system (2025–26).

**NOA** — Notice of assignment: pay the factor.

**Non-owned trailer** — Insurance for trailers the carrier pulls but doesn’t own.

**Out-of-service** — Order barring a company, driver or vehicle from operating.

**SAFER** — FMCSA public company snapshot lookup.

**Scheduled autos** — Policy covers only listed vehicles.

**SMS** — FMCSA Safety Measurement System.

**USDOT number** — FMCSA company identifier.

**USDOT suffix** — Letter after a new USDOT number showing entity type.

**W-9** — IRS form giving a taxpayer ID to a payer.

pages.title: Three hundred loads. Which two do you call?
pages.markdown:
6

Module 6 · Load boards

Three hundred loads.  
Which two do you call?

The background is a real DAT Power search from your OMNITECH manual: a Charlotte search showing 284 results. Speed matters, because good loads are often covered within minutes. But speed without screening books the wrong loads.

pages.title: A marketplace, not a contract
pages.markdown:
Lesson 6.1 · How it works

# A marketplace, not a contract

![](/assets/diagrams/m06/market.jpg)

### Who uses load boards

- **Brokers** post loads they need trucks for, and search posted trucks.
- **Carriers and dispatchers** search loads and post available trucks.
- Boards add tools: **rate data**, **broker credit and days-to-pay**, reviews, alerts, “book now”.

The biggest U.S. boards are **DAT** and **Truckstop**; others include 123Loadboard. Big brokers also run their own apps and portals.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] A posting is not a promise**
>
> Postings can be old, already covered, missing details, or fake (Module 8). Rates can change on the phone. **Nothing is booked until the carrier signs a rate confirmation.**

> **[FACT] Access reminder (Module 0)**
>
> DAT lets carriers with authority add a **seat for their dispatcher**. Truckstop requires active carrier authority to search loads. Never borrow logins.

### Where a carrier’s loads come from

| Source | How it works | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Load boards** | Search posted loads, call or email the broker, or book instantly where offered | New carriers; finding freight anywhere, fast |
| **Truck postings** | Post the empty truck; brokers call you | Thin markets; slow nights |
| **Repeat brokers** | Brokers you have hauled for email their lanes or call first | Better rates and trust over time |
| **Broker apps / portals** | Large brokers let set-up carriers book loads inside their own app | After the carrier is onboarded with that broker (Module 5) |
| **Direct shippers** | The carrier contracts with a shipper directly | Established carriers; not your first month |

pages.title: Four real boards, one logic
pages.markdown:
Lesson 6.1 · Real screens

# Four real boards, one logic

![](/assets/diagrams/m06/gallery.jpg)
> **[KEY RULE] Learn the columns, not the colours**
>
> Every board shows the same core facts: **age · pickup date · equipment · origin + deadhead · destination · trip miles · length/weight · company · credit/pay signals · rate**. Once you can read one, you can read them all, even after a redesign.

#### DAT One

The largest U.S. board. Broker **credit score** and **days to pay**, market rates (RateView), truck postings with alarms, TriHaul route suggestions (higher plans).

#### Truckstop

Needs active carrier authority to search. **Bond backing**, **RMIS** tags, **Book It Now** loads, rate insights and backhaul suggestions.

#### Others

123Loadboard (in your manual) and similar boards, plus brokers’ own apps. Fewer loads on some, but the same columns and the same screening logic.

Features and plan names change often. Check the board’s own site before telling a carrier what a plan includes; never quote prices from memory.

pages.title: The search form
pages.markdown:
Lesson 6.2 · Searching

# The search form

![](/assets/diagrams/m06/form.jpg)

### DAT’s definitions (help centre)

- **Origin** — “where your truck is or will be.”
- **DH-O** — “how far you are willing to drive to get a load.”
- **Destination** — city, state or zones; “leaving it blank is the equivalent to ‘anywhere’.”
- **Weight** — “the maximum cargo weight you can haul.”
- **Search back** — shows loads posted or refreshed in the last X hours.

> **[KEY RULE] Fill it from facts**
>
> Weight = the truck’s confirmed legal max (Module 2). Dates = when the driver is really empty and legal (Module 4). Equipment = what the truck really is. A search built on wishes finds loads you can’t haul.

> **[TRY IT] Try it**
>
> Truck 12 prefers the Southeast. Which destination would you type: blank, “Charlotte, NC”, or “Z3, Z2”? What changes in the results? (Answer at the back.)

### Five search mistakes beginners make

| Mistake | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- |
| **Weight left at the default** | You see loads the truck can’t legally carry and waste calls |
| **Wrong date** | Loads pick up before the driver is empty or legal to drive |
| **“VR” or “any van” for a plain van** | Reefer-only and special loads fill your screen |
| **Huge DH-O from a big market** | Hundreds of far-away loads bury the close ones |
| **Search back of 24 h** | You call on old postings that were covered hours ago |

pages.title: Deadhead circles and zones
pages.markdown:
Lesson 6.2 · Deadhead

# Deadhead circles and zones

![](/assets/diagrams/m06/dhmap.jpg)

### Choosing the circle size

| Situation | DH-O |
| --- | --- |
| Big freight market (Chicago, Dallas, Atlanta) | 25–75 mi |
| Medium city, decent freight | 75–100 mi |
| Rural area / thin board | 100–150+ mi |

Practice guidelines, not rules. The carrier decides how much deadhead it accepts.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Deadhead is unpaid but not free**
>
> Every empty mile costs fuel, driver pay, tyres and hours (Module 4). A load 90 miles away uses nearly 2 hours of the driver’s clock before loading even starts.

> **[FACT] Zones**
>
> A destination of **Z3** covers AL, FL, GA, MS and TN in one search (Module 3). Type several: **Z3, Z2**.

pages.title: The results screen
pages.markdown:
Lesson 6.2 · Results

# The results screen

![](/assets/diagrams/m06/board.jpg)
![](/assets/diagrams/m06/columns.jpg)

pages.title: Open a load before you call
pages.markdown:
Lesson 6.2 · Load details

# Open a load before you call

![](/assets/diagrams/m06/detail.jpg)

### The 20-second pre-call check

1. **Fit:** equipment, length, weight, commodity.
2. **Time:** pickup window vs truck availability; delivery if shown.
3. **Lane:** direction, zones, next-load market.
4. **Money:** posted rate ÷ total miles vs carrier minimum.
5. **Broker:** credit score, days to pay, reviews, MC.

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Say it out loud — drill 8: the first 15 seconds**
>
> **“Hi, this is Jawad with Blue Line Transport, MC 1298456. I’m calling about your load LL-448210, Chicago to Charlotte, picking up Wednesday. Is it still available?”**  
>   
> If yes: **“Great. What’s the commodity and weight, and what are the pickup and delivery appointments?”** Rate comes after the facts (Module 8).

pages.title: Will this broker pay — and how fast?
pages.markdown:
Lesson 6.3 · Broker signals

# Will this broker pay — and how fast?

### DAT signals

| Signal | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Credit score (CS)** | DAT’s credit rating for the company, calculated with Equifax from days-to-pay trends, collections, bankruptcy alerts and other data. Higher is better; new brokers may have no score. |
| **Days to pay (DTP)** | Average days the company takes to pay invoices. Around 30 is normal; 45–60+ is slow. |
| **Reviews** | Star ratings from carriers. |

### Truckstop signals

| Signal | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Bond backing** | Shows the broker’s surety bond status |
| **RMIS verification** | Broker uses RMIS onboarding |
| **Factorable / new / private** | Load tags: can the carrier’s factor buy this invoice? |
| **Rate insights** | Pricing context before you call |

**Real Truckstop search** (your manual): Charlotte → anywhere and Ontario, CA → AZ, with rate, Book It Now, company, O-DH/D-DH, distance and weight columns.

> **[KEY RULE] Ask your factoring company**
>
> If the carrier factors, the factor may refuse to buy invoices from low-credit brokers. Many factors offer a **broker credit check**. Check it before booking a load from an unfamiliar broker.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Signals are not verification**
>
> A good score doesn’t prove the person on the phone really works for that broker. Identity theft and double brokering are covered in Module 8.

pages.title: Posting trucks and alarms
pages.markdown:
Lesson 6.4 · Posting

# Posting trucks and alarms

![](/assets/diagrams/m06/post.jpg)

### When to post

- As soon as you know when and where the truck will be empty, ideally the day before.
- Post each truck separately with its real details.
- Update the posting if the time or location changes; remove it when booked.

> **[FACT] What happens next**
>
> Brokers searching for trucks see your posting and call or email. Be ready to answer: the truck’s location, availability, equipment, and a rate. Keep the carrier’s minimum in mind (Module 7).

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] When a broker calls about your posting**
>
> **“Blue Line Transport, this is Jawad.”** Broker: “I see your truck in Joliet. I have a load to Atlanta.”  
> **“Sure. What’s the pickup location and time, the delivery appointment, the commodity and weight?”** Then: **“What are you paying on it?”** If it works, get the load details in writing before committing.

|  | Searching loads | Posting trucks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Who calls** | You call the broker | The broker calls you |
| **Speed** | Fast when the board is busy | Slower; works while you do other things |
| **Use it when** | Always, first | Thin markets, odd equipment, late nights, and always as a backup |

pages.title: A search routine and good habits
pages.markdown:
Lesson 6.4 · Discipline

# A search routine and good habits

![](/assets/diagrams/m06/routine.jpg)

| Habit | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **One saved search per truck** | Refresh with one click; alarms work per search or posting |
| **Short search-back (2–4 h)** | Old postings are often covered; fresh ones get answered |
| **Sort by age or pickup** | See new loads first; don’t scroll randomly |
| **Blank destination, then zones** | See everything, then narrow to the carrier’s preferred regions |
| **Note every call** | Load ID, broker, contact, offer, answer: you will call again |
| **Widen slowly** | Increase DH-O or zones only if the board is thin |

> **[FACT] Your clock vs their clock**
>
> When it is **8:00 AM in Chicago (CT)**, it is **6:00 PM in Pakistan** during U.S. daylight time (March–November) and **7:00 PM** in winter. Many brokers post fresh loads at the start of their business day, so the first two hours of your shift matter most.

> **[KEY RULE] Friday rule of thumb**
>
> On Friday, brokers post loads for Monday pickup. If a truck will be empty over the weekend, search Monday pickups on Friday and ask the carrier if the driver is taking a weekend break.

pages.title: The funnel: screen fast, call few
pages.markdown:
Lesson 6.4 · Screening

# The funnel: screen fast, call few

![](/assets/diagrams/m06/funnel.jpg)

### The five-filter scan (per load, ~10 seconds)

1. **Can we haul it?** Equipment, weight, length, hazmat.
2. **Can we get there?** Deadhead, pickup date and time, hours.
3. **Can we deliver it?** Appointment feasible (Module 4).
4. **Does it go somewhere good?** Lane, carrier preference, next load.
5. **Is it worth calling?** Rate per total mile, broker signals.

> **[KEY RULE] Call in order**
>
> Call the best load first, but have the second and third ready. If the first is gone, you lose seconds, not the evening.

### Worked example: three loads through the five filters

| Filter | Load 1 · Chicago → Charlotte | Load 5 · Aurora → Memphis | Load 11 · Chicago → Birmingham |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1 Haul it?** | V, 53 ft, 42,000 lb OK | 46,500 lb > 44,500 STOP | VA = air-ride required STOP |
| **2 Get there?** | 40 mi DH, Wed OK | — | — |
| **3 Deliver it?** | Thu FCFS 8–4 ET OK | — | — |
| **4 Good lane?** | Southeast OK | — | — |
| **5 Worth calling?** | $2.56/total mi, CS 96 CALL | — | — |

Stop at the first failed filter. Two of these three loads take two seconds each.

pages.title: Backhauls and triangles
pages.markdown:
Lesson 6.4 · Beyond one load

# Backhauls and triangles

![](/assets/diagrams/m06/triangle.jpg)

### Search the next leg first

Before booking Joliet → Charlotte, run a quick search: **Charlotte (DH-O 75) → Z4, Z6** for Thursday or Friday. Many decent loads back toward the Midwest means the truck is well placed. Few or cheap loads means you should value the outbound load lower, or pick a different destination.

> **[FACT] Tools that help**
>
> DAT’s guide describes **TriHaul** (DAT One Pro), which suggests triangular routes to reduce deadhead. Truckstop highlights backhauls to reduce deadhead. Rate history tools (DAT RateView) come in Module 7.

### Headhaul, backhaul, triangle

| Term | Meaning | For Truck 12 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Headhaul** | A lane with lots of freight and fewer trucks: rates are usually stronger | Depends on the market that week: check, don’t assume |
| **Backhaul** | The return direction, often with more trucks than loads: rates are usually weaker | A load back toward Joliet after the Southeast run |
| **Triangle** | Three legs instead of an out-and-back, to avoid a weak return lane | Joliet → Charlotte → Atlanta → Midwest |

> **[TRY IT] Try it**
>
> Truck 12 books Load 7 to Jacksonville, FL. Write the next search. (Suggested: origin Jacksonville, DH-O 75, destination Z4, Z6 or blank, van, full, 53 ft, 44,500 lb, delivery day + 1. Check the load count before booking the outbound leg.)

**p.6.**

Blank = all destinations: most results, including bad lanes. “Charlotte, NC” = only near Charlotte (DH-D). “Z3, Z2” = the whole Southeast (AL, FL, GA, MS, TN, MD, NC, SC, VA, WV). Best for this carrier’s preference.

**1.**

It is only an advertisement. Details and rates can change; the deal is made by phone, email or book-now, and is binding only with a signed rate confirmation.

**2.**

Deadhead to origin / from destination. Too high = more loads, but more unpaid miles and hours.

**3.**

Anywhere. Use zones: Z3 (and Z2).

**4.**

Time since posted or refreshed. Old loads are often covered; fresh loads get booked quickly.

**5.**

Creditworthiness from days-to-pay trends, collections, bankruptcies (via Equifax). DTP = average days to pay.

**6.**

$1,800 ÷ 750 = **$2.40** per total mile.

**7.**

Brokers searching trucks (including for unposted freight) can find and call you.

**8.**

Remove or update it immediately.

**9.**

Can we haul it? Get there? Deliver it? Does it go somewhere good? Is it worth calling (rate, broker)?

**10.**

A good outbound load into a dead market can lose money on the next leg. Knowing the reload options sets its real value.

**11.**

Any three: bond backing, RMIS verification, factorable / new / private tags, rate insights, broker ratings.

**12.**

Possible fraud or bait. Verify identity and authority carefully (Module 8), check with the factor, or skip it.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.markdown:
Reference

# Glossary

**Age** — Time since a posting was created or refreshed.

**Alarm / alert** — Notification when new matching loads appear.

**Backhaul** — Load that brings the truck back toward home or a good market.

**Book now** — Book online without a call; still produces a rate confirmation.

**Credit score (CS)** — DAT broker credit rating.

**DH-O / DH-D** — Deadhead to origin / from destination.

**Days to pay (DTP)** — Average payment time.

**Factorable** — Load whose invoice a factor will buy.

**F / P** — Full or partial load.

**Load board** — Online marketplace of loads and trucks.

**Post a truck** — Advertise available capacity.

**Private loads** — Loads visible only to selected carriers.

**Rate per mile** — Rate ÷ miles (loaded, or total including deadhead).

**Reference ID** — The broker’s load number on the board.

**Saved search** — Stored search criteria for quick refresh.

**Search back** — Only show loads posted in the last X hours.

**Trip** — Loaded miles from pickup to delivery.

**TriHaul** — DAT tool suggesting triangular routes.

**Zone** — Region code (Z0–Z9) for searches.

### Board codes you’ll see (DAT)

| Code | Meaning | Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **V** | Van (dry van) | **F** | Flatbed |
| **VA** | Van with air-ride | **SD** | Step deck |
| **VM** | Van with team | **R** | Reefer |
| **VC** | Van with curtains (curtainside) | **VR** | Van or reefer: either can haul it |
| **MV** | Moving van | **F / P** | Full or partial load |

Codes follow Module 2. Boards add and rename types; hover or open the equipment list on the board to confirm.

# How to use this module

In Module 6 you screened loads against Mike’s minimum of **$2.40 per total mile**. Where did that number come from, and is it still right? This module teaches you to **build the number yourself** and to judge a whole week, not a single load.

### Truck 12’s money facts (practice)

#### Blue Line Transport · Truck 12

Fixed costs **$1,300 a week** (truck + trailer payments, insurance, ELD, phone, board seat) · driver Carlos paid **$0.60 a mile** · **6.5 mpg** · repairs, tyres, tolls **$0.26 a mile** · runs about **2,500 total miles a week** · dispatch fee **6%** · factoring **3%**.

These are practice numbers for learning. A real carrier gives you its own, or you build them together (Lesson 7.1).

### Study rhythm (about 6 hours)

- **Session 1 (1.5 h):** cost per mile, fixed vs variable, fuel.
- **Session 2 (1.5 h):** break-even, minimum rate, the rate con.
- **Session 3 (1 h):** rate tools, load-to-truck, seasons.
- **Session 4 (2 h):** rate per day, the week plan, drill 9, practice.

> **[KEY RULE] Bring a calculator**
>
> Every page has numbers. Do the math yourself before you read the answer. Speed comes from repetition.

Contents

> **[FACT] Carrier-side, always**

pages.title: “Is $2,050 a good rate?” It depends. On what, exactly?
pages.markdown:
7

Module 7 · Load economics

“Is $2,050 a good rate?”  
It depends. On what, exactly?

On what the truck costs to run, what diesel costs this week, what the lane usually pays, how many days the load takes, and where it leaves the truck. By the end of this module you’ll answer with numbers, not feelings.

pages.title: Where the money goes
pages.markdown:
Lesson 7.1 · Cost per mile

# Where the money goes

![](/assets/diagrams/m07/cost_stack.jpg)

### Cost per mile, in one line

**Cost per mile = all costs for a period ÷ all miles in that period**, loaded and empty. If Truck 12 spends $5,900 in a week and runs 2,500 miles, it costs **$2.36 a mile**.

Use **total miles**: an empty mile burns the same fuel and pays the same driver as a loaded one.

> **[FACT] ATRI benchmark (real data)**
>
> The American Transportation Research Institute surveys carriers every year. For 2025 it reported an average **$2.336 per mile**, a record, and **$1.854** without fuel. Driver wages were 81.8¢ and repairs 21.5¢ a mile. Use it to sanity-check a carrier’s numbers, not as their numbers.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “Every carrier costs about $2 a mile”**
>
> Cost depends on the truck payment, the driver pay, insurance, fuel price and miles run. Two trucks on the same lane can differ by 50¢ a mile. Always use the carrier’s own numbers.

pages.markdown:
Lesson 7.1 · Fixed vs variable

# Truck 12’s cost sheet

| Fixed (per week) | $ / week | $ / mile\* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Truck payment | 600 | 0.24 |
| Trailer payment | 200 | 0.08 |
| Insurance (liability, cargo, physical damage) | 350 | 0.14 |
| ELD, phone, board seat, permits, accounting | 150 | 0.06 |
| **Total fixed** | **1,300** | **0.52** |

\*At 2,500 total miles a week.

| Variable (per mile) | $ / mile |
| --- | --- |
| Fuel ($6.38 ÷ 6.5 mpg) | 0.98 |
| Driver pay (Carlos) | 0.60 |
| Repairs & maintenance | 0.18 |
| Tyres | 0.05 |
| Tolls & misc. | 0.03 |
| **Total variable** | **1.84** |

**Operating cost = $0.52 + $1.84 = $2.36 a mile.**

![](/assets/diagrams/m07/fixed_var.jpg)
> **[KEY RULE] Idle days are expensive**
>
> Fixed costs don’t stop on weekends or when a truck waits for a load. Keeping the truck moving lowers the cost of every mile. That’s why rate per day matters (Lesson 7.5).

pages.title: Fuel: the swing cost
pages.markdown:
Lesson 7.2 · Diesel

# Fuel: the swing cost

![](/assets/diagrams/m07/diesel.jpg)

### Fuel per mile

**Fuel cost per mile = diesel price ÷ mpg.** A heavy 53′ van usually gets about 6–7 mpg. Hills, speed, weight, weather and idling change it. The carrier knows its real number from fuel receipts and the ELD or fuel card.

Each **$1.00** rise in diesel adds about **15¢ a mile** at 6.5 mpg (1 ÷ 6.5 = $0.154). On 2,500 miles that’s about **$385 a week**.

> **[FACT] Where to check**
>
> **EIA Gasoline and Diesel Fuel Update**, published every week for the U.S. and by region. Week of 28 Sep 2026: **$6.382**, against **$3.754** a year earlier.

> **[REAL-WORLD TIP] Pakistan tip**
>
> Put the EIA page in your Monday routine, just like the load board. When diesel moves more than about 25¢, tell the carrier and re-check the minimum rate together.

pages.title: How fuel gets paid
pages.markdown:
Lesson 7.2 · Fuel surcharge

# How fuel gets paid

![](/assets/diagrams/m07/fsc.jpg)

### Worked example

A broker offers **“$1,400 linehaul plus fuel”** for 700 loaded miles and uses DAT’s method: ($6.382 − $1.25) ÷ 6.0 = $0.855 a mile.

Fuel = 700 × $0.855 = **$599**. All-in = $1,400 + $599 = **$1,999** = $2.86 per loaded mile. If deadhead is 50 miles: $1,999 ÷ 750 = **$2.67 per total mile**.

> **[KEY RULE] Always convert to all-in**
>
> Compare loads on the **all-in total ÷ total miles**. Two brokers can say “$1,400” and mean very different money.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Get it in writing**
>
> If the rate is “linehaul + FSC”, the rate confirmation must show how fuel is paid: a fixed amount, or the formula and the diesel price week. Otherwise the carrier may be paid only the linehaul.

### What a rate can include

| Part | Meaning | Module |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Linehaul** | Pay for moving the load from A to B, without fuel | This module |
| **Fuel surcharge** | Extra pay that follows the diesel price | This module |
| **Accessorials** | Detention, layover, lumper, extra stops, TONU | Module 10 |
| **Deductions** | Money taken off for broken rules (tracking, late POD) | Next pages · Module 9 |

pages.title: Break-even and minimum rate
pages.markdown:
Lesson 7.3 · Break-even

# Break-even and minimum rate

![](/assets/diagrams/m07/breakeven.jpg)

### Three numbers every dispatcher knows

| Number | Truck 12 |
| --- | --- |
| **Operating cost** | $2.36 per total mile |
| **Break-even** | $2.59: below this, every mile loses money |
| **Target minimum** | $2.70: break-even plus the carrier’s profit cushion |

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Why not just add 9%?**
>
> $2.36 + 9% = $2.57, which is too low. The fees are 9% of the **rate**, not of the cost. At $2.57 the fees are 23¢ and the carrier keeps $2.34, less than cost. Dividing by 0.91 fixes it.

> **[KEY RULE] The carrier sets the minimum**
>
> You calculate and explain. Mike decides his profit cushion and when to accept less for a good reason.

### Truck 12 break-even at different diesel prices and miles

| Diesel ($/gal) | Fuel / mi | 2,000 mi / week | 2,500 mi / week | 3,000 mi / week |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $4.50 | $0.69 | $2.42 | $2.27 | $2.18 |
| $5.00 | $0.77 | $2.51 | $2.36 | $2.27 |
| $5.50 | $0.85 | $2.59 | $2.45 | $2.36 |
| $6.00 | $0.92 | $2.67 | $2.53 | $2.43 |
| **$6.38 (Sep 2026)** | **$0.98** | $2.74 | **$2.59** | $2.50 |
| $7.00 | $1.08 | $2.85 | $2.70 | $2.61 |

Practice numbers: $1,300 fixed a week, $0.86 other variable costs a mile, 6.5 mpg, 9% fees. Print this table for your carrier and update it when costs change.

pages.title: Per loaded mile vs per total mile
pages.markdown:
Lesson 7.3 · Using it

# Per loaded mile vs per total mile

Load boards and rate tools show rates per **loaded** (trip) mile. Your break-even is per **total** mile. Convert before you compare:

**Rate per total mile** = all-in rate ÷ (deadhead + loaded miles)

**Load 1:** $2,050 ÷ 760 loaded = $2.70 “on the board”. With 40 deadhead: $2,050 ÷ 800 = **$2.56**. That’s 3¢ under break-even.

### The other direction: what should I ask for?

**Ask = target × total miles.** Load 1: $2.70 × 800 = **$2,160**. Walk-away (break-even): $2.59 × 800 = **$2,072**.

> **[REAL-WORLD TIP] The $2.40 story**
>
> Mike set $2.40 in spring, when diesel was about $5.00. Break-even then was **$2.36**, so $2.40 left 4¢. Diesel went to $6.38 and break-even became $2.59. Nobody updated the minimum, and Truck 12 started losing about 19¢ on every “minimum” mile.

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Tell the carrier early**
>
> **“Mike, with diesel at $6.38 our break-even on Truck 12 is about $2.59 a mile. Our $2.40 minimum now loses money. Can we set a new minimum around $2.70?”**
