pages.title: Read the rate con for money
pages.markdown:
Lesson 7.3 · Real document

# Read the rate con for money

![](/assets/diagrams/m07/rc_annot.jpg)

> **[CHECKLIST] Money checklist for any rate con**
>
> 1. All-in total, or linehaul + fuel?
> 2. Miles shown: loaded only?
> 3. Accessorials listed (detention, lumper, TONU)?
> 4. Deductions and fines in the notes?
> 5. Payment terms: days, quick-pay fee, factor’s address?

> **[FACT] Fees that come off the top**
>
> **Factoring:** commonly about 1.5–3% (recourse) or 2.5–5% (non-recourse) per invoice, plus possible transfer and same-day fees (FreightWaves). **Dispatch:** often 5–10% of gross; 6–7% is common for vans (industry guides). Truck 12 uses 3% and 6%.

### Follow Load 1’s $2,050 to the carrier’s pocket

| Step | Amount | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rate confirmation, all-in | $2,050.00 | Chicago → Charlotte, 760 loaded + 40 deadhead |
| − Factoring 3% | − $61.50 | Paid within a day or two instead of waiting for the broker |
| − Dispatch 6% | − $123.00 | Your employer’s fee (or your pay) |
| **= Carrier keeps** | **$1,865.50** | 91% of the rate |
| − Cost of 800 miles at $2.36 | − $1,888.00 | Fuel, driver, repairs + share of weekly fixed costs |
| **= Result** | **− $22.50** | A small loss: why you counter toward $2,160 |

pages.title: What is the lane really paying?
pages.markdown:
Lesson 7.4 · Market rates

# What is the lane really paying?

![](/assets/diagrams/m07/rateview.jpg)

### How to read a lane range

- **Below the low end:** the posted rate is weak. Counter with confidence.
- **Around the average:** fair. Negotiate a little, decide on the whole trip.
- **Above the high end:** strong, or something is unusual (urgent load, hard pickup, fraud: check Module 8).

Rate tools usually need a paid subscription. Many carriers give their dispatcher access with the board seat.

> **[KEY RULE] Spot vs contract**
>
> **Spot** = one load, priced today, broker to carrier. **Contract** = rates agreed for months between shipper and carrier. You mostly work spot. DAT reports both, and they can move in different directions.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Don’t quote from memory**
>
> Rates change every week. Never tell a carrier “Chicago to Charlotte pays $2.60” from last month. Look it up again.

### No rate tool? Four other ways to judge a rate

| Method | How | Watch out |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Compare similar posts** | Search the same lane and day; note posted rates on 3–5 comparable loads | Many loads post without a rate |
| **Your own history** | Your load economics cards for that lane over the last weeks | Old weeks may not match today |
| **Board market data** | Many boards show lane averages or rate insights beside the load | Check the date range and whether fuel is included |
| **Ask the broker** | “What’s your budget on this one?”, then counter from your numbers (Module 8) | Their first number is rarely their best |

Lesson 7.4 · Supply and demand

# Hot markets, cold markets

![](/assets/diagrams/m07/ltr.jpg)

### National snapshot (for context only)

| DAT, August 2026 | Spot linehaul | Fuel surcharge | ≈ Spot all-in | Contract linehaul |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Van** | $2.19 | $0.70 | $2.89 | $2.41 |
| **Reefer** | $2.61 | $0.77 | $3.38 | $2.65 |

Per loaded mile, national averages. “All-in” = linehaul + surcharge, added for this course. DAT called August’s 20¢ van drop the steepest August pullback on record.

> **[REAL-WORLD TIP] What this means for Truck 12**
>
> A national van average of about $2.89 per loaded mile is only about **$2.51 per total mile** once you add 15% deadhead. That’s below Truck 12’s $2.59 break-even. In a soft market with expensive diesel, lane choice and negotiation decide whether the week makes money.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Averages hide lanes**
>
> Some lanes pay far above the national average and some far below. Use the national number to understand the market’s mood. Use lane tools for real decisions.

pages.title: The freight year
pages.markdown:
Lesson 7.4 · Seasons

# The freight year

![](/assets/diagrams/m07/season.jpg)

### Questions seasons help you ask

- Is it produce season in the destination? (Reefers get scarce; van rates can rise too.)
- Is a holiday coming? (Plan pickups before docks close; expect a slow day after.)
- Is it quarter-end? (Shippers push volume in the last days.)
- Is weather coming? (Hurricane or winter storm: add time and ask about delays.)

> **[FACT] Roadcheck 2026**
>
> CVSA’s International Roadcheck ran **12–14 May 2026**: 72 hours of North American roadside inspections. Some drivers take those days off, so capacity can tighten briefly.

> **[KEY RULE] Weekly rhythm too**
>
> Mondays often bring fresh freight; Friday afternoons bring loads for Monday; weekends are thin in many markets. Watch your own board to learn your lanes.

pages.markdown:
Lesson 7.5 · Lane planning

# Plan the week, not the load

![](/assets/diagrams/m07/plans.jpg)

All three plans start with Truck 12 empty in Joliet on Wednesday morning. Each has a first load from the Module 6 board and a practice reload. **Before you read the next page**, decide which plan you would pitch to Mike, and why.

| Plan | Wednesday | Thursday | Friday | Weekend |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | Load 1, drive toward Charlotte | Deliver ~noon ET; wait | Reload Charlotte → Indianapolis | Deliver Sat |
| **B** | Load 7, drive south | Drive | Deliver Jacksonville; reload | Deliver Nashville Sat/Sun |
| **C** | Load 2, drive to Atlanta | Deliver AM; reload Atlanta PM | Deliver Columbus ~noon | Free for a short load or restart |

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] A reload you found is not booked**
>
> Plan C depends on the Atlanta load still being there on Thursday. Ask the broker if you can book it now, or keep two backups. A plan is only as good as its weakest leg.

> **[CHECKLIST] What the numbers don’t show**
>
> Broker credit and days to pay (Module 6), appointment risk, weather, the driver’s home time, and whether the carrier wants to be in that area. Ask Mike before you decide.

pages.title: Per mile, per day, per week
pages.markdown:
Lesson 7.5 · Rate per day

# Per mile, per day, per week

![](/assets/diagrams/m07/perday.jpg)

### Rate per day

**Revenue per day = trip revenue ÷ days the truck is committed**, from dispatch until it is empty again and ready.

Truck 12 needs about **$6,500 a week** (2,500 mi × $2.59) to break even, which is about **$1,300 per working day** over five days.

| Plan | Margin vs break-even | Hours used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | −$144 | ~34 of 40 |
| B | −$498 | ~40 of 40 |
| C | +$35 and 8 h left for a short load | ~32 of 40 |

Margin = revenue − (total miles × $2.59).

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “Always take the highest rate per mile”**
>
> Short loads with high per-mile rates can pay less per day. Long loads into weak markets can look rich and still lose the week. Measure **per total mile**, **per day** and **where the truck ends up**.

> **[KEY RULE] Hours are money too**
>
> Plan B uses all 40 of Carlos’s remaining hours (Module 4). Plan C leaves room for one more short load before a 34-hour restart.

pages.title: Pitch the plan to the carrier
pages.markdown:
Lesson 7.5 · Talking money

# Pitch the plan to the carrier

### What a good pitch contains

1. **The load:** lane, miles, pickup and delivery.
2. **The money:** offered rate, your counter, rate per total mile.
3. **The comparison:** against break-even and the market.
4. **The reason:** the next leg, days, hours, where the truck ends.
5. **The question:** “Do you want me to book it?”

> **[KEY RULE] The carrier decides**
>
> Never book below the carrier’s minimum without asking. Some carriers let you book above target on your own: get that permission in writing (Module 1 dispatch agreement).

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Say it out loud · drill 9: pitching a plan**
>
> **“Mike, I have Bolingbrook to Atlanta, 715 miles, 12 empty, picks up Wednesday at 9, delivers Thursday at 1. The broker offered $1,600. I got them to $1,750, which is $2.41 a mile, under our $2.59 break-even by itself. But Atlanta is strong: I have a Thursday reload to Columbus for $1,700, so the two loads average $2.62, and Carlos is back near home Friday with hours left. Do you want me to book both?”**

> **[TRY IT] Your turn**
>
> Write and say the pitch for **Plan A**. Be honest that the trip averages $2.49, 10¢ under break-even, and suggest what you would try to improve it.

### Words that make money talk clear

| Say | Instead of |
| --- | --- |
| “$2.56 per total mile” | “good money” / “decent rate” |
| “3 cents under break-even” | “a bit low” |
| “$1,380 a day for 2.5 days” | “quick load” |
| “Atlanta shows many outbound loads today” | “Atlanta is always hot” |

pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers: practice

**1.**

Fixed $1,500 ÷ 2,800 = **$0.54**. Fuel $6.38 ÷ 6.0 = $1.06; variable = 1.06 + 0.62 + 0.20 + 0.05 + 0.03 + 0.10 = **$2.06**. Operating = **$2.60**. Break-even = $2.60 ÷ 0.92 = **$2.83**.

**2a.**

Fuel $5.50 ÷ 6.5 = $0.85. Cost = 0.52 + 0.85 + 0.86 = $2.23. ÷ 0.91 = **$2.45**.

**2b.**

Fixed $1,300 ÷ 2,000 = $0.65. Cost = 0.65 + 1.84 = $2.49. ÷ 0.91 = **$2.74**.

**3.**

FSC = (6.38 − 1.25) ÷ 6.0 = **$0.855**/mi. × 700 = **$599**. All-in = **$1,999**. ÷ 750 total mi = **$2.67**, 8¢ above break-even.

**4.**

X: $1,100 ÷ 320 = **$3.44**/total mi, **$1,100**/day. Y: $2,400 ÷ 1,000 = **$2.40**/total mi, **$1,200**/day. Y earns more per day but is below break-even per mile. X is better only if a good reload is ready the next morning; ask about both destinations before choosing.

**5.**

$700 − $150 − $150 = **$400**. Lost $300 = **43%**.

|  | A | B | C |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Revenue | $3,500 | $3,950 | $3,450 |
| Total mi | 1,405 | 1,715 | 1,317 |
| Per total mi | $2.49 | $2.30 | **$2.62** |
| vs $2.59 | −$144 | −$498 | +$35 |
| Days · per day | 3.5 · $1,000 | 4 · $990 | **2.5 · $1,380** |
| Hours | ~34 | ~40 | ~32 |
| Ends | Indianapolis, Sat | Nashville, Sun | Columbus, Fri |
| Rank | 2 | 3 | **1** |

**6.**

Any two: counter Load 1 toward $2,160 (+$110 lifts the trip to $2.57); negotiate the Indianapolis reload up by $150 (with the Load 1 counter too: $3,760 = $2.68); find a Thursday reload instead of Friday to save a day; pick a reload that ends closer to Joliet to cut next week’s deadhead.

**7.**

Example: “At $6.38 diesel Truck 12 costs about $2.36 a mile, and after 9% fees we need $2.59 just to break even. At $2.40 we lose about 19¢ a mile, around $475 on a 2,500-mile week. I suggest a $2.70 minimum and we review it whenever diesel moves 25¢.”

pages.title: Answers: module check
pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers: module check

**1.**

All costs ÷ all miles for a period. Empty miles cost fuel, pay and wear too, so leaving them out makes the truck look cheaper than it is.

**2.**

Fixed: truck payment, trailer payment, insurance, ELD/phone/board seat, permits. Variable: fuel, driver pay per mile, repairs, tyres, tolls.

**3.**

The weekly fixed amount is shared across more miles: $1,300 ÷ 2,000 = $0.65, ÷ 3,000 = $0.43.

**4.**

$5.00 ÷ 6.5 = $0.77 → $6.38 ÷ 6.5 = $0.98: **+21¢** a mile.

**5.**

Break-even = cost per mile ÷ (1 − fee %). Fees are a percentage of the rate, and the rate is the unknown. Adding the fees to the cost undercounts them.

**6.**

$2.36 · $2.59 · $2.70 (practice, diesel $6.38).

**7.**

($6.00 − $1.25) ÷ 6.0 = **$0.79** a mile.

**8.**

All-in = one total that already includes fuel. Linehaul + FSC = base pay plus a separate fuel amount; convert to all-in to compare.

**9.**

The spread of recently reported paid rates (middle 50%) around the average. RateView needs at least 7 records from 3 different companies.

**10.**

Load posts ÷ truck posts for one market and equipment type. Levels differ by market and equipment (flatbed runs much higher than van), so “high” only means high compared with that market’s normal.

**11.**

It leads to a strong reload or good end location; it uses fewer days (more per day); it fits the driver’s hours; it avoids a weak market.

**12.**

$150 if tracking is refused or disabled; $150 if POD is not sent within 72 hours. $300 total.

> **[FACT] Try-it answer (page 17)**
>
> Plan A pitch example: “Mike, Plan A is Load 1 to Charlotte for $2,050, then Charlotte to Indianapolis Friday for $1,450. Together that’s $3,500 on 1,405 miles, $2.49 a mile, about 10¢ under break-even. I’d try to get Load 1 up to $2,160 and look for a Thursday reload. Do you want me to try?”

pages.title: Glossary
pages.markdown:
Reference

# Glossary

**All-in rate** — One total that includes fuel.

**Break-even** — Rate per total mile where revenue after fees equals cost.

**Contract rate** — Rate agreed for months between shipper and carrier.

**Cost per mile** — All costs ÷ all miles in a period.

**Deduction** — Money taken off the pay for a broken rule.

**Dispatch fee** — Dispatcher’s pay, often a % of gross.

**EIA** — U.S. Energy Information Administration; publishes weekly diesel prices.

**Factoring** — Selling invoices for fast pay, for a fee (recourse / non-recourse).

**Fixed cost** — Paid every week regardless of miles.

**Fuel surcharge (FSC)** — Pay that follows the diesel price.

**Headhaul / backhaul** — Strong direction / weaker return direction.

**Linehaul** — Base rate without fuel.

**Load-to-truck ratio** — Load posts ÷ truck posts, per market and equipment.

**Market Conditions** — DAT’s hot/cold supply-demand map.

**Operating cost** — Fixed + variable cost per mile.

**Rate per day** — Trip revenue ÷ days the truck is committed.

**Rate per total mile** — All-in rate ÷ (deadhead + loaded).

**RateView** — DAT’s tool for recent paid lane rates.

**Spot rate** — One-off price for a single load.

**Target minimum** — Break-even plus the carrier’s profit cushion.

**Variable cost** — Grows with each mile.

**Walk-away rate** — Lowest rate you’d accept: usually break-even.

### Formula card

| What | Formula | Truck 12 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed per mile | weekly fixed ÷ weekly total miles | $1,300 ÷ 2,500 = $0.52 |
| Fuel per mile | diesel price ÷ mpg | $6.38 ÷ 6.5 = $0.98 |
| Operating cost | fixed per mile + variable per mile | $2.36 |
| Break-even | operating cost ÷ (1 − fee %) | $2.36 ÷ 0.91 = $2.59 |
| Target minimum | (cost + profit per mile) ÷ (1 − fee %) | $2.46 ÷ 0.91 = $2.70 |
| Fuel surcharge (DAT method) | (EIA diesel − $1.25) ÷ mpg | ($6.38 − 1.25) ÷ 6 = $0.86 |
| Rate per total mile | all-in ÷ (deadhead + loaded) | $2,050 ÷ 800 = $2.56 |
| Ask price | target × total miles | $2.70 × 800 = $2,160 |
| Revenue per day | trip revenue ÷ days committed | $3,450 ÷ 2.5 = $1,380 |

pages.title: Freight fraud: what you’re up against
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.1 · The problem

# Freight fraud: what you’re up against

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/theft.jpg)

### Six schemes that hit carriers and dispatchers

| Scheme | How it works | How the carrier loses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Double brokering** | A load is re-sold, often by someone using a stolen carrier or broker identity | Hauls it and never gets paid |
| **Broker impersonation** | Fake emails and phones copy a real broker’s name | Unpaid load, stolen packet, or worse |
| **Carrier identity theft** | Criminals use *your* carrier’s MC/DOT to book loads and steal freight | Claims, police calls, blocked by brokers |
| **Fictitious pickup** | A fake carrier picks up real freight and disappears | Brokers tighten rules; honest carriers get more checks |
| **Phishing** | “Load details” links steal board, email or factoring logins | Account takeover, diverted payments |
| **Payment diversion** | Fake NOA or bank-change letters redirect the broker’s payment | The money goes to the thief |

pages.title: How a “normal” load goes unpaid
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.1 · Double brokering

# How a “normal” load goes unpaid

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/dbl.jpg)

### Why it works

Everyone in the chain sees something normal: a shipper hands over freight, a truck shows up, the load delivers. The only one who notices is the carrier, weeks later, when the invoice bounces between companies that don’t know each other.

The fix is upstream: **vet the broker before booking** (Lesson 8.2) and **check the BOL at pickup** (page 11).

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “Re-brokering is fine if everyone gets paid”**
>
> If you are a carrier (or its dispatcher), you haul the loads you accept. Handing a load to another carrier is brokering. Without broker registration and the $75,000 security it is unlawful, whether or not everyone gets paid.

> **[KEY RULE] One test**
>
> If the shipper’s paperwork, the broker on your rate con and the company that calls you don’t all line up, stop and verify before the truck moves.

### Protect your carrier’s identity

| Habit | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Lock the FMCSA login** | The owner keeps the FMCSA/Motus login private with multi-factor authentication; thieves change contact details to hijack authority |
| **One official email and phone** | Keep them current on the FMCSA record and tell brokers to trust only those |
| **Use identity platforms** | Setup platforms such as Highway let brokers confirm they are dealing with the real carrier |
| **Watch for strange calls** | A broker asking about a load you never booked = possible identity theft. Tell the carrier the same day |
| **Don’t post documents publicly** | MC certificate, COI and W-9 go only to verified brokers, never to social media groups |

pages.title: Real broker or copy?
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.1 · Impersonation

# Real broker or copy?

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/emails.jpg)

### Protect your own accounts

- Turn on **multi-factor authentication** for email, load boards and the factoring portal.
- Never open “rate con” or “load details” links from unknown senders. Log in to the platform yourself.
- Never share login codes, even with someone claiming to be “support”.
- Send carrier documents only through setup platforms or verified addresses.

> **[FACT] FMCSA’s advice**
>
> FMCSA says to confirm broker and carrier phone numbers using SAFER, remember that “even insurance certificates can be fraudulent,” and stop if someone asks you to misrepresent your company, proposes blind loads, offers unusually high rates or pressures a quick deal.

> **[REAL-WORLD TIP] Your carrier can be impersonated too**
>
> If a broker calls asking about a load you never booked, someone may be using Blue Line’s MC. Tell Mike immediately. Carriers can warn brokers through setup platforms and report it to FMCSA.

pages.title: Twelve red flags
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.1 · Red flags

# Twelve red flags

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/flags.jpg)

### The “two flags” rule

One flag has innocent explanations: a new broker has to start somewhere, and a hot load can pay well. **Two or more flags together**, like brand-new authority with a gmail address and a rate $300 above the rest, is the classic fraud pattern. Stop and tell the carrier.

| Flags | Action |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | Normal checks, book |
| 1 | Verify that point on an official channel |
| 2+ | Stop · tell the carrier · probably pass |

> **[CHECKLIST] Brokers check carriers, too**
>
> Brokers use setup platforms and monitoring services (like the Carrier411 screen on page 3) to vet carriers, looking at authority age, insurance, safety, and reports such as “cancelled after accepting load”. Every cancellation you cause can follow your carrier.

> **[KEY RULE] Stay polite**
>
> “I just need to verify a couple of things before we book” is normal business. Real brokers respect it. Fraudsters push back or disappear.

### Innocent explanation or fraud pattern?

| Flag | Could be innocent | Fraud pattern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **High rate** | Late load, hard pickup, holiday, tight market; the broker explains why | High rate + new broker + pressure; no clear reason |
| **New authority** | New office of an experienced team; normal contacts, platform setup | New + free email + cell only + unusual payment instructions |
| **Pickup change** | Broker updates the rate con and the shipper confirms | Change by phone only; “meet at a truck stop”; new consignee |
| **New bank details** | Carrier switched factors, with an NOA release letter | Email-only change, urgent, different company name on the account |

pages.title: Vetting a broker in seven steps
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.2 · The check

# Vetting a broker in seven steps

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/vetting.jpg)

### Where each check happens

| Check | Where |
| --- | --- |
| 1–2 Authority, bond | FMCSA SAFER and L&I (free, public) |
| 3 Contact | Broker’s website, SAFER, board profile |
| 4 History | SAFER/L&I dates, board reviews, your notes |
| 5 Credit | DAT credit score and days to pay, factor’s check |
| 6 Tools | Highway for Carriers (free), board profile |
| 7 Rate con | The document itself, against all of the above |

> **[FACT] Highway for Carriers**
>
> Launched in March 2025 and free for carriers. Search a broker by name, MC or DOT to confirm authority, activity and credit standing, and see potential fraud risks. Carriers also use it for broker setups (Module 5).

> **[KEY RULE] Save what you learn**
>
> Keep a simple broker list: name, MC, official phone, email domain, pay speed, notes. It turns 5 minutes into 30 seconds next time.

pages.title: Reading a broker’s record
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.2 · FMCSA records

# Reading a broker’s record

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/safer_b.jpg)

### Carrier record vs broker record

| Field | Carrier (Module 5) | Broker |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entity type | CARRIER | BROKER |
| Authority | Motor carrier of property | Broker of property |
| Money filing | BIPD insurance ($750,000+) | BMC-84 bond or BMC-85 trust ($75,000) |
| Power units | 1 or more | Usually 0 |

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Some companies are both**
>
> A company can hold carrier and broker authority. Check which one applies to **this load**: the rate con should name it as broker, and the broker authority must be active.

> **[REAL-WORLD TIP] Motus changes (Module 5)**
>
> FMCSA is moving registration into Motus and adding USDOT status suffixes for new registrants. Broker MC numbers still appear on existing records. Always use the live FMCSA site.

pages.title: Broker security and unpaid loads
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.2 · The $75,000 rule

# Broker security and unpaid loads

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/bond.jpg)

### If a broker doesn’t pay: the carrier’s escalation ladder

| # | Step | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Check the terms** | Rate con payment terms (for example 30 days), quick-pay option, documents required (signed BOL/POD, invoice) |
| 2 | **Resend and confirm** | Resend invoice and POD to the address on the rate con; ask for the expected pay date in writing |
| 3 | **Factor collections** | If the carrier factors, the factor chases payment; non-recourse terms may cover credit failures |
| 4 | **Bond claim** | Carrier files a claim against the broker’s BMC-84 surety or BMC-85 trust (provider listed on L&I) |
| 5 | **Report** | FMCSA National Consumer Complaint Database; board reviews and credit reports |
| 6 | **Legal** | Carrier’s attorney or a collections agency for larger amounts |

You support the carrier with documents and dates. The carrier (or its factor) owns the claim.

pages.title: The last check: paperwork at the dock
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.2 · At pickup

# The last check: paperwork at the dock

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/bolcheck.jpg)

> **[CHECKLIST] Driver’s 60-second pickup check**
>
> Before leaving the dock the driver sends you a photo of the BOL. You compare: shipper, consignee, commodity, pieces, weight, seal, reference numbers, and **which carrier and broker the shipper expects**.

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] If something doesn’t match**
>
> **“Carlos, please don’t leave yet. The BOL shows 5,729 pounds and our rate con says 2,000. I’m calling the broker now and will call you back in five minutes.”**

### What the driver confirms before the truck moves

| Item | Check against | If different |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shipper name and address | Rate con pickup | Stop; call the broker |
| Carrier and broker the shipper expects | Your carrier and your broker | Stop: possible double brokering |
| Pieces, weight, commodity | Rate con | Call the broker; get the update in writing |
| Seal number | Write it on the BOL; photo | Note any broken or missing seal |
| Delivery address | Rate con consignee | Never change it on a phone call alone |

pages.title: The six-step response
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.3 · When something is wrong

# The six-step response

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/respond.jpg)

### Example: the lookalike email

A “Lakeshore Logistics” rep emails from **lakeshore-logistics-llc.com** asking for your packet. You **stop**, **verify** by calling Lakeshore’s number from its website (they have no such rep), **tell Mike**, **protect** (no documents were sent), **report** to Lakeshore, the load board and FMCSA, and **record** the domain on your do-not-use list.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Don’t play detective**
>
> Don’t confront, threaten or “trap” a suspected fraudster. Stop the transaction, protect the carrier, and report to the proper channels.

> **[KEY RULE] Write it down immediately**
>
> Times, numbers, emails, screenshots. Reports and claims go faster with evidence, and memory fades by the next shift.

### Who to tell, and when

| Who | When |
| --- | --- |
| **The carrier (Mike)** | Always, first, in writing |
| **The real broker** | Someone is impersonating them, or their load is being re-sold |
| **The load board** | Fake postings, fake accounts, phishing through the board |
| **The factor** | Payment redirection, fake NOA, suspicious broker credit |
| **FMCSA NCCDB** | Identity theft, unauthorized brokering, broker non-payment |
| **FBI IC3 / FTC / police** | Money lost, cargo stolen, cyber fraud (the carrier files; you supply evidence) |

pages.title: Stay on the carrier’s side
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.3 · Your legal lines

# Stay on the carrier’s side

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/legal.jpg)

### How to introduce yourself honestly

**“Hi, this is Jawad, dispatcher for Blue Line Transport, MC 1298456.”** If asked where you are: **“I work remotely for Blue Line. Mike, the owner, can be reached at the number on our FMCSA record.”**

Being honest about your role costs you nothing with good brokers and protects your carrier if anyone checks.

> **[FACT] The law in one line**
>
> A person may provide interstate brokerage only if registered as a broker with FMCSA and meeting the financial security requirement (49 U.S.C. 14916). Penalties can reach $10,000 per violation, and officers and principals can be personally liable.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “Dispatchers can share loads between their carriers”**
>
> If you dispatch for two carriers and move a load booked by one to the other, you are acting as a broker. Each carrier books and hauls its own loads.

pages.title: Prepare before you dial
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.4 · Negotiation

# Prepare before you dial

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/prep.jpg)

### Five principles

1. **Facts first, rate second.** Confirm the load details before you talk money (drill 8).
2. **Know your numbers.** Target, walk-away, market range. Say them in dollars.
3. **Anchor with a reason.** Your first number sets the range. Tie it to miles, market or timing.
4. **Move in shrinking steps.** Big first step, smaller after. It signals you are near your limit.
5. **Be ready to walk.** Politely, with an open door: “If it changes, call me.”

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “Always accept the posted rate to win loads”**
>
> Posted rates are often an opening number. Brokers expect carriers to counter, and many lanes have room. Accepting every first offer trains brokers to lowball your carrier.

> **[KEY RULE] Carrier-side, not personal**
>
> You aren’t fighting the broker. You both want the load covered. Your job is to get a fair price for your carrier’s truck, and a respectful tone gets better rates over time.

pages.title: Load 2, step by step
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.4 · A full negotiation

# Load 2, step by step

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/ladder.jpg)

### Say it out loud · drill 10: the negotiation

| Who | Line |
| --- | --- |
| **You** | “Hi, this is Jawad with Blue Line Transport, MC 1298456, calling about your Bolingbrook to Atlanta load for Wednesday. Is it still available?” |
| Broker | “Yes, it is.” |
| **You** | “Great. What’s the commodity and weight, and what are the pickup and delivery appointments?” |
| Broker | “Paper products, 38,500 pounds. Pickup Wednesday 9 to 11, delivery Thursday 1 PM.” |
| **You** | “Okay. What are you paying on it?” |
| Broker | “$1,600.” |
| **You** | “For 727 miles with a same-day pickup I need $2,000. This lane has been running around $2.60 a mile.” *(Then stop talking.)* |
| Broker | “I can go $1,700.” |
| **You** | “Meet me at $1,800 and I’ll book it now.” |
| Broker | “$1,750 is the best I can do.” |
| **You** | “Let me confirm with my carrier. I’ll call you back in five minutes.” |

pages.title: Broker lines and calm answers
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.4 · Tactics

# Broker lines and calm answers

![](/assets/diagrams/m08/lines.jpg)

### Things to trade besides the rate

| Ask | Why it’s worth money |
| --- | --- |
| **Detention terms** | Paid waiting after a set free time (Module 10) |
| **Lumper paid by broker** | Unloading fees can be $100+ |
| **Quick pay terms** | Cash faster, lower or no factoring fee |
| **Extra stop pay** | Each stop costs time and hours |
| **Later pickup / wider window** | Lets the truck finish or rest properly |
| **Backhaul or next load** | Solves the reload problem (Module 7) |

> **[KEY RULE] Silence is a tool**
>
> After you say your number, stop. The first person to fill the silence usually moves. Count to five in your head.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Never bluff about facts**
>
> Don’t invent another offer, a fake appointment or a false truck location. Brokers talk to each other, and one lie costs your carrier more than any single load.

pages.title: Closing the deal cleanly
pages.markdown:
Lesson 8.4 · Closing

# Closing the deal cleanly

### Before you say “send the rate con”

1. **Total, all-in:** “So that’s $1,750 all-in, including fuel?”
2. **Appointments:** pickup and delivery times, FCFS or appointment, time zone.
3. **Details:** commodity, weight, pieces, equipment, tracking app.
4. **Accessorials:** detention after how many hours and at what rate, lumper, TONU.
5. **Payment:** terms, quick pay, where to send invoices.
6. **Carrier approval:** Mike says yes (or the load is within his written limits).
7. **Setup:** broker has (or will get) the packet through its platform.

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] The close**
>
> **“Mike confirmed. We’ll take it at $1,750 all-in. Detention after two hours, and lumper covered by you, correct? Please send the rate confirmation to our dispatch email and the setup link if you need one. Thank you!”**

> **[CHECKLIST] When the rate con arrives**
>
> Read it line by line **before** anyone signs: rate, all-in, dates, addresses, commodity, weight, accessorials, deductions, payment terms, broker name and MC (Module 9 goes deeper). If anything differs from the call, ask for a corrected rate con.

> **[KEY RULE] Walking away well**
>
> **“I understand. I can’t do it under $1,850 today. If it’s still open later, call me at this number.”** Many loads come back an hour later at your price.

### Five negotiation mistakes

| Mistake | Instead |
| --- | --- |
| Asking “what’s your best?” then accepting it | Counter with your number and a reason |
| Negotiating per mile on loaded miles | Talk totals; you know your total-mile math |
| Splitting the difference too early | Shrinking steps: $2,000 → $1,800 → final |
| Agreeing, then “forgetting” detention and lumper | Confirm accessorials before the rate con |
| Booking before the carrier approves | “Let me confirm with my carrier: five minutes.” |

pages.markdown:
Practice

For each broker decide: PASS CAUTION STOP, and write the flag(s) and your next action. All names, domains and details are fictional.

| # | Broker · load | What your checks show | Decision · flags · next action |

| **A** | **Lakeshore Logistics** Load 1 · $2,050 | Broker authority active since 2011 · BMC-84 $75,000, no cancellation · email @lakeshorelogistics.com matches website · office phone matches website and SAFER · CS 96, DTP 28 |  |
| **B** | **Prime Direct Freight LLC** Load 10 · $2,300 | Broker authority granted 3 weeks ago · BMC-84 on file · email primedirectfreight@gmail.com · calls from a cell · rate ~$300 above similar loads · “book in 5 minutes, email me your packet” |  |

### Quick quiz: flag or fine?

| # | Situation | Flag / fine? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | A broker with 10 years of authority pays $150 over the lane average for a same-day pickup, and says why |  |
| 2 | A broker asks you to tell the shipper you are “ABC Transport” instead of Blue Line |  |
| 3 | After booking, the broker texts a new delivery address and asks the driver to go straight there |  |
| 4 | A broker asks for your carrier packet through its Highway setup link |  |
| 5 | An email with “Rate con attached, click to view” comes from an address you don’t know |  |

Answers: 1 fine (explained) · 2 flag: misrepresenting identity · 3 flag: verify with the broker’s official number and a corrected rate con · 4 fine · 5 flag: phishing risk · 6 flag: credit risk, tell Mike

pages.title: Four negotiation role-plays
pages.markdown:
Practice

# Four negotiation role-plays

Prepare each with the prep card (page 14): numbers, alternatives, leverage, non-rate asks. Then practise out loud, and when ready, ask Claude to play the broker.

#### Role-play 1 Posted load, room to push

Load 1 · Chicago → Charlotte · posted $2,050 · 760 loaded + 40 DH · practice lane range $2.45–$2.85 per loaded mile ($1,862–$2,166)

**Your numbers:** Target $2,160 · walk-away $2,072 · anchor about $2,250

#### Role-play 2 Broker calls on your posted truck

Joliet → Nashville · 470 loaded + 15 DH · broker offers $1,150 ($2.37 per total mile) · pickup today 2 PM

**Your numbers:** Target $1,310 (485 × $2.70) · ask $1,400 · walk-away $1,256

#### Role-play 3 Rich rate, weak destination

Load 7 · Kankakee → Jacksonville · $2,700 · 1,085 total mi · reloads out of Jacksonville are thin and cheap

**Your numbers:** Ask $2,930+ or pass · use the reload problem as your reason

#### Role-play 4 Slow facility, protect the driver

A load you like at a fair rate, but the shipper is known for 4-hour waits

**Your numbers:** Keep the rate · negotiate detention after 2 h in writing (practice: $50/h) and a later pickup window

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] How to start a role-play with me**
>
> Type: **“Role-play 2. You’re the broker. I’m Jawad from Blue Line.”** I’ll stay in character, push back realistically, and give you a score and feedback at the end.

> **[CHECKLIST] Score yourself**
>
> Facts before rate? A number with a reason? Shrinking steps? Stayed at or above walk-away? Confirmed all-in and accessorials? Polite close either way?

pages.title: Module 8 check
pages.markdown:
Module 8 · Check yourself

# Module 8 check

1. What is double brokering, and why does the carrier often end up unpaid?
2. Name four of the twelve red flags.
3. Which two FMCSA lookups confirm a broker’s authority and financial security? Which forms should you see?
4. Under the rule in force since 16 January 2026, what happens when a broker’s security drops below $75,000?
5. Someone emails claiming to work for a broker you know. How do you verify them?
6. The BOL at pickup names a different carrier than yours. What do you tell the driver, and what do you do?
7. Name three places FMCSA says to report freight fraud.
8. Why can’t a dispatcher move a load from one of their carriers to another?
9. What is a walk-away number, and where does it come from?
10. What does “anchor with a reason” mean? Give an example sentence.
11. Name three things you can negotiate besides the rate.
12. What must you confirm before asking for the rate confirmation?

### Skills self-check

| Skill | Can do | Need practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run the seven broker checks in under 5 minutes | ☐ | ☐ |
| Read a broker’s SAFER and L&I record (authority, BMC-84/85) | ☐ | ☐ |
| Spot an impersonator email and verify through official channels | ☐ | ☐ |
| Compare BOL and rate con at pickup | ☐ | ☐ |
| Follow the six-step response when something is wrong | ☐ | ☐ |
| Negotiate with target, walk-away and a reasoned anchor (drill 10) | ☐ | ☐ |
| Close cleanly: all-in, accessorials, terms, carrier approval | ☐ | ☐ |

pages.title: Answers: vet six brokers
pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers: vet six brokers

| # | Decision | Flags and next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | PASS | No flags. Complete setup on its platform, negotiate (target $2,160), read the rate con. |
| B | STOP | Four flags: 3-week-old authority, free email, cell only, rate well above market, plus pressure and packet by email. Tell Mike, pass, note it on your list. |
| C | STOP | Impersonation: lookalike domain, wrong phone, official office has no “Dan”. Send nothing. Tell Peachtree, Mike and the board; report to FMCSA NCCDB. If you want the real load, book it through Peachtree’s official contact. |
| D | CAUTION | Legitimate but slow payer (CS 71, DTP 58) with a factor limit. Ask Mike if he accepts slower pay; ask for quick-pay terms; stay under the factor limit. |
| E | STOP | No broker authority: brokering without authority, and a double-brokering risk. Decline politely. |
| F | CAUTION | Bond cancellation pending (BMC-36). Ask the broker if a replacement bond is filed; recheck L&I. If not, a load paying in 30 days is risky: pass or ask for quick pay. |

**Bonus.**

“Hi, this is Jawad, dispatcher for Blue Line Transport. I’m verifying a contact: someone named Dan emailed from peachtree-freight-llc.com about your Bolingbrook–Atlanta load. Does Dan work with you, and is that your domain?” Then to Mike: “Stopped a fake Peachtree contact (lookalike domain, no such employee). Sent nothing. Reported to Peachtree and the board. Real load still available through their office.”

**RP 2.**

Walk-away check: 485 × $2.59 = $1,256. Target 485 × $2.70 = $1,310 (rounded). Anchor near $1,400; $1,150 would lose money.

**RP 1.**

Ask $2,250 ($2.96 per loaded mile, just above the range, leaving room to come down); accept ≥ $2,160 or check with Mike between $2,072 and $2,160.

**RP 3.**

$2,700 ÷ 1,085 = $2.49, 10¢ under break-even, into a weak reload market. Ask $2,930 (1,085 × $2.70) with the reason “Jacksonville reloads are thin; I’ll likely deadhead out.” If the broker won’t pass about $2,810 (break-even), pass unless Mike wants the lane.

**RP 4.**

Keep the rate; ask for “detention after 2 hours at $50 an hour, on the rate con” and a pickup window that fits Carlos’s hours. Confirm how to report arrival times (in/out on the BOL, tracking app). Module 10 covers detention claims.

pages.title: Answers: module check
pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers: module check

**1.**

Re-selling a load you took as a carrier, often via stolen identities. The real broker pays whoever it contracted with (the fraudster), who never pays your carrier.

**2.**

Any four: rate far above market; brand-new authority; free or lookalike email; cell-only; pressure; hide your identity; new bank details; asks for logins; pickup changes; names don’t match; odd equipment; asks you to pay.

**3.**

SAFER (entity type BROKER, broker authority active) and L&I (BMC-84 surety bond or BMC-85 trust fund, $75,000, no cancellation).

**4.**

The provider notifies FMCSA; FMCSA notifies the broker, who has 7 business days to restore it or show an error; otherwise its authority is suspended.

**5.**

Find the broker’s phone yourself (website, SAFER, board profile), call, and ask for the person by name. Compare the email domain with the website.

**6.**

“Don’t leave yet.” Call the broker on its official number (and the shipper if needed), tell Mike, and move only when it’s resolved in writing.

**7.**

FMCSA NCCDB (nccdb.fmcsa.dot.gov), FMCSA Contact Center 1-800-832-5660, FTC, FBI IC3 or state attorney general, DOT OIG hotline.

**8.**

It is brokering: arranging transport by another carrier for compensation requires broker registration and $75,000 security (49 U.S.C. 14916).

**9.**

The lowest rate you’ll accept: usually break-even × total miles (Module 7), lower only when the carrier agrees for a strategic reason such as a strong reload.

**10.**

Open with a number backed by facts. “For 727 miles with a same-day pickup I need $2,000. The lane has been around $2.60 a mile.”

**11.**

Detention terms, lumper paid, quick pay, stop pay, pickup window, a backhaul.

**12.**

All-in total, appointments, commodity and weight, accessorials, payment terms, carrier approval, setup.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.markdown:
Reference

# Glossary

**BMC-84** — Broker’s $75,000 surety bond filing.

**BMC-85** — Broker’s $75,000 trust fund filing.

**BMC-36** — Notice cancelling a bond or trust.

**Anchor** — First number that sets the negotiation range.

**Blind load** — Shipment where the parties’ identities are hidden; can be legitimate, but a red flag if you’re asked to misrepresent yourself.

**Bond claim** — Carrier’s claim against a broker’s surety or trust for unpaid freight.

**Double brokering** — Re-selling a load taken as a carrier, without authority or disclosure.

**Fictitious pickup** — Theft where a fake carrier collects real freight.

**Highway for Carriers** — Free tool for carriers to verify brokers.

**Identity theft** — Using another company’s MC/DOT or name.

**Impersonation** — Posing as a real broker with lookalike contacts.

**L&I** — FMCSA Licensing & Insurance: authority and filings.

**NCCDB** — FMCSA’s National Consumer Complaint Database.

**Phishing** — Fake links or messages that steal logins.

**SAFER** — FMCSA company snapshot: entity type, status, contacts.

**Target** — The rate you aim for: target × total miles.

**Walk-away** — Lowest acceptable rate; usually break-even.

**Unauthorized brokering** — Arranging carriage without broker registration and security; unlawful.

# Sources

| Source | What it supports | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **FMCSA** | Broker and carrier fraud and identity theft: prevention tips and reporting channels | fmcsa.dot.gov/mission/help |
| **FMCSA** | Broker and Freight Forwarder Financial Responsibility rule: Educational and Compliance Guide ($75,000; BMC-84/85/36; 2 business days; 7 business days; compliance 16 Jan 2026) | fmcsa.dot.gov |
| **U.S. Code** | 49 U.S.C. 14916 Unlawful brokerage activities ($10,000 per violation; joint and several liability) | govinfo.gov |
| **Verisk CargoNet** | 2025 cargo theft analysis: ~$725M losses, 2,646 incidents, $273,990 average, theft by deception | cargonet.com |

pages.title: The life of a load
pages.markdown:
Lesson 9.1 · The big picture

# The life of a load

![](/assets/diagrams/m09/lifecycle.jpg)

### Who does what

| Person | Main jobs on this load |
| --- | --- |
| **You** | Check rate con, brief driver, track, update broker, collect and send documents |
| **Driver** | Pickup, count, seal, drive legally, deliver, get signatures, send photos |
| **Carrier (Mike)** | Signs the rate con (or authorizes you), chooses payment path, owns disputes |
| **Broker** | Sends rate con and tracking, handles shipper and receiver, pays |

> **[KEY RULE] Write it down**
>
> Every call, message and change goes into the load notes with the time and time zone. If there’s a dispute in six weeks, your notes are the carrier’s evidence.

> **[FACT] One load at a time, then many**
>
> Real dispatchers run several trucks at once. The steps are the same; a simple tracker (page 16) keeps each load’s next action visible.

pages.title: The clauses that cost money
pages.markdown:
Lesson 9.1 · Real rate con

# The clauses that cost money

![](/assets/diagrams/m09/rc_terms.jpg)

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “The rate con is just a receipt for the rate”**
>
> It is the contract for this load. It usually refers to the broker–carrier agreement signed at setup, and together they set the rules: payment, fines, liability and accessorials.

> **[FACT] Right to see the record**
>
> FMCSA requires brokers to keep a record of each brokered transaction for three years, and **each party to the transaction has the right to review it** (49 CFR 371.3).

### Common rate con clauses and how to respond

| Clause | What it means | Your move |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Tracking required** | Deduction if tracking is refused or stops | Set up tracking before pickup; tell the driver |
| **POD deadline** | Fine if the POD arrives late (e.g. 72 h) | Send the POD the same day |
| **Late delivery fine** | Money off if late, sometimes a fixed amount | Ask for a grace period, or removal when the delay isn’t the carrier’s fault |
| **Detention terms** | Free time, hourly rate, cap, notice required | Know the notice rule (e.g. call when 2 h reached) and log in/out times |
| **TONU** | Pay if the load cancels on arrival, or “not liable” | Ask for TONU on loads with long deadhead |
| **No re-brokering** | Carrier must haul the load itself | Always true for you (Module 8) |
| **Cargo liability** | Carrier responsible for loss, damage, shortage | Check the carrier’s cargo insurance limits cover the freight value |

pages.title: Check every rate con against the call
pages.markdown:
Lesson 9.1 · Checklist

# Check every rate con against the call

| # | Check | Against |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Broker** | Name, MC, address, contact = your vetting (Module 8) |
| 2 | **Carrier** | Legal name, MC, USDOT exactly right |
| 3 | **Equipment** | The truck you offered (dry van, 53′, no air-ride) |
| 4 | **Stops** | Addresses, dates, times, time zones, FCFS/appointment, reference numbers |
| 5 | **Freight** | Commodity, pieces, weight, temperature if any |
| 6 | **Money** | Rate, all-in or linehaul + FSC, total |
| 7 | **Accessorials** | Detention, lumper, TONU, extra stops as agreed |
| 8 | **Rules** | Tracking, fines, deductions, POD deadline |
| 9 | **Payment** | Terms, quick pay, where to send invoices |

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] When something is wrong**
>
> **“Hi, this is Jawad with Blue Line, about load PF-20931. The rate con shows $1,650 and a reefer. We agreed $1,750 for a dry van. Could you send a corrected rate con, please?”**

> **[KEY RULE] Fix it before anyone signs**
>
> Never sign “and fix it later”. Once signed, the wrong rate or missing detention is what the carrier agreed to. Ask for a corrected version; check it again.

> **[CHECKLIST] After signing**
>
> Save the signed copy in the load folder (page 15), send the setup documents if requested, and only then send the dispatch sheet to the driver.

The practice rate con for Load 2, with six deliberate errors, is on page 17.

pages.title: Briefing the driver
pages.markdown:
Lesson 9.2 · Dispatch

# Briefing the driver

![](/assets/diagrams/m09/dsheet.jpg)
> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Confirm by phone**
>
> **“Carlos, you’re set for PF-20931: Bolingbrook, pickup number 5-5-8-1-2, window 9 to 11 Central tomorrow. Delivery Atlanta Thursday 1 PM Eastern. Can you read back the pickup number and the appointment?”**

### Before the driver rolls

- Signed rate con saved; setup complete with the broker.
- Dispatch sheet sent and read back by the driver.
- Tracking link sent and accepted (or ELD tracking connected).
- Hours checked: the plan fits the driver’s clocks (Module 4).
- Route checked: truck entrance, parking, any low bridges or restricted roads.
- Broker has the driver’s name, truck and trailer numbers, and cell if required.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] If the driver says the plan won’t work**
>
> Listen. The driver sees hours, weather and fatigue you don’t. Adjust the plan, tell the broker early, and never push him to drive over his hours (Module 4, coercion is prohibited).

> **[REAL-WORLD TIP] Driver information sharing**
>
> Brokers often ask for the driver’s name and number for tracking and check calls. Share only what the carrier approves, through the broker’s official channel.

Lesson 9.2 · The plan

# Load 2, hour by hour

![](/assets/diagrams/m09/timeline.jpg)

### Your time vs their time

| U.S. zone | Pakistan time (PKT = UTC+5) |
| --- | --- |
| Eastern (EDT, UTC−4) | +9 hours · 1 PM ET = 10 PM PKT |
| Central (CDT, UTC−5) | +10 hours · 9 AM CT = 7 PM PKT |
| After U.S. clocks go back (EST/CST, early Nov) | add 1 more hour: +10 / +11 |

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] The most common dispatch mistake**
>
> Mixing time zones: telling a driver “1 PM” when the appointment is Eastern and he’s still in Central time. Always say the zone out loud: **“1 PM Eastern.”**

pages.title: At the shipper
pages.markdown:
Lesson 9.3 · Pickup

# At the shipper

![](/assets/diagrams/m09/pickup.jpg)

### Live load vs drop and hook

| Type | What happens | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Live load** | Driver waits while the shipper loads | In/out times for detention |
| **Drop and hook** | Driver drops an empty trailer, takes a pre-loaded one | Seal, SLC, trailer number, condition |
| **Preloaded** | Trailer loaded before arrival | SLC, seal photo, weight |

> **[FACT] The law behind SLC**
>
> When the bill of lading shows the shipper loaded the goods, federal law (49 U.S.C. 80113) limits the carrier’s liability for damage caused by improper loading. The driver still must refuse a load that is visibly unsafe.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Overweight or unsafe load?**
>
> If the load looks overweight, poorly secured or not as described, the driver doesn’t leave. Scale it if needed (Module 2) and call the broker. Safety comes before the appointment.

pages.title: Check calls and tracking
pages.markdown:
Lesson 9.3 · Transit

# Check calls and tracking

![](/assets/diagrams/m09/chat.jpg)

### Tracking apps

Brokers track loads with tools such as **Descartes MacroPoint** or **Trucker Tools**. MacroPoint can pull location from the carrier’s **ELD** (preferred: no app needed), from a TMS, or from a driver phone app. It says it tracks only during the load session.

The rate con for #12354 deducted **$150** if the driver refused or disabled tracking. Make sure it is running before the truck leaves.

> **[KEY RULE] Check-call rhythm**
>
> At dispatch · at shipper · loaded (BOL photo) · every 3–4 hours or at breaks · any delay, immediately · at receiver · empty (POD photo).

> **[REAL-WORLD TIP] Pakistan tip**
>
> Use one group chat per truck with the carrier included, plus a pinned message with the current load. Everyone sees the same information, and nothing depends on your shift.

pages.title: The proof of delivery
pages.markdown:
Lesson 9.4 · Delivery

# The proof of delivery

![](/assets/diagrams/m09/pod_annot.jpg)

### Clean vs exception POD

| POD shows | What you do |
| --- | --- |
| **Clean** | Photo/scan, send with invoice today |
| **Short** | Driver photographs the count and trailer; call broker before leaving |
| **Damaged** | Photos of damage and packaging; exact note on POD |
| **Refused** | Don’t leave or dump freight; broker gives written instructions |

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Ask the driver for the right photo**
>
> **“Carlos, please send the full signed page, flat, in good light, so I can read the stamp, the count and the name.”**

> **[FACT] Records to keep**
>
> Bills of lading and delivery records: at least 1 year under FMCSA’s record rules (49 CFR 379, Appendix A).

pages.title: Three documents, one story
pages.markdown:
Lesson 9.4 · The paper trail

# Three documents, one story

![](/assets/diagrams/m09/chain.jpg)

### Spot the mismatch

Compare #12354’s rate con and BOL: rate con weight **2,000 lb**, BOL weight **5,729 lb** (Module 8, page 11). The POD shows 10 units received, matching the BOL. A broker AP team may ask about the weight difference before paying. That’s why you resolve mismatches at pickup, in writing.

> **[FACT] What a BOL must include**
>
> Under 49 CFR 373.101: consignor and consignee names; origin and destination; number of packages; description of the freight; weight, volume or measurement when used for rating.

### What each document proves

| Document | Proves | Issued by | Carrier keeps |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Rate con** | The price and rules agreed | Broker | Signed copy |
| **BOL** | What was handed to the carrier, and in what condition | Shipper | Driver’s copy + photo |
| **POD** | What the receiver accepted, and any exceptions | Receiver signs the BOL/receipt | Signed copy |
| **Receipts** | Costs paid on the broker’s behalf (lumper, scale) | Facility / vendor | Original + scan |
| **Invoice** | What the carrier asks to be paid | Carrier (you prepare) | Copy + sent email |

pages.title: The invoice
pages.markdown:
Lesson 9.4 · Invoicing

# The invoice

![](/assets/diagrams/m09/invoice.jpg)

### Invoice packet checklist

- Invoice with its own number, load #, BOL #, dates, amounts
- Signed rate con (or corrected version)
- Signed BOL/POD, readable
- Receipts for any reimbursed costs (lumper, scale)
- Detention proof: in/out times and broker approval (Module 10)

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Deadlines are money**
>
> Some rate cons set a POD deadline (72 hours on #12354) and fine or deduct after it. Send the packet the same day the truck empties.

> **[KEY RULE] One email, one load**
>
> Subject: “Invoice BL-1024 · Load PF-20931 · POD attached”. Attach PDFs, not links. Save the sent email in the load folder.

### Why invoices get held, and the fix

| Reason | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| POD unreadable or missing a page | Ask the driver to rescan flat, full page; send PDF |
| Amount doesn’t match the rate con | Invoice only what’s on the (corrected) rate con, plus approved extras |
| Wrong load or reference number | Copy the broker’s load # exactly from the rate con |
| Sent to the wrong address | Use the AP email on the rate con, or the factor if factored |
| Detention added without proof or approval | Attach in/out times and the broker’s written approval (Module 10) |

pages.title: Keeping the records
pages.markdown:
Lesson 9.4 · Files

# Keeping the records

![](/assets/diagrams/m09/files.jpg)

### Close-out checklist (after payment)

1. Payment amount matches the invoice (or the deduction is explained).
2. Payment confirmation saved in the load folder.
3. Invoice tracker marked paid.
4. Broker notes updated: pay speed, service, issues.
5. Load economics card updated with the real result (Module 7).

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Privacy**
>
> Carrier documents contain bank details, tax IDs and driver information. Keep them in the carrier’s system only, with a strong password and MFA. Never forward them from personal accounts.

### Photo and scan standards for drivers

| Good | Bad |
| --- | --- |
| Whole page, flat, all four corners visible | Cut-off edges, folded page, finger over text |
| Daylight or cab light, no shadow | Dark cab, flash glare on the stamp |
| Scanner app → one PDF, all pages | Five separate blurry photos |
| Signature, stamp and count readable | “It was signed, trust me” |

pages.title: Answers
pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers

**E1.**

(1) MC 1298465 → **1298456**. (2) 53′ Reefer → **dry van**. (3) Delivery Wed 14 Oct → **Thu 15 Oct**, 1 PM ET. (4) Rate $1,650 → **$1,750**. (5) “No detention” → **after 2 h, $50/h**. (6) Lumper on carrier → **paid by broker**. Question: the **$250 late fine**: ask to remove it or define “late” (grace period, delays caused by the shipper or receiver).

**E2.**

Load/broker, tracking, pickup (shipper, address, window 10–2 CT, PU# 88120, 24 plts, 42,000 lb, canned goods), delivery (Charlotte, FCFS 8–4 ET, DEL# C-4410), notes: seal on BOL, BOL photo, lumper receipt, call if delayed. Rate only if Mike allows.

**E3.**

“Carlos, please don’t leave yet.” Two problems: 20 vs 22 pallets, and a **different carrier name** (possible double brokering or wrong paperwork). Call Peachtree on its official number; don’t move until the count and carrier are corrected in writing (Module 8).

**E4.**

1) Driver stays; photos of the pallet, packaging and POD note. 2) Call the broker immediately. 3) Follow written instructions for the refused pallet (return, hold, salvage). 4) Tell Mike. 5) Record everything; send POD with the exception note. Claims: Module 10.

**E5.**

7–9 PM PKT · Thu 10:00 PM PKT · Thu 7:35 AM PKT · 8:00 AM Chicago (CT).

**E6.**

Example: “LL-448210 loaded 12:40 CT, 24 plts, 42,000 lb, seal \_\_\_, ETA Thu 9:30 ET.” · “LL-448210 on site Charlotte 9:25 ET (FCFS).” · “LL-448210 delivered 11:50 ET clean, POD attached.”

**E7.**

(a) $2,050 in ~30 days · (b) $2,009 in ~1–5 days · (c) $1,988.50 in ~1–2 days. Factoring or quick pay is fastest; standard pays the most.

**Bonus.**

03\_BOL\_pickup.jpg · 04\_POD\_signed.pdf · 06\_Invoice\_BL-1024.pdf, inside 2026-10-14\_PF-20931\_Bolingbrook-Atlanta.

**1–4.**

See page 4 (steps) · signed rate con = contract; only people the carrier authorizes sign · tracking deductions, POD deadlines, fines, liability, no TONU · driver info with time zones; rate at carrier’s choice.

**5–8.**

Consignor/consignee, origin/destination, packages, description, weight/volume · shipper load and count when the driver couldn’t see or count · any change to the plan, delay, damage, refusal · counts match, nothing short/damaged, signed; for damage: photos, exact note, call broker.

**9–12.**

Invoice, signed rate con, signed BOL/POD, receipts, detention proof · to the factor named in the NOA, so the broker pays the right party · 1 year · 10:00 PM PKT Thursday.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.markdown:
Reference

# Glossary

**BOL** — Bill of lading: receipt and contract for the shipment.

**Check call** — Status update from the driver or to the broker.

**Clean POD** — Signed delivery with no shortage or damage noted.

**Dispatch sheet** — The driver’s load instructions.

**Drop and hook** — Swap trailers instead of waiting to load.

**Exception** — Shortage, overage, damage or refusal noted on the POD.

**FCFS** — First come, first served: no fixed appointment.

**Invoice packet** — Invoice + rate con + POD + receipts.

**Live load/unload** — Driver waits while freight is loaded or unloaded.

**OS&D** — Over, short and damaged.

**POD** — Proof of delivery: the signed BOL or delivery receipt.

**PU# / DEL#** — Pickup or delivery reference numbers.

**Quick pay** — Broker pays early for a fee.

**Rate con** — Rate confirmation: the load contract.

**Seal** — Numbered tag locking the trailer doors.

**SLC** — Shipper load and count.

**TONU** — Truck ordered, not used: pay if a load cancels on arrival.

**Tracking** — Location sharing with the broker (ELD or app).

# Sources

| Source | What it supports | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **eCFR** | 49 CFR 373.101: required information on motor carrier bills of lading | ecfr.gov |

Start here

# How to use this module

Module 9 showed Load 2 going perfectly. Real weeks don’t. Receivers make trucks wait, loads cancel at the gate, highways close, trucks break, freight arrives crushed. This module teaches you to **protect the driver, the schedule and the carrier’s money** when that happens.

### Practice terms used in this module

#### Blue Line’s usual asks (practice values)

Detention **2 h free, then $50/h** · layover **$250/day** · TONU **$150** · extra stop **$75** · driver assist **$75** (only if agreed) · lumper **paid or reimbursed by broker**.

Real terms differ by broker and load. The rate con always decides (Module 9).

### Study rhythm (about 5 hours)

- **Session 1 (1.5 h):** accessorials, detention clock, lumpers, TONU and layover.
- **Session 2 (1.5 h):** problems on the road, late ETA call (drill 12), breakdowns, accidents.
- **Session 3 (2 h):** claims, evidence kit, practice situations and check.

Contents

**L10.1** Accessorials: getting paid for extra time and work4

**L10.2** Problems on the road9

**L10.3** Cargo claims and evidence13

Practice: six situations · detention math15

Answer key · Glossary · Sources18

> **[KEY RULE] Three rules for every problem**
>
> **People first** (is the driver safe?) · **call early** (brokers forgive problems, not surprises) · **write it down** (times, names, photos, instructions).

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Not legal advice**
>
> Claims and accidents can involve insurers and lawyers. Your job is fast, accurate information to the carrier; the carrier and its insurer make the decisions.

pages.title: Hours of waiting are hours of pay, if you can prove them.
pages.markdown:
10

Module 10 · When things go wrong

Hours of waiting are hours of pay,  
if you can prove them.

ATRI found drivers were detained at 39% of stops in 2023, and fleets were paid for fewer than half of the detention invoices they sent. The difference between paid and unpaid is almost always the same: times, notice and proof.

pages.title: The accessorials menu
pages.markdown:
Lesson 10.1 · Accessorials

# The accessorials menu

![](/assets/diagrams/m10/menu.jpg)

### Three conditions for getting paid

1. **Agreed:** on the rate con, or approved by the broker in writing before or during the event.
2. **Proven:** times, receipts, messages, photos (evidence kit, page 14).
3. **Invoiced properly:** a separate line on the invoice, with the proof attached, sent with the POD.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Correction: “Accessorials are automatic”**
>
> Brokers pay what the rate con says and what you can prove. A driver who waited four hours without anyone telling the broker usually gets nothing.

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Ask at booking**
>
> **“What are your detention terms: free time, rate, and how do you want to be notified?”** Then check the answer on the rate con.

pages.title: The detention clock
pages.markdown:
Lesson 10.1 · Detention

# The detention clock

![](/assets/diagrams/m10/dclock.jpg)

### Your detention routine

| When | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Arrival | Driver checks in; photo of the check-in sheet or gate time; tracking shows arrival |
| 15 min before free time ends | Email/message the broker: “Driver on site since 12:00 for 1 PM appt, not yet in a door. Free time ends 3 PM; please notify the receiver and approve detention after 3.” |
| Departure | In and out times written on the BOL/POD and signed by the facility |
| Same day | Detention line on the invoice with times and the notice message attached |

> **[FACT] Hours of service still apply**
>
> Waiting at a dock is usually on-duty time and uses the 14-hour window (Module 4). Long detention can push a driver out of hours, which is why detention can also mean a missed next load.

> **[KEY RULE] Know the fine print**
>
> Some brokers pay only if the driver arrived on time, only after written notice, or only up to a daily cap. Ask once, write it down for that broker, and follow it every time.

pages.title: Detention by the numbers
pages.markdown:
Lesson 10.1 · Why it matters

# Detention by the numbers

![](/assets/diagrams/m10/dstats.jpg)

### The detention notice (template)

**Subject:** Detention notice · Load PF-20931 · Atlanta  
  
Hi Dana, our driver Carlos arrived at 12:00 PM ET for the 1:00 PM appointment and is still waiting for a door. Free time ends at 3:00 PM ET. Please let the receiver know, and confirm detention will apply at $50/h after 3:00 PM per the rate confirmation. Check-in photo attached. Thank you, Jawad · Blue Line Transport

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] If the broker says “we don’t pay detention on this one”**
>
> **“Understood. The rate con lists detention after two hours at $50. Can you point me to where it says otherwise?”** If it truly isn’t there, note it for next time and add detention terms to your negotiation checklist.

> **[REAL-WORLD TIP] Pakistan tip**
>
> Detention often starts in your early morning shift (U.S. afternoon). Set reminders at “free time minus 15 minutes” for every live appointment on your tracker.

pages.title: Lumper fees
pages.markdown:
Lesson 10.1 · Lumpers

# Lumper fees

![](/assets/diagrams/m10/lumper.jpg)

### Driver script at the receiver

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Carlos to the receiver**
>
> **“Before I pay anything, I need to call my dispatcher. Can I get the amount and who to make it out to?”** Then he calls you, and you call the broker.

> **[CHECKLIST] The lumper receipt must show**
>
> Facility name and address · date and time · amount · load or PO number · how it was paid · signature or stamp. A handwritten note on a napkin will not be reimbursed.

### Driver assist vs lumper

| Situation | What it is | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Lumper** | Facility’s paid crew unloads | Broker pays or reimburses; get a receipt |
| **Driver assist** | Driver loads/unloads or counts by hand | Only if agreed in advance and paid; driver can refuse unsafe work |
| **No-touch** | Driver stays in the truck | Normal for most full truckload freight |

pages.title: Three common situations
pages.markdown:
Lesson 10.1 · TONU, layover, refusals

# Three common situations

![](/assets/diagrams/m10/scen.jpg)

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] TONU call**
>
> **“Hi, this is Jawad with Blue Line, load PF-20931. Our driver is at the shipper and was told the load is cancelled. He drove 90 miles empty for this. Per the rate con, we’ll invoice the $150 TONU. Can you confirm the cancellation by email?”**

> **[KEY RULE] Layover is about rest too**
>
> If the driver must wait overnight, make sure he has a legal and safe place to park. The layover payment doesn’t replace the next load he may lose, so tell Mike quickly so he can decide.

### Accessorial request emails: subject lines that get paid

| Type | Subject line | Attach |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Detention** | Detention request · PF-20931 · Atlanta · 1 h 30 billable | POD with in/out times, notice email, tracking |
| **TONU** | TONU · PF-20931 · cancelled on arrival 8:10 AM CT | Rate con, check-in photo, cancellation message |
| **Layover** | Layover · PF-20931 · held overnight per your instruction | Instruction message, times |
| **Lumper** | Lumper reimbursement · PF-20931 · $185 | Receipt, approval message |

Send the request the same day, then add the approved amount to the invoice (Module 9).

pages.title: First moves for eight problems
pages.markdown:
Lesson 10.2 · Problems

# First moves for eight problems

![](/assets/diagrams/m10/problems.jpg)
> **[FACT] Why “call early” works**
>
> A broker who hears about a delay three hours before the appointment can move the appointment, tell the receiver and keep the customer calm. A broker who finds out from the receiver at 1:05 PM loses trust in your carrier, and may fine it.

### The problem log (one line per event)

| Time (zone) | What happened | Who was told | Decision / next step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10:05 AM ET | I-24 closure; truck stopped 2 h | Broker (call + email), Mike | New ETA 2:50 PM ET; broker asking receiver |
| 10:40 AM ET | Receiver moved appointment to 3:00 PM | Driver, Mike | Confirmed in writing; tracker updated |
|  |  |  |  |

Practice rows. The log goes in the load folder (Module 9) and is your evidence if fines, detention or claims come up later.

pages.title: The late ETA call
pages.markdown:
Lesson 10.2 · Running late

# The late ETA call

![](/assets/diagrams/m10/late.jpg)

### Drill 12: say it out loud

Read the call-first script above aloud three times. Then change the facts: **flat tyre at mile 42, repair 90 minutes**, and give a new ETA with the same structure: **load · what happened · new ETA · request · written follow-up**.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Never make up a reason**
>
> If the driver overslept or left late, say “the driver is running behind” and give an honest ETA. Brokers check tracking; invented traffic destroys trust.

> **[KEY RULE] Update again if it slips**
>
> If the new ETA changes by more than about 30 minutes, call again. One accurate update beats three hopeful ones.

### Quick ETA table (at a realistic 50 mph average)

| Miles left | 50 | 100 | 150 | 200 | 250 | 300 | 400 | 500 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Driving time** | 1:00 | 2:00 | 3:00 | 4:00 | 5:00 | 6:00 | 8:00 | 10:00 |

Add fuel, traffic and check-in time, then check the driver’s hours (Module 4). Above about 500 miles, a 10-hour break usually falls in between.

pages.title: When the truck or the reefer fails
pages.markdown:
Lesson 10.2 · Breakdowns and reefers

# When the truck or the reefer fails

![](/assets/diagrams/m10/breakdown.jpg)

#### Reefer problem checklist

Unit running? Setpoint matches the BOL? Continuous or cycle mode as required? Fuel level? Alarms? Download the temperature record. Tell the broker **before** the freight warms, and follow written instructions (Module 2).

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Recovery is the broker’s decision**
>
> If Truck 12 can’t be repaired in time, the broker decides whether to wait or send a recovery truck. Your carrier must not hand the load to another carrier on its own: that’s brokering (Module 8).

> **[FACT] Evidence for repairs**
>
> Keep the repair order, tow receipt and times. If the broker agrees to reschedule rather than cancel, get the new appointment in writing.

pages.title: Safety events
pages.markdown:
Lesson 10.2 · Accidents and weather

# Safety events

![](/assets/diagrams/m10/accident.jpg)

### Weather and hours

The driver decides whether it is safe to drive. FMCSA’s **adverse driving conditions** exception can allow up to 2 extra hours of driving (and extend the 14-hour window by up to 2 hours) when conditions such as snow, fog or unusual traffic weren’t known at dispatch. It is for finishing safely, not for pushing through a storm.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Coercion is prohibited**
>
> Carriers, shippers, receivers and brokers may not pressure a driver to break hours-of-service or other safety rules (49 CFR 390.6, Module 4). Never say “just push through.”

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] The weather call to the broker**
>
> **“Load PF-20931: heavy snow on I-75 north of Atlanta. The driver has stopped at a safe location. New ETA tomorrow 8 AM Eastern, weather permitting. I’ll update you by 6 AM.”**

pages.title: Cargo claims
pages.markdown:
Lesson 10.3 · Claims

# Cargo claims

![](/assets/diagrams/m10/claims.jpg)

### How claims reach the carrier

| Step | Who |
| --- | --- |
| Damage found | Receiver notes it on the POD; driver photographs |
| Claim filed | Shipper or its insurer, usually through the broker |
| Carrier response | Carrier, with its cargo insurer |
| Salvage | Damaged freight sold or disposed of to reduce the loss (49 CFR 370.11) |

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Payment offsets**
>
> Some brokers hold or deduct freight payment while a claim is open, depending on the broker–carrier agreement. Tell Mike, read the agreement, and respond with evidence. Don’t ignore the claim hoping it goes away.

> **[KEY RULE] Protect the carrier’s insurance**
>
> Tell the carrier the same day so it can notify its cargo insurer on time. Late notice can create problems with coverage.

pages.title: The evidence kit
pages.markdown:
Lesson 10.3 · Evidence

# The evidence kit

![](/assets/diagrams/m10/evidence.jpg)

### Damage photo checklist for drivers

1. Wide shot of the trailer interior before unloading, if possible.
2. Close-ups of each damaged item and its label.
3. The seal (intact or broken) and the seal number.
4. The POD notation, readable.
5. Anything that shows cause: load bars, straps, shifting, wet floor.

> **[FACT] A notation is not a claim**
>
> Under 49 CFR 370.3, a note on a delivery receipt doesn’t count as a claim by itself. A claim is a written demand identifying the shipment, asserting liability and stating an amount. Notes and photos are the evidence for that claim.

> **[REAL-WORLD TIP] Securement matters**
>
> Your M2 photos of load bars and blocked cargo show what prevents most shifting damage. Ask the driver to secure partial or light loads, and photograph it.

pages.title: Six situations
pages.markdown:
Practice

# Six situations

For each: what do you do first, who do you tell, what evidence do you collect, and what do you say? Answers at the back.

#### Situation 1 Waiting at the shipper

Truck 12 arrives 7:40 AM CT for an 8:00 AM appointment. At 9:45 AM Carlos is still not in a door. Rate con: 2 h free, then $50/h, notice required before free time ends.

**Write:** your first three actions and the exact words to the broker.

#### Situation 2 Lumper at the receiver

Receiver in Atlanta says unloading is by lumpers, $185, card or money code only. Rate con: “lumper paid by broker with receipt.”

**Write:** your first three actions and the exact words to the broker.

#### Situation 3 Cancelled at the gate

Carlos drives 95 miles empty to Rockford, IL. Shipper: “We shipped it with another carrier this morning.” Rate con: TONU $150.

**Write:** your first three actions and the exact words to the broker.

#### Situation 4 Breakdown with a reefer

A reefer load (practice) of produce set at 34°F. The truck loses an air line 180 miles from delivery. Repair ETA 3 hours; the reefer unit is running.

**Write:** your first three actions and the exact words to the broker.

#### Situation 5 Short and damaged

Receiver counts 21 pallets, not 22, and marks one pallet “wet, damaged.” The BOL shows 22 pallets, seal 4471023 intact, SLC written.

**Write:** your first three actions and the exact words to the broker.

#### Situation 6 Snow and hours

Heavy snow ahead. Carlos has 2 hours of driving left and the appointment is in 3 hours. The broker texts: “Customer needs it today, can he push?”

**Write:** your first three actions and the exact words to the broker.

pages.markdown:
Practice

# Detention math and the accessorial invoice

### 7 · Detention calculations

Terms for all three: **2 hours free from the appointment time (or arrival, if later), then $50 per hour, billed in full 15-minute blocks (rounded down)**. Detention is void if the driver arrives after the appointment.

| # | Appointment | Arrived | Out | Billable time | Amount |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a | 8:00 AM | 7:40 AM | 12:05 PM |  |  |
| b | 1:00 PM | 12:00 PM | 4:40 PM |  |  |
| c | 6:00 AM | 6:20 AM | 11:30 AM |  |  |
| d | FCFS 8 AM–4 PM | 9:00 AM | 1:30 PM |  |  |

For d (first come, first served), assume free time starts at arrival.

### 8 · Build the invoice

Load 2 on a bad day: linehaul **$1,750**; detention from 7b; the carrier paid a **$185** lumper with its own card (broker approved, receipt attached). Write the invoice lines and the total.

| Line | Amount | Proof attached |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Line haul, all-in |  |  |
| Detention |  |  |
| Lumper reimbursement |  |  |
| **Total** |  |  |

> **[TRY IT] 9 · Write the claim response note**
>
> Situation 5 becomes a claim: the shipper claims $1,400 for the missing and damaged pallets. Write a short, factual note from Jawad to Mike: what happened, what evidence you have (BOL, seal, SLC, photos), and what Mike should do next.

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Drill 12 variations**
>
> Give the late-ETA call for: (a) flat tyre, 90-minute repair; (b) receiver moved the appointment; (c) the driver needs his 10-hour break before delivery.
