pages.title: Answers: situations and math
pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers: situations and math

**S1.**

Free time runs 8:00–10:00 AM CT (arrived early, clock starts at the appointment). Send the detention notice now, before 10:00, with the check-in time. Ask Carlos to get in/out times on the BOL.

**S2.**

Carlos pays nothing yet. Call the broker: “Lumper $185 at the receiver; rate con says broker pays. How will you pay it?” Get a money code or direct payment; receipt with load #.

**S3.**

Photo of the gate/check-in, tracking arrival. Call the broker: cancellation in writing; invoice TONU $150 with proof. Tell Mike; start searching for a reload near Rockford.

**S4.**

Driver safe; roadside service. Call the broker: location, 3 h repair, reefer running at 34°F, new ETA. Temperature record downloaded. Broker decides on waiting or recovery.

**S5.**

Photos, exact POD note (21 received, 1 wet/damaged), seal intact and SLC on BOL. Call the broker before Carlos leaves; tell Mike the same day. Evidence supports that loading/counting was the shipper’s.

**S6.**

Safety first: no pushing. “The driver will stop at a safe place; with the snow and his hours he can’t deliver today. New ETA tomorrow 8 AM.” Tell Mike. Coercion is prohibited.

**7a.**

Clock 8:00 → out 12:05 = 4 h 05 min − 2 h = 2 h 05 → 8 full blocks = 2 h → **$100**.

**7b.**

1:00 → 4:40 = 3 h 40 − 2 h = 1 h 40 → 6 full blocks = 1 h 30 → **$75**.

**7c.**

Arrived after the appointment: detention void → **$0** (unless the broker agrees otherwise).

**7d.**

9:00 → 1:30 = 4 h 30 − 2 h = 2 h 30 → **$125**.

**8.**

Line haul $1,750.00 (rate con) · detention $75.00 (times on POD + notice email) · lumper $185.00 (receipt + broker approval) · **total $2,010.00**.

**9.**

Example: “Mike, the shipper claims $1,400 on PF-20931. Facts: BOL 22 pallets, seal 4471023 intact at delivery, SLC written at pickup, receiver counted 21 and noted 1 wet. Photos and POD attached. Please notify your cargo insurer and reply to the broker in writing; I’ll send the full file.”

pages.title: Answers: module check
pages.markdown:
Answer key

# Answers: module check

**1.**

Detention: paid waiting after free time. Layover: held overnight or a day. TONU: truck ordered, not used (cancelled after dispatch). Lumper: paid unloading crew.

**2.**

Usually at the appointment time (or arrival, if later). Arriving early is the carrier’s choice, not the facility’s delay.

**3.**

Terms on the rate con, times proven (tracking, BOL in/out), notice to the broker when required; then invoice with proof.

**4.**

A shipper or receiver that requires loading/unloading help must provide it or pay for it, and coercing a carrier to load or unload is unlawful.

**5.**

Driver calls you; you confirm with the broker who pays and how; payment method agreed; receipt obtained.

**6.**

Work out an honest ETA with hours, call the broker before the appointment, confirm in writing and ask for a new time.

**7.**

The broker (with its customer). Handing the load to another carrier without the broker arranging it is brokering.

**8.**

Setpoint on the BOL, unit download/temperature record, pulp temperatures, precool proof, times and messages.

**9.**

A fatality, an injury treated away from the scene, or a vehicle towed for disabling damage. Never admit fault, promise payment or guess.

**10.**

A notation records what was seen at delivery; a claim is a written demand identifying the shipment, asserting liability and stating an amount (49 CFR 370.3).

**11.**

At least 9 months to file a claim; at least 2 years to sue after written denial (49 U.S.C. 14706).

**12.**

Acknowledge within 30 days; pay, decline or offer within 120 days, with written status every 60 days if not resolved (49 CFR 370.5, 370.9).

pages.title: Glossary
pages.markdown:
Reference

# Glossary

**Accessorial** — Extra charge beyond the linehaul.

**Adverse driving conditions** — HOS exception adding up to 2 h when unexpected conditions arise.

**Carmack Amendment** — 49 U.S.C. 14706: carrier liability for cargo loss or damage.

**Claim** — Written demand with shipment, liability and amount.

**Detention** — Paid waiting after free time.

**Driver assist** — Driver helps load or unload, if agreed and paid.

**Free time** — Waiting allowed before detention starts (often 2 h).

**Layover** — Truck held overnight or to the next day.

**Lumper** — Paid unloading crew at a facility.

**Money code** — Payment code issued so a driver can pay a fee.

**Notice** — Message telling the broker free time is ending.

**Offset** — Broker holding payment against a claim.

**Out of service** — Vehicle or driver barred from moving until fixed.

**Recovery** — Moving freight after a breakdown, arranged by the broker.

**Salvage** — Selling damaged freight to reduce a loss.

**TONU** — Truck ordered, not used.

# Sources

| Source | What it supports | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **U.S. Code** | 49 U.S.C. 14706 Carmack Amendment: liability; 9-month claim and 2-year suit minimums | law.cornell.edu |
| **U.S. Code** | 49 U.S.C. 14103 Loading and unloading: shipper/receiver provide or pay; coercion unlawful | law.cornell.edu |
| **eCFR** | 49 CFR 370: claim contents, 30-day acknowledgment, 120-day disposition, salvage | ecfr.gov |
| **eCFR** | 49 CFR 390.5 accident definition; 390.6 coercion prohibited | ecfr.gov |
| **FMCSA** | Hours of service summary, including the adverse driving conditions exception | fmcsa.dot.gov |
| **ATRI** | Detention research (Sept 2024, 2023 data): 39.3% of stops, 135M hours, $15.1B cost, <50% of invoices paid, 14.6% faster driving | truckingresearch.org |
| **User-supplied** | OMNITECH manual: rate con #12354 (no-TONU clause); detention, driver and reefer photos | your files |

> **[FACT] Practice values**
>
> Accessorial amounts, the Load 2 “bad day”, situations and claim amounts are fictional practice values. Rules and statistics are from the sources above (checked September 2026).

# How to use this module

This is the last handbook. The first half prepares **you**: your hours, your desk, your pay, your health and your first carrier. The second half tests **everything**: a five-day simulation with three trucks, where Claude plays the brokers, the driver and the carrier.

### Study rhythm (about 8 hours)

- **Session 1 (1.5 h):** time zones, setup, pay and tax, routine, first carrier.
- **Sessions 2–6 (1 h each):** one simulation day each, with that day’s role-plays.
- **Session 7 (1.5 h):** weekly report, capstone, final checklist.

### How the role-plays work

1. Read the day card and prepare your numbers.
2. Copy the start line from page 13 into the chat with Claude.
3. Talk (type or use voice) as you would on a real call.
4. Claude stays in character until the call ends, then scores you with the rubric (page 14) and shows a better version.
5. Repeat any role-play scoring below 7/10.

Contents

**L11.1** Working from Pakistan4

**L11.2** The simulation week9

**L11.3** Capstone and final checklist16

Your next 30 days · Sources18

Certificate of completion20

> **[KEY RULE] Treat it like a real week**
>
> Keep a load tracker, write handover notes, save “documents” in folders, and log every call. The habits are the real test.

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Not tax or legal advice**
>
> Pakistan tax and banking rules in Lesson 11.1 are as reported in 2026. Confirm with a qualified adviser and your bank before you start work.

pages.title: The truck is 12,000 km away. Your reliability has to be local.
pages.markdown:
11

Module 11 · Remote and ready

The truck is 12,000 km away.  
Your reliability has to be local.

Carriers hire remote dispatchers for night-time coverage, sharp numbers and clean paperwork, and they fire them for missed calls, wrong time zones and silence during outages. This module makes sure your setup is as professional as your skills.

pages.title: Your clock and theirs
pages.markdown:
Lesson 11.1 · Time

# Your clock and theirs

![](/assets/diagrams/m11/clocks.jpg)

### Practice conversions

| U.S. time (date) | PKT |
| --- | --- |
| Wed 14 Oct, 9 AM CT | Wed 7 PM |
| Thu 15 Oct, 1 PM ET | Thu 10 PM |
| Mon 2 Nov, 9 AM CT (after the change) | Mon 8 PM |
| Tue 3 Nov, 4 PM PT | Wed 5 AM |

> **[FACT] Why the date matters**
>
> Late U.S. afternoons are already **tomorrow** in Pakistan. When you write notes, use the U.S. date and time for loads (that’s what brokers and drivers use) and add PKT only for your own schedule.

> **[REAL-WORLD TIP] Set two clocks**
>
> Put U.S. Eastern and Central clocks on your phone and computer next to PKT. Most load boards and tracking apps can also show times in the facility’s zone.

pages.title: A desk that doesn’t fail
pages.markdown:
Lesson 11.1 · Setup

# A desk that doesn’t fail

![](/assets/diagrams/m11/setup.jpg)

### Start-of-shift checklist (10 minutes)

1. Power and backup internet working; headset tested.
2. Read the handover note; check every truck’s status.
3. EIA diesel (Mondays); any weather alerts on active lanes.
4. Load board, email, tracking and chat groups open.
5. Message the carrier: “Online and covering. Status: …”

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Use the carrier’s number, not your own**
>
> Brokers call back the numbers on the carrier’s FMCSA record and setup packet. Use the carrier’s U.S. business line (usually a softphone app); never give out a personal Pakistani number for business calls.

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] If your connection drops mid-call**
>
> Call back immediately from the backup: **“Sorry, I lost the line. This is Jawad from Blue Line again, about load PF-20931.”** Then tell the carrier if the outage continues.

pages.title: Getting paid and staying legal
pages.markdown:
Lesson 11.1 · Money

# Getting paid and staying legal

![](/assets/diagrams/m11/payflow.jpg)

### How carriers usually pay dispatchers

| Model | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| **Percentage** | A share of gross revenue (industry guides: often 5–10%; Module 7) |
| **Weekly flat fee** | Fixed amount per truck or per week |
| **Salary / hourly** | Employed or contracted by a dispatch company |

Whatever the model, it must be written in your dispatch agreement, and paid by the carrier only.

> **[CHECKLIST] Your weekly invoice to the carrier**
>
> Week dates · list of loads (load #, lane, gross) · fee calculation · total · payment details. Keep copies with the bank credit advice for tax filing.

> **[FACT] Keep your own records**
>
> Agreement, invoices, bank advices and tax filings, stored safely. They prove your income source if your bank or FBR asks.

pages.title: A night-shift routine you can keep
pages.markdown:
Lesson 11.1 · Health

# A night-shift routine you can keep

![](/assets/diagrams/m11/shift.jpg)

### Five habits of long-lasting night dispatchers

- Fixed sleep and wake times, seven days a week if possible.
- Light exercise and daylight before the shift.
- Water and real meals; limit caffeine in the last four hours of the shift.
- Short breaks every 90 minutes: stand, stretch, rest your eyes.
- A clear stop: handover note sent, laptop closed.

> **[KEY RULE] Coverage agreements**
>
> Agree in writing which hours you cover, who covers weekends and holidays, and how emergencies reach someone while you sleep.

> **[REAL-WORLD TIP] Pakistan realities**
>
> Plan around load-shedding schedules, Ramadan timings, and family events. Tell the carrier early about any day you can’t cover, just as you’d want to hear early about a late truck.

pages.title: From trainee to working dispatcher
pages.markdown:
Lesson 11.1 · Your first carrier

# From trainee to working dispatcher

![](/assets/diagrams/m11/first.jpg)

### What your dispatch agreement should cover (Module 1)

| Clause | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| **Services and hours** | What you do (search, book, track, paperwork) and when you are on duty |
| **Authority** | What you may book or sign without asking; the minimum rates |
| **Fee and payment** | Amount, schedule, method; paid only by the carrier |
| **No brokering** | You never assign loads to other carriers or collect freight payments |
| **Data and accounts** | The seat and accounts belong to the carrier; confidentiality; returning data if you part ways |
| **Ending the agreement** | Notice period; handover of open loads and documents |

> **[CHECKLIST] Your Tuesday checklist**
>
> Vet every new broker (Module 8) · check each rate con against your call (Module 9) · dispatch sheets with time zones · tracker updated · post any truck still empty.

> **[KEY RULE] Remember the limits**
>

pages.markdown:

# Days 3–5: execute, fix, close

| Day | Event | Your task · role-play |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Wed** | Carlos calls at 6:30 AM CT: 11 h of driving left, worried about parking near the Atlanta receiver | Role-play C (you’re Jawad, Claude is Carlos) |
| **Wed** | Truck 3 has waited 3 hours at a receiver on its Wednesday reload out of Charlotte; broker says “no detention on this one” | Role-play F · detention notice and invoice line |
| **Wed** | Maria sends the BOL: setpoint 36°F continuous, 20 pallets, seal 88412 | Check against the rate con; update broker |
| **Thu** | Truck 7 stuck behind an I-44 closure near Joplin, MO; delivery appointment at risk | Role-play E (drill 12) · problem log |
| **Thu** | A “broker” offers Truck 3 a Friday load at $3.40 a mile: new MC, gmail, “book in 5 minutes” | Role-play G · six-step response (Module 8) |
| **Thu** | Truck 12’s next rate con shows $1,950 instead of the $2,050 agreed, and no detention | Role-play D · correction email |
| **Fri** | PODs from all trucks; one lumper receipt ($185) from Truck 7 in Chicago | Invoices, folders, invoice tracker |
| **Fri** | Dwayne home by 6 PM ET; Truck 12 and 7 weekend plans | Weekend handover note |
| **Fri** | Weekly review call with Mike | Role-play H · weekly report (page 15) |

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Thursday is the real test**
>
> Three problems in one shift. Prioritize: **safety and hard deadlines first** (Truck 7’s appointment), then **fraud** (don’t let Truck 3 book a trap), then **money** (the rate con fix, before anyone signs).

> **[REAL-WORLD TIP] Write the handover**
>
> At the end of each simulated shift, write a handover note (Module 9 template). Claude can review it: paste it and ask, “What’s missing?”

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Useful follow-up prompts**
>

> **[FACT] Voice practice**
>
> If your Claude app supports voice, use it: speaking under time pressure is the skill brokers notice first. Otherwise type exactly what you would say.

> **[KEY RULE] Honest scoring helps you**
>

pages.title: The capstone: one message, every skill
pages.markdown:
Lesson 11.3 · Capstone

# The capstone: one message, every skill

WHATSAPP · MIKE (BLUE LINE) · MON 5:30 PM PKT (7:30 AM CT)

“Jawad, Truck 12 empties in **Memphis tomorrow 8 AM CT**. Carlos has **38 hours** left on his 70 and has to be **home in Joliet by Saturday night**. Find something paying toward Chicago. Also, **Harbor Point** wants our packet for a load next week, but I heard something about their bond. And diesel jumped to **$6.70** this week. Is our $2.70 minimum still OK? Let me know tonight.”

### Your tasks

1. **Numbers (Module 7):** recalculate Truck 12’s break-even and target at $6.70 diesel ($1,300 fixed, 2,500 mi/week, $0.86 other variable, 6.5 mpg, 9% fees).
2. **Search (Module 6):** write the search: origin, DH-O, destination, equipment, weight, date.
3. **Feasibility (Modules 3–4):** can Carlos deliver and still be home by Saturday within 38 hours?
4. **Choose (Modules 6–7):** compare the three loads below.
5. **Vetting (Module 8):** what do you do about Harbor Point?
6. **Communicate (all):** write your reply to Mike, and make the first call to the broker (drill 8).

| # | Lane | Loaded + DH | Details | Posted | Broker |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| L1 | Memphis, TN → Chicago, IL | 530 + 10 | Dry van · 42,000 lb · Tue 10 AM CT · deliver Wed 8 AM CT | $1,550 | CS 94 · DTP 30 · 9 yrs |
| L2 | Memphis, TN → Indianapolis, IN | 465 + 25 | Dry van · 40,000 lb · Tue 9 AM CT · deliver Wed 7 AM ET | $1,300 | CS 91 · DTP 34 |
| L3 | West Memphis, AR → Joliet, IL | 540 + 12 | Dry van · 44,000 lb · Tue 11 AM CT · deliver Wed 10 AM CT | $1,450 | CS 88 · DTP 38 |

Model answer on page 19. When you’re done, ask Claude: “Capstone review. Here is my answer: …” for a scored review.

### Capstone scoring (10 points)

| Part | Points | Full marks when… |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Numbers | 3 | Break-even and target correct to the cent, with working |
| Search + feasibility | 2 | Sensible search; hours and home time checked |
| Load choice | 2 | Rate per total mile for all three; clear decision and backup |
| Vetting | 1 | Checks L&I, holds the packet, uses the setup platform |
| Communication | 2 | Reply to Mike is short, numeric and ends with a question; drill 8 opening correct |

Lesson 11.3 · Review

# Your course, and your next 30 days

![](/assets/diagrams/m11/coursemap.jpg)

### A 30-day plan

| When | What |
| --- | --- |
| **Week 1** | Review Modules 0–5 with the course map; redo drills 1–7 aloud daily; run role-plays C and D. |
| **Week 2** | Review Modules 6–10; one full simulation day per evening; role-plays A, B, E, F, G at medium difficulty. |
| **Week 3** | Hard-difficulty role-plays; capstone; build your “proof pack”: two practice load folders, your best role-play transcripts, a sample weekly report. |
| **Week 4** | Set up your desk (power, internet, headset, security); approach carriers or dispatch companies; ask for a paid trial week. |

> **[SAY IT OUT LOUD] Your 20-second introduction to a carrier**
>
> **“I’m Jawad, a trained carrier-side dispatcher working from Pakistan. I cover your U.S. business day, book to your minimums, vet every broker, and send clean paperwork the same day. Can I show you a sample week?”**

> **[WARNING / CORRECTION] Stay on the right side**
>
> No paid “job guarantees”, no renting authority, no shared logins, no broker money in your account. Your reputation is your career.

pages.title: Capstone model answer
pages.markdown:
Answer key · Sources

# Capstone model answer

**1.**

Fuel $6.70 ÷ 6.5 = $1.03. Cost = 0.52 + 1.03 + 0.86 = $2.41. Break-even = 2.41 ÷ 0.91 = **$2.65**. Target = (2.41 + 0.10) ÷ 0.91 = **$2.76**. The $2.70 minimum is now only 5¢ above break-even.

**2.**

Origin Memphis, DH-O 50 · destination Chicago area or zone covering IL (Z6) · dry van, full, 53 ft · 44,500 lb · pickup Tue.

**3.**

L1: ~540 mi ≈ 11 h driving + loading/unloading ≈ 14 h on duty: fits 38 h, delivers Wed morning, then ~45 mi to Joliet. Home long before Saturday, with hours left for a short Thursday/Friday load.

**4.**

L1 $1,550 ÷ 540 = **$2.87** (above $2.76) → BOOK after checks. L2 $2.65 = break-even, and ends 180 mi from home → pass. L3 $2.63 below break-even, slower-paying broker, but ends at home → only if L1 is gone; counter to ≥ $1,525.

**5.**

Check L&I: if a BMC-84 cancellation is pending, ask Harbor Point whether a replacement bond is filed. Don’t send the packet until it is resolved; send it only through their setup platform.

**6.**

“Mike: at $6.70 diesel break-even is $2.65, so I suggest a $2.76 minimum. For Truck 12 I’m calling on Memphis→Chicago, $1,550 ($2.87), pickup Tue 10 AM CT, Carlos home Wed with hours to spare. Harbor Point shows a bond cancellation pending, so I’m holding the packet until they confirm a replacement. OK to book L1?”
